title: Lua
description: A complete, from-zero guide to the Lua programming language: installing Lua on Windows and Linux, syntax, tables, metatables, coroutines, the standard library, LuaRocks packages, embedding Lua in C, and building and shipping Lua programs.

Getting Started.What Is Lua:
Lua is a lightweight, fast, embeddable scripting language, created in Brazil in 1993. It's designed from the ground up to be simple, small, and easy to embed inside larger applications written in C or other languages — which is exactly how most people actually encounter Lua, even without realizing it. As of this guide, the current stable release is **Lua 5.5** (released December 2025), though — as [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) covers in detail — most real-world Lua deployment (games, Neovim, Redis, OpenResty) still runs on 5.1 through 5.4, so this guide teaches core Lua in a way that transfers directly across all of them, calling out 5.5-specific features explicitly wherever they appear.

## Why people choose Lua

- **Extremely small and fast.** The entire Lua interpreter compiles to a few hundred kilobytes and starts up almost instantly. Lua is consistently one of the fastest scripting languages in real-world benchmarks among interpreted languages, thanks to a carefully optimized register-based virtual machine — and Lua 5.5 pushes this further with more compact array storage and incremental garbage collection.
- **Designed to be embedded.** Unlike Python or Ruby, which are usually the "main" language of a project, Lua was built from day one to be dropped *into* a larger C/C++ application as a scripting layer — this is covered in depth in [Embedding and C Interop](/lua/why-embed-lua/).
- **One core data structure: the table.** Lua doesn't have separate array, dictionary, set, and object types — a single, flexible **table** type covers all of these roles. This is one of Lua's most distinctive design decisions and gets its own extensive section, [Tables](/lua/tables-as-arrays/).
- **Small, easy-to-learn syntax.** Lua's entire language reference fits comfortably in far fewer pages than most languages' — there's remarkably little to memorize before you're productive.

## What Lua is *not* particularly suited for

Lua doesn't ship with a large "batteries included" standard library the way Python does — no built-in HTTP client, no built-in JSON parsing, no built-in database drivers. This is a deliberate design choice: Lua expects the host application embedding it (or a package from LuaRocks, Lua's package manager, covered in [LuaRocks and Packages](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) to provide whatever additional functionality is needed. This makes Lua less immediately "batteries included" than some competitors, but keeps the core language small and predictable.

## Where you'll actually encounter Lua

- **Game development** — Lua is the scripting language behind World of Warcraft's UI addons, Roblox (a heavily modified variant called Luau), the Love2D game framework, Garry's Mod, and many other game engines that expose Lua as a way to script game logic without recompiling the engine itself.
- **Neovim configuration** — modern Neovim uses Lua as its primary configuration and plugin language (replacing Vimscript for most new plugin development).
- **Nginx / OpenResty** — Lua scripting is used to customize web server request handling at a very high performance level.
- **Redis** — Lua is built into Redis for writing atomic, server-side scripts.
- **Embedded/IoT devices** — Lua's tiny footprint makes it popular for scripting on resource-constrained hardware.

## What's new if you already know Lua 5.4

If you've used Lua before, [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) has a full practical summary of 5.5's changes — the headline items are explicit `global` variable declarations (which can make accidentally-created globals a compile error instead of a silent bug), read-only `for`-loop control variables, and named vararg tables. Nothing you already know about Lua 5.4 stopped working; 5.5 is an additive, compatible release at the level this guide teaches.

## How this guide is organized

This guide assumes **zero prior Lua knowledge**, but assumes you've programmed before in *some* language. It proceeds: installation → syntax and types → control flow and functions → tables (Lua's signature feature) → strings and pattern matching → metatables and object-oriented programming → modules → error handling → coroutines → I/O → the standard library → LuaRocks packages → embedding in C → tooling → a full worked project.

Next: [Installing Lua on Linux](/lua/installing-lua-on-linux/) or [Installing Lua on Windows](/lua/installing-lua-on-windows/).
Getting Started.Installing Lua on Linux:
## Arch Linux

Lua is available directly through `pacman`:

```bash
sudo pacman -S lua
```

This installs the latest Lua 5.x release available in Arch's repos. As of this guide, that's **Lua 5.5** (Arch tracks upstream closely, so you should get 5.5.x shortly after each release) — check with `lua -v` after installing. Arch also packages `luarocks` (Lua's package manager, covered in [Installing LuaRocks](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) separately:

```bash
sudo pacman -S luarocks
```

If your project or a host application you're targeting specifically needs Lua 5.4 rather than 5.5 (per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/), this is common for existing games and embedding hosts), the AUR carries version-pinned packages (e.g. `lua54`), or you can build 5.4 from source using the instructions below with the appropriate version number.

## Verifying the install

```bash
lua -v
# Lua 5.5.1  Copyright (C) 1994-2026 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
```

## Other Linux distributions

Most distributions package Lua similarly:

```bash
# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install lua5.4    # Debian/Ubuntu package names are typically still version-pinned;
                              # check `apt search lua5` for a 5.5 package once available in your release

# Fedora
sudo dnf install lua         # Fedora has tracked 5.5 since shortly after its release

# openSUSE
sudo zypper install lua5
```

Debian/Ubuntu in particular tend to install version-suffixed binaries (`lua5.4` rather than plain `lua`) since multiple Lua versions can coexist — see [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) for why this matters and how to handle it, and check your distribution's package repository directly for whichever specific version you need.

## Building from source (getting the latest version, or a specific one)

Package managers sometimes lag behind the latest upstream release, or you may specifically want an older version for compatibility with a particular project or game engine. Building from source is simple, since Lua has no external dependencies beyond a C compiler:

```bash
curl -R -O https://www.lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.1.tar.gz
tar zxf lua-5.5.1.tar.gz
cd lua-5.5.1
make linux test
sudo make install
```

`make linux` builds with the correct platform-specific flags (readline support for the interactive prompt, dynamic library flags, etc.); `make test` runs a quick sanity check; `sudo make install` installs to `/usr/local` by default. Substitute `5.4.9` (the final 5.4 release) in place of `5.5.1` in the URL above if you specifically need Lua 5.4.

## Checking which Lua you're actually running

If you have multiple Lua installations (e.g. a distro package and a from-source build), confirm which one is first on your `PATH`:

```bash
which lua
lua -v
```

Getting Started.Installing Lua on Windows:
Lua doesn't have as unified an "official installer" story on Windows as some languages, but there are several straightforward, reliable options.

## Option 1: winget (simplest, recommended)

```powershell
winget install DEVCOM.Lua
```

Or search for available Lua packages:

```powershell
winget search lua
```

Check the installed version afterward with `lua -v`; if you need to pin a specific version (5.5 vs an older 5.4, per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), the LuaBinaries option below gives more direct control.

## Option 2: Pre-built binaries from LuaBinaries

The Lua project's official binary distribution page (`luabinaries.sourceforge.net`) provides pre-compiled Windows executables. Download the appropriate `.zip` for your system (typically `lua-5.5.1_Win64_bin.zip`, or `lua-5.4.9_Win64_bin.zip` if you specifically need 5.4), extract it somewhere permanent like `C:\lua`, and add that folder to your `PATH`:

1. Search Windows for "Edit the system environment variables."
2. Click **Environment Variables**, select **Path** under System variables, click **Edit**, then **New**, and add `C:\lua`.
3. Open a **new** PowerShell/Command Prompt window and verify:

```powershell
lua -v
```

## Option 3: Chocolatey

If you use the Chocolatey package manager:

```powershell
choco install lua
```

## Option 4: WSL

Since Lua's Windows story is a bit less polished than its Linux story, many developers prefer running Lua inside **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)** and following the Linux install instructions exactly:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

Then inside the resulting Ubuntu shell, follow [Installing Lua on Linux](/lua/installing-lua-on-linux/). This guide's examples work identically either way — pick native Windows if you're specifically scripting a Windows application (like a game that expects a native Lua DLL) or WSL if you just want a smooth, Linux-like development experience.

## A note on LuaJIT as an alternative

Many Windows Lua users, especially in game development contexts, actually want **LuaJIT** (a fast, JIT-compiled alternative implementation, covered in [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) rather than the reference "PUC-Lua" implementation covered on this page. LuaJIT remains based on Lua 5.1 semantics and has not adopted 5.5's features (or 5.3/5.4's, in most cases) — if a specific game engine or framework's documentation mentions LuaJIT specifically, follow that framework's own bundled installation instructions rather than installing standalone Lua 5.5, since the versions and feature sets differ substantially.

## Verifying the install

```powershell
lua -v
```

Getting Started.Your Editor Setup:
## VS Code

Install the **Lua** extension by **sumneko** (also published as "Lua Language Server," now maintained under the `LuaLS` organization) — this is the de facto standard Lua tooling for VS Code, providing autocompletion, inline diagnostics, go-to-definition, and hover documentation.

1. Open the Extensions panel (`Ctrl+Shift+X`).
2. Search for "Lua" and install the one published by `sumneko`/`LuaLS`.
3. Open any `.lua` file — the language server activates automatically.

## Neovim

Since Neovim itself is configured in Lua, Lua tooling in Neovim tends to be particularly well polished. Using `nvim-lspconfig` with the `lua_ls` language server:

```lua
require('lspconfig').lua_ls.setup({})
```

On Arch Linux, `lua-language-server` is available directly via pacman:

```bash
sudo pacman -S lua-language-server
```

## Other editors

- **Sublime Text** — the "Lua" package (via Package Control) provides syntax highlighting; combine with a LSP client package for full language server features.
- **IntelliJ / JetBrains IDEs** — the "Lua" plugin (search the JetBrains Marketplace) adds full Lua support.
- **ZeroBrane Studio** — a dedicated, lightweight Lua IDE, purpose-built for Lua (and popular in game development circles for its built-in debugger support with several game engines).

## Installing the language server standalone

If your editor needs the language server binary directly, the `lua-language-server` project provides prebuilt binaries on its GitHub releases page for Linux, Windows, and macOS — extract it and point your editor's LSP client configuration at the extracted binary.

## Formatting: StyLua

Lua doesn't have an official formatter bundled with the language itself (unlike Rust's `rustfmt`), but **StyLua** has become the de facto community standard:

```bash
cargo install stylua   # if you have a Rust toolchain (see the Rust guide!)
# or download a prebuilt binary from StyLua's GitHub releases
```

```bash
stylua my_script.lua        # format a file in place
stylua --check my_script.lua  # check without modifying, useful for CI
```

Most editor Lua extensions can be configured to run StyLua automatically on save, similar to how `rustfmt` works for Rust.

Getting Started.Hello World:
## Your first script

Create a file called `hello.lua`:

```lua
print("Hello, world!")
```

Run it:

```bash
lua hello.lua
```

That's genuinely the entire program — no `main` function required, no imports needed for basic output. Lua scripts execute top-to-bottom as a sequence of statements, starting immediately at the top of the file.

## The interactive prompt (REPL)

Lua ships with an interactive interpreter, useful for quick experiments:

```bash
lua
```

```
Lua 5.5.1  Copyright (C) 1994-2026 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
> print("Hello, world!")
Hello, world!
> 2 + 2
4
> local x = 10
> print(x * 2)
20
> os.exit()
```

Typing an expression alone (like `2 + 2`) at the REPL prints its value automatically — useful for quickly checking how something behaves without writing a full script.

## A slightly larger first example

```lua
-- a simple greeting script
local function greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end

print(greet("Lua"))

for i = 1, 3 do
    print("Count: " .. i)
end
```

```bash
lua hello.lua
```

```
Hello, Lua!
Count: 1
Count: 2
Count: 3
```

A few things to notice right away, each covered fully in upcoming pages: `--` starts a comment ([Comments and Formatting](/lua/comments-and-formatting/)), `..` concatenates strings ([Operators](/lua/operators/)), `local` declares a variable scoped to the current block ([Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/)), and `for i = 1, 3 do ... end` is Lua's numeric for-loop syntax ([Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/)).

Next: [The lua and luac Commands](/lua/the-lua-and-luac-commands/).
Getting Started.The lua and luac Commands:
## lua: running scripts

```bash
lua script.lua              # run a script
lua                           # start the interactive REPL
lua -e "print(2 + 2)"          # run a one-line snippet directly from the command line
lua -i script.lua                # run a script, THEN drop into an interactive prompt
                                    # (useful for inspecting state after the script runs)
```

## Passing arguments to a script

```bash
lua script.lua arg1 arg2 arg3
```

Inside `script.lua`, these are available via the global `arg` table:

```lua
print(arg[1]) -- "arg1"
print(arg[2]) -- "arg2"
print(#arg)   -- 3 (the number of arguments)
```

This is covered fully in [Command Line Arguments](/lua/command-line-arguments/).

## luac: compiling to bytecode

`luac` compiles Lua source into precompiled bytecode — this doesn't make Lua "compiled" in the sense of producing a standalone native executable (it still requires a Lua interpreter to run the bytecode), but it can speed up startup for large scripts by skipping the parsing step, and is sometimes used to obscure source code (though bytecode is still fairly easy to decompile, so don't rely on it for genuine security).

```bash
luac -o script.luac script.lua   # compile to bytecode
lua script.luac                    # run the compiled bytecode directly — the lua
                                      # interpreter accepts both source and bytecode
```

```bash
luac -p script.lua   # parse-only, check for syntax errors without producing output —
                        # useful as a quick "does this even parse" check, similar in
                        # spirit to Rust's `cargo check`
```

## A note on the standalone interpreter's name

Depending on how Lua was packaged for your system, the executable might be named `lua`, `lua5.4`, `lua5.1`, etc. (Debian/Ubuntu in particular tend to version-suffix it, since multiple Lua versions can be installed side by side). If a plain `lua` command isn't found, try `lua5.4`, or check what got installed with `ls /usr/bin/lua*` on Linux.

Next: [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/).
Getting Started.Lua Versions Explained:
Understanding Lua's version landscape early will save you real confusion later, since — unlike many languages — several genuinely different Lua versions and implementations remain in active, simultaneous use across different ecosystems.

## The official versions: 5.1 through 5.5

Lua has no "Lua 2" or radically different major version the way Python 2→3 was — instead, it's had a steady sequence of 5.x releases, each introducing some new features and occasionally small breaking changes:

- **Lua 5.1** (2006) — still widely used because it's the version **LuaJIT** (covered below) is based on, and many game engines and embedded systems standardized on it years ago and never moved.
- **Lua 5.2** (2011) — introduced `goto`, removed some deprecated 5.1 features.
- **Lua 5.3** (2015) — added a genuine integer subtype (previously all numbers were floats) and built-in bitwise operators.
- **Lua 5.4** (2020) — adding the integer-division operator `//`, to-be-closed variables, and generational garbage collection. Still extremely widely deployed — most current game engines, Neovim, Redis, and OpenResty target 5.1-5.4, so this remains genuinely essential knowledge even though it's no longer the newest release.
- **Lua 5.5** (December 2025) — the current stable version as of this guide, adding explicit `global` variable declarations, read-only numeric/generic `for`-loop control variables, named vararg tables, more compact array storage (up to 60% less memory for large arrays), and incremental major garbage collection. **This guide's primary examples target Lua 5.5**, with the differences from 5.4 called out explicitly wherever they matter — almost everything shown works unchanged on 5.1-5.4 too, since 5.5 is a compatible, additive release at the level this guide teaches.

## What's actually new in Lua 5.5 — a practical summary

The full details are covered in context throughout the guide (particularly [Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/) for `global` declarations, [Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/) for read-only loop variables, and [Variadic Functions](/lua/variadic-functions/) for named vararg tables), but as a quick orientation:

- **`global` declarations** — Lua now lets you explicitly declare `global x` (optionally `global<const> x` for a read-only global), and `global<const> *` at the top of a chunk locks down *all* undeclared assignments as errors. This directly formalizes the "always use `local`, watch out for accidental globals" discipline this guide has emphasized throughout — in 5.5, that discipline can be enforced by the language itself rather than relying purely on habit or a linter like `luacheck`.
- **Read-only loop control variables** — in both the numeric `for` and generic `for` loops, the control variable is now a `const` local, so accidentally reassigning it inside the loop body is a compile error rather than a silent bug.
- **Named vararg tables** — `function f(...args)` (a name after the dots) binds `args` directly as a table-like view of the extra arguments, with `args.n` giving the count — reducing the need for the `{...}`/`select("#", ...)` dance from [Variadic Functions](/lua/variadic-functions/) in common cases.
- **Floats print more precisely** — the default string conversion for floats now prints enough digits to read the exact value back correctly, avoiding silent precision loss when a float is converted to a string and back.
- **Large arrays use far less memory** — an internal storage optimization, transparent to your code, but worth knowing about if you're working with large array-like tables and memory footprint matters.
- **Nothing from 5.4 was removed at the level this guide teaches.** 5.5 is compatible with idiomatic 5.4 code; the reference manual's formal incompatibilities list is narrow and mostly affects edge cases (numeral parsing corner cases, some C API details) rather than everyday scripting.

## LuaJIT: a separate, extremely popular implementation

**LuaJIT** is not "a newer Lua" — it's a completely separate implementation (by Mike Pall) of the **Lua 5.1** language, with a highly optimized Just-In-Time compiler that makes it, in many benchmarks, one of the fastest dynamic language implementations that exists. LuaJIT is extremely widely used specifically *because* of its speed — it powers Neovim's Lua runtime, many game engines, and OpenResty/Nginx's Lua scripting.

The practical implication: if you're scripting for a specific engine or tool (Neovim, a game engine, OpenResty), **check which Lua/LuaJIT version it actually uses** before assuming every feature from this guide's examples is available — LuaJIT is based on 5.1 syntax/semantics, with some 5.2 features backported, and does not have Lua 5.3/5.4/5.5-only features (the native integer type, the `//` operator, `global` declarations, named vararg tables) without special handling.

## Why this fragmentation happens, and how to navigate it

Because Lua is designed to be embedded, the application embedding it "owns" the decision of which Lua version to ship — a game released in 2012 might have permanently locked in Lua 5.1 (or LuaJIT) for its entire lifetime, regardless of what's currently "latest" upstream. This is completely normal in the Lua ecosystem, unlike languages where a single, centrally-controlled runtime version is expected. As of this guide, Lua 5.5 is genuinely new — most existing host applications you'll encounter still target 5.1 through 5.4, so treat 5.5-specific features (`global` declarations, named vararg tables) as things to use freely in your own standalone 5.5 scripts, but not to assume are available when writing for someone else's embedding host until you've confirmed its version.

**Practical rule of thumb**: when writing a script for a specific host application (a game, Neovim, Redis), check that application's own documentation for which Lua version it targets, and write compatible code for that version specifically — don't assume "latest Lua" features are available. When writing standalone scripts/tools with the `lua` command on your own machine, you control the version and can freely use whatever your installed `lua -v` reports.

Syntax Basics.Comments and Formatting:
## Comments

```lua
-- a single-line comment

--[[
   a multi-line block comment
   spanning several lines
--]]

--[==[
   a block comment that itself contains ]] safely,
   using extra = signs to avoid ambiguity
]==]
```

Single-line comments start with `--` and run to the end of the line. Block comments use `--[[ ... ]]`. The `--[==[ ... ]==]` variant (matching numbers of `=` signs between the brackets) exists specifically so a block comment can safely contain a literal `]]` inside it without prematurely closing.

## No enforced formatting standard, but strong conventions

Unlike Rust (which has one dominant official formatter), Lua has no built-in formatter and a looser community convention overall — but the following are close to universal:

- **Indentation**: either 2 or 4 spaces, fairly evenly split by community preference; pick one and be consistent within a project. (**StyLua**, from [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/), defaults to 4 spaces if you want an automated formatter to just decide for you.)
- **snake_case** for variables and functions: `local user_name`, `function calculate_total()`.
- **PascalCase** is commonly used for "class"-like tables (covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)): `local Animal = {}`.
- **SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE** for genuine constants, though Lua has no built-in `const` keyword (covered next page) — this is purely a naming convention signaling intent.

```lua
local MAX_RETRIES = 5
local user_name = "ferris"

local function calculate_total(items)
    -- ...
end
```

## `end` closes blocks — no braces

Unlike C-family languages, Lua doesn't use `{ }` to delimit blocks — every block-opening keyword (`function`, `if`, `for`, `while`, `do`) is closed with a matching `end`:

```lua
if x > 0 then
    print("positive")
end

function greet()
    print("hello")
end
```

This is one of the first visual differences newcomers notice, and it's consistent throughout the entire language — every block construct covered in upcoming pages follows this same `keyword ... end` pattern.

Syntax Basics.Variables and Scope:
## Global by default — a crucial early distinction

This is one of the most important things to learn early, and it's the **opposite** default from most modern languages: a variable assignment in Lua is **global** unless you explicitly declare it `local`.

```lua
x = 10        -- GLOBAL, visible everywhere, including other files/chunks
local y = 20   -- LOCAL, scoped to the current block only

print(x, y)   -- 10   20
```

## Why you should almost always use local

Global variables in Lua are stored in a shared global table (accessible as `_G`), meaning every global you create is visible from literally anywhere in your program, including other files, other libraries, and code you didn't write — a recipe for accidental name collisions and hard-to-track bugs in any program beyond a trivial script.

```lua
-- BAD habit, avoid this:
count = 0
function increment()
    count = count + 1  -- modifies the GLOBAL count — any other code using "count" breaks
end

-- GOOD habit:
local count = 0
local function increment()
    count = count + 1  -- modifies the local count, safely scoped
end
```

**Practical rule: always write `local` in front of every variable declaration unless you have a specific, deliberate reason to create a global.** This single habit prevents the large majority of scoping bugs beginners hit in Lua.

## New in Lua 5.5: explicit global declarations

Lua 5.5 adds a `global` statement that lets you declare a global variable explicitly, and — more importantly — lets you lock down *accidental* global creation as a compile-time error, turning the discipline above from a habit into something the language itself can enforce:

```lua
global counter -- explicitly declares "counter" as a global, ahead of using it
counter = 0

global<const> MAX_PLAYERS = 4 -- a read-only global — reassigning it later is an error
```

The genuinely powerful part is declaring this at the top of a chunk (a file, per [Chunks and Blocks](/lua/chunks-and-blocks/)):

```lua
global<const> * -- from this point in the chunk, EVERY global must be explicitly declared;
                  -- any undeclared assignment (a typo, or a forgotten `local`) is now a
                  -- compile-time error instead of a silent, hard-to-find bug

local count = 0 -- fine, this is local
countt = 1        -- ERROR: countt was never declared as a global — this likely catches
                    -- a typo that, in 5.4 and earlier, would have silently created a
                    -- stray global and compiled without complaint
```

If you're writing new Lua 5.5 code, `global<const> *` at the top of your entry-point script (or every module file) is a genuinely good habit — it gives you, for free, exactly the protection that linters like `luacheck` (covered later in [Style Guide and Linting](/lua/style-guide-and-linting/)) previously had to catch after the fact. If you're targeting Lua 5.1-5.4 (still the majority of real-world hosts, per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), this feature isn't available, and the discipline of "always write `local`" plus a linter remains your best defense.

## Block scoping

`local` variables are scoped to the innermost enclosing block (`do...end`, a function body, a loop body, an `if` body):

```lua
local x = 10

do
    local x = 20 -- a NEW local variable, shadows the outer x within this block
    print(x)      -- 20
end

print(x) -- 10, unaffected — the outer x was never touched
```

```lua
if true then
    local message = "inside the if"
    print(message)
end

-- print(message) -- ERROR: message doesn't exist here, it went out of scope
```

## Declaring multiple variables at once

```lua
local a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
print(a, b, c) -- 1  2  3

local x, y = 10          -- y is nil — fewer values than variables is fine
print(x, y)              -- 10  nil

local p, q = 1, 2, 3     -- extra value (3) is simply discarded
print(p, q)              -- 1  2
```

Lua handles mismatched counts gracefully in both directions: missing values become `nil` (covered next page), and extra values are silently dropped. This behavior — used deliberately and constantly throughout idiomatic Lua — is explored further in [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/).

## Checking if a global exists (a common defensive pattern)

```lua
if type(some_global) == "nil" then
    print("not defined")
end

-- or, more idiomatically:
if some_global == nil then
    print("not defined")
end
```

Next: [Chunks and Blocks](/lua/chunks-and-blocks/).
Syntax Basics.Chunks and Blocks:
## What a "chunk" is

In Lua terminology, a **chunk** is simply a piece of Lua code — typically, an entire file, but also a string passed to `load()`, or code typed at the REPL. Every chunk is, internally, treated as the body of an anonymous function — this is why you'll sometimes see Lua's own error messages or documentation refer to "the main chunk" as if it were a function; it effectively is one.

```lua
-- this whole file is "a chunk" — implicitly wrapped as a function body
local x = 10
print(x)
```

This matters practically in one specific way: a chunk can `return` a value, just like a function, and this is exactly the mechanism [modules](/lua/writing-a-module/) use — a module file is a chunk that returns a table of functions.

```lua
-- greet.lua — this chunk returns a value
return function(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end
```

## Blocks

A **block** is a sequence of statements, optionally ending in a `return` or `break` — you've already seen several kinds: the body of a `function`, the body of an `if`, the body of a loop, or an explicit `do...end`.

```lua
do
    -- this is a block, with its own local scope — a standalone
    -- grouping construct with no loop or condition attached
    local temp = compute_something()
    print(temp)
end
-- temp is gone here — it only existed within the do...end block
```

A bare `do...end` block, with no attached `if`/`for`/`while`, is a genuinely useful tool purely for scoping — it lets you introduce `local` variables that are guaranteed to disappear afterward, keeping your broader scope clean of temporary helper variables.

## Statement separators

Semicolons are **entirely optional** in Lua, and rarely used in practice (unlike JavaScript or C, where they're either required or near-universal by convention):

```lua
local x = 1
local y = 2
print(x + y)

-- also completely valid, though unusual style:
local x = 1; local y = 2; print(x + y)
```

The only time a semicolon is genuinely useful is disambiguating certain edge cases involving function calls that start with `(`, where Lua's parser might otherwise interpret two consecutive lines as one expression — this is a rare enough edge case that most Lua style guides simply recommend never using semicolons at all, for consistency.

Next: [Operators](/lua/operators/).
Syntax Basics.Operators:
## Arithmetic

```lua
print(5 + 3)   -- 8
print(5 - 3)   -- 2
print(5 * 3)   -- 15
print(5 / 3)   -- 1.6666666666667 — ALWAYS produces a float, even for integer operands!
print(5 // 3)  -- 1 — floor (integer) division, Lua 5.3+
print(5 % 3)   -- 2 — modulo
print(5 ^ 2)   -- 25.0 — exponentiation, always produces a float
print(-5)      -- unary negation
```

**Important**: `/` always produces a float result in Lua, even when both operands are integers (`5 / 3` is `1.6666...`, not `1`) — this is different from many languages where integer division truncates by default. Use `//` (floor division, Lua 5.3+) when you specifically want integer-style division.

## Comparison

```lua
print(5 == 3)   -- false
print(5 ~= 3)   -- true  -- NOTE: Lua uses ~= for "not equal", not != or <>
print(5 > 3)    -- true
print(5 < 3)    -- false
print(5 >= 5)   -- true
print(5 <= 4)   -- false
```

`~=` for "not equal" is one of Lua's more distinctive syntax choices — easy to forget if you're coming from a C-family language expecting `!=`.

## Logical operators: and, or, not

Lua spells out its logical operators as words, not symbols:

```lua
print(true and false)  -- false
print(true or false)   -- true
print(not true)         -- false
```

`and`/`or` in Lua don't just return `true`/`false` — they return one of their **actual operands**, evaluated with short-circuiting, which makes them useful for more than plain boolean logic (this is covered thoroughly in the section on `nil`/booleans, since it relies on understanding truthiness first — see [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/)).

```lua
local x = nil
local y = x or "default"  -- "default", since x is falsy
print(y)

local a = 5
local b = a and "positive" -- "positive", since a is truthy — the RESULT of `and`
                              -- is the second operand when the first is truthy
print(b)
```

## String concatenation: ..

```lua
local greeting = "Hello, " .. "World!"
print(greeting) -- "Hello, World!"

local name = "Lua"
local version = 5.4
print("Using " .. name .. " " .. version) -- numbers are auto-converted to strings
```

`..` is Lua's dedicated string concatenation operator — `+` is reserved purely for arithmetic and will error (or attempt numeric coercion and fail) if used on non-numeric strings.

## The length operator: #

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(#s) -- 5, the string's byte length

local t = {10, 20, 30}
print(#t) -- 3, the table's "array part" length — covered in Tables
```

## Operator precedence, briefly

Lua follows fairly standard precedence (`not`/unary minus highest, then `^`, then `*`/`/`/`//`/`%`, then `+`/`-`, then `..`, then comparisons, then `and`, then `or` lowest) — when in doubt, use parentheses for clarity; there's no penalty for being explicit.

Next: [Expressions and Statements](/lua/expressions-and-statements/).
Syntax Basics.Expressions and Statements:
Like most languages, Lua distinguishes between **expressions** (things that produce a value) and **statements** (things that perform an action). This distinction is more relaxed in Lua than in Rust, but still worth understanding clearly.

## Statements

```lua
local x = 5          -- an assignment statement
if x > 0 then         -- an if statement
    print("positive")
end
for i = 1, 3 do        -- a for statement
    print(i)
end
```

Statements don't produce a usable value — you can't do `local y = (if x > 0 then ... end)` the way you might in some functional languages; `if` in Lua is purely a control-flow statement, not an expression (unlike Rust, where `if` *does* produce a value — this is a genuine difference between the two languages worth remembering if you're learning both).

## Expressions

```lua
5 + 3              -- an arithmetic expression
"hello" .. "world" -- a concatenation expression
x > 0               -- a comparison expression, evaluates to true/false
some_function()      -- a function call expression, evaluates to its return value(s)
```

## Simulating "if as an expression" with and/or

Because Lua's `if` is a statement, not an expression, a common idiom for a quick conditional value uses `and`/`or`'s short-circuiting behavior instead (leaning on the truthiness rules from [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/)):

```lua
local age = 15
local category = (age >= 18) and "adult" or "minor"
print(category) -- "minor"
```

This reads as: *"if `age >= 18` is truthy, evaluate to `"adult"`; otherwise, evaluate to `"minor"`."* It works because of how `and`/`or` short-circuit and return actual operand values, not just booleans. **Caveat**: this idiom breaks if the "true" branch's value could itself be `false` or `nil` — `condition and false or "other"` always evaluates to `"other"`, regardless of `condition`, because `condition and false` itself is falsy, so Lua falls through to the `or` branch regardless. For anything beyond simple, always-truthy values in both branches, prefer a plain `if`/`else` assigning to a `local` declared beforehand:

```lua
local category
if age >= 18 then
    category = "adult"
else
    category = "minor"
end
```

## Function calls as statements vs expressions

A function call can be used as a standalone statement (when you only care about its side effects) or as part of a larger expression (when you care about its return value):

```lua
print("hello")              -- statement: called purely for its side effect

local result = math.max(3, 7) -- expression: the return value is used
print(math.max(3, 7) + 1)      -- expression, nested inside another expression
```

This wraps up syntax basics. Next: [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/).

Types and Values.Nil and Booleans:
## nil: Lua's "nothing" value

```lua
local x
print(x) -- nil — an uninitialized local is nil by default

local y = nil
print(y == nil) -- true
```

`nil` represents the absence of a useful value — similar in spirit to Python's `None`, JavaScript's `null`/`undefined`, or (conceptually, though implemented very differently) Rust's `Option::None`. Any variable that hasn't been assigned a value is `nil`. Assigning `nil` to a table field effectively **deletes** that key entirely (covered fully in [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/)).

## Booleans: true and false

```lua
local is_active = true
local is_done = false

print(type(is_active)) -- "boolean"
```

## Truthiness: the rule that trips up every newcomer

This is one of the most important rules in the entire language, and it differs from almost every other language you might already know: **in Lua, everything is truthy except `false` and `nil`.**

```lua
if 0 then print("0 is truthy!") end          -- prints! 0 is NOT falsy in Lua
if "" then print("empty string is truthy!") end -- prints! "" is NOT falsy in Lua
if {} then print("empty table is truthy!") end   -- prints! {} is NOT falsy in Lua

if false then print("won't print") end
if nil then print("won't print") end
```

If you're coming from Python, JavaScript, C, or most other languages, this will trip you up at least once — `0` and `""` are falsy in many of those languages, but **not** in Lua. Only the literal values `false` and `nil` are falsy; everything else, including `0`, empty strings, and empty tables, counts as true in a boolean context.

## How this affects and/or idioms

This rule is exactly why the `x or default` idiom from the previous page works cleanly for `nil` checks but can misfire if `0` or `""` are meant to be valid, intentional values:

```lua
local count = 0
local display_count = count or 10  -- display_count is 0, NOT 10 — 0 is truthy!
print(display_count) -- 0
```

If you specifically need to distinguish "no value was given" (`nil`) from "a falsy-looking but legitimate value was given" (`0`, `false`), compare against `nil` explicitly rather than relying on `or`:

```lua
local function get_count(count)
    if count == nil then
        count = 10 -- only fall back to a default if genuinely not provided
    end
    return count
end

print(get_count(0))  -- 0, correctly preserved
print(get_count())    -- 10, the default
```

Next: [Numbers](/lua/numbers/).
Types and Values.Numbers:
## One number type, with two subtypes

Since Lua 5.3, the `number` type has two internal subtypes: **integer** and **float**. Before 5.3, Lua had only floats internally. This page covers 5.3+ behavior, which is what you'll encounter on any modern Lua install (including LuaJIT-based Lua 5.1 environments, integers are always represented as floats — see [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) if you need to work with an older target).

```lua
print(type(10))     -- "number" — both integers and floats report the SAME type() result
print(math.type(10))   -- "integer" — math.type() distinguishes the subtype
print(math.type(10.0)) -- "float"
print(math.type(10/2)) -- "float" — / ALWAYS produces a float, as covered in Operators
```

`type()` treats integers and floats as one unified `"number"` type — you only need `math.type()` if you specifically need to distinguish the internal representation, which is relatively rare in everyday scripting.

## Integer vs float literals

```lua
local a = 10      -- integer literal
local b = 10.0    -- float literal (the .0 makes it a float)
local c = 1e3      -- float literal, scientific notation: 1000.0
local d = 0x1F       -- integer literal, hexadecimal: 31
```

## Arithmetic and automatic promotion

```lua
print(5 + 3)     -- 8 (integer + integer = integer)
print(5 + 3.0)   -- 8.0 (integer + float = float — "promoted")
print(5 / 2)     -- 2.5 (/ ALWAYS produces a float)
print(5 // 2)    -- 2 (// floor division stays integer if both operands are integers)
print(5.0 // 2)   -- 2.0 (// on a float operand produces a float)
```

## Common math functions

```lua
print(math.floor(3.7))   -- 3
print(math.ceil(3.2))     -- 4
print(math.abs(-5))        -- 5
print(math.max(3, 7, 2))    -- 7
print(math.min(3, 7, 2))     -- 2
print(math.sqrt(16))          -- 4.0
print(math.pi)                  -- 3.1415926535898
print(math.huge)                  -- inf, positive infinity
```

A full reference of `math` library functions is in [math Library](/lua/math-library/).

## Converting between strings and numbers

```lua
print(tonumber("42"))     -- 42
print(tonumber("3.14"))    -- 3.14
print(tonumber("abc"))      -- nil — not a valid number, returns nil rather than erroring
print(tonumber("10", 2))     -- 2 — parse "10" as base-2 (binary): 10 binary = 2 decimal

print(tostring(42))    -- "42"
print(tostring(3.14))   -- "3.14"
```

`tonumber` returning `nil` (rather than throwing an error) on invalid input is a common and useful pattern for validating user input — check for `nil` before using the result:

```lua
local input = "not a number"
local n = tonumber(input)
if n == nil then
    print("Invalid number: " .. input)
else
    print("Got: " .. n)
end
```

## Integer overflow behavior

Lua integers wrap around silently on overflow (similar to Rust's release-mode behavior, but always, not just in an "optimized" build) — there's no panic or error:

```lua
print(math.maxinteger)          -- 9223372036854775807 (on a typical 64-bit build)
print(math.maxinteger + 1)        -- -9223372036854775808 — wraps around silently
```

Next: [Strings](/lua/strings/).
Types and Values.Strings:
## String literals

```lua
local s1 = "double quotes"
local s2 = 'single quotes' -- functionally identical to double quotes in Lua
local s3 = [[
a long string literal,
spanning multiple lines,
with no escape processing at all
]]
```

Unlike some languages, Lua treats `'single'` and `"double"` quoted strings as **completely equivalent** — pick whichever you prefer, though most style guides lean toward double quotes for consistency. The `[[...]]` "long string" syntax is useful for multi-line text (like embedded SQL, help text, or templates) and — notably — does **not** process escape sequences like `\n` inside it; it's taken completely literally, including actual line breaks.

## Escape sequences (in quoted strings, not long strings)

```lua
print("Line 1\nLine 2")    -- newline
print("Tab:\there")          -- tab
print("Quote: \"quoted\"")    -- escaped double quote
print('It\'s here')             -- escaped single quote
print("Backslash: \\")           -- literal backslash
print("Unicode: \u{1F600}")        -- unicode escape (Lua 5.3+)
```

## Strings are immutable

Just like in Rust, Python, and most other languages, Lua strings are **immutable** — every "modification" (concatenation, uppercasing, replacing) actually produces a brand new string, leaving the original unchanged:

```lua
local s = "hello"
local upper = s:upper() -- creates a NEW string
print(s)      -- "hello" — unchanged
print(upper)  -- "HELLO"
```

## String indexing and length

Unlike Rust (which deliberately disallows byte-indexing a `String` for UTF-8 safety reasons, as covered in the Rust guide's [Working With Text](/rust/working-with-text/)), Lua strings are simpler: they're just raw byte sequences, with no built-in Unicode awareness at the language level.

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(#s)         -- 5, the byte length
print(s:sub(1,1))  -- "h" — Lua string indices are 1-BASED, not 0-based!
print(s:sub(-1))    -- "o" — negative indices count from the end
print(s:sub(2,4))    -- "ell"
```

**Lua strings (and, as you'll see in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/), Lua's array-like tables) are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed.** This is a fundamental, pervasive difference from almost every C-family language, Python, JavaScript, and Rust — the very first element is index `1`, not `0`. This trips up virtually every newcomer to Lua at least once; it's worth deliberately internalizing early.

## Method-call syntax on strings

You may have noticed `s:upper()` and `s:sub(1,1)` above using a colon `:` rather than a dot `.`. This is Lua's **method call syntax**, equivalent to calling `string.upper(s)` but more convenient — this shorthand is covered in full in [Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/) once you understand how functions and tables interact, and used extensively once we reach [Tables](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) and object-oriented patterns.

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(s:upper())        -- "HELLO", shorthand for:
print(string.upper(s))  -- "HELLO", the equivalent explicit form
```

The full string library is covered in depth starting with [String Library Basics](/lua/string-library-basics/).

Next: [The type Function and Type Coercion](/lua/the-type-function-and-type-coercion/).
Types and Values.The type Function and Type Coercion:
## The type() function

Lua has exactly **eight** basic types, and `type()` tells you which one any value is:

```lua
print(type(nil))          -- "nil"
print(type(true))          -- "boolean"
print(type(42))             -- "number"
print(type("hello"))         -- "string"
print(type({}))               -- "table"
print(type(print))             -- "function"
print(type(coroutine.create(function() end))) -- "thread"
-- the 8th type, "userdata", represents opaque data from host C code —
-- you won't create these directly in pure Lua scripts, but you'll encounter
-- them when embedding Lua in C (see Embedding and C Interop) or using libraries
-- that wrap C objects (like file handles)
```

That's the entire type system — dramatically smaller than most languages. There's no separate integer/float *type* at the `type()` level (both report `"number"`, as covered in [Numbers](/lua/numbers/)), no separate array/dictionary/object types (all are `"table"`), and no class type (classes are a pattern built on tables, covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)).

## Automatic coercion: string ↔ number

Lua automatically converts between strings and numbers in certain contexts — this is convenient but can also be a source of subtle bugs if you're not aware of it:

```lua
print("10" + 5)      -- 15 — the string "10" is coerced to a number
print("10" .. 5)       -- "105" — the number 5 is coerced to a string, then concatenated
print("3.14" * 2)       -- 6.28

print("abc" + 1)        -- ERROR: attempt to perform arithmetic on a string value
                           -- (coercion only works if the string actually looks like a number)
```

Arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, etc.) automatically try to coerce string operands to numbers. Concatenation (`..`) automatically coerces number operands to strings. This is genuinely convenient for quick scripts, but relying on it heavily in larger programs can make bugs harder to spot — being explicit with `tonumber()`/`tostring()` (from the previous page) is generally considered better practice once code grows beyond a quick script.

## No coercion for comparisons

Unlike arithmetic and concatenation, **comparison operators do not coerce types**:

```lua
print(10 == "10")  -- false! different types are NEVER equal, no coercion happens here
print(10 == 10)     -- true
```

This is a deliberate and important exception — `==` in Lua always returns `false` when comparing values of different types, with zero exceptions, unlike JavaScript's infamous `==` coercion rules. If you want to compare a string and a number for equality, convert one explicitly first:

```lua
local input = "10"
if tonumber(input) == 10 then
    print("matches!")
end
```

## Checking multiple types safely

```lua
local function describe(value)
    local t = type(value)
    if t == "number" then
        return "a number: " .. value
    elseif t == "string" then
        return "a string: " .. value
    elseif t == "nil" then
        return "nothing"
    else
        return "something else: a " .. t
    end
end

print(describe(42))       -- "a number: 42"
print(describe("hi"))       -- "a string: hi"
print(describe(nil))          -- "nothing"
print(describe({}))             -- "something else: a table"
```

This wraps up types and values. Next: [If, Then, Else](/lua/if-then-else/).

Control Flow.If, Then, Else:
```lua
local number = 7

if number < 5 then
    print("less than five")
elseif number == 5 then
    print("exactly five")
else
    print("greater than five")
end
```

Every branch keyword — `if`, `elseif`, `else` — and the whole construct is closed with one final `end`. Note `elseif` is a single word (not `else if`), and there's no limit to how many `elseif` branches you can chain.

## The condition can be any value — remember truthiness

Unlike Rust (which requires a literal `bool`), Lua's `if` condition accepts **any** value, evaluated according to the truthiness rule from [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/) — only `false` and `nil` are falsy:

```lua
local name = "Ferris"

if name then
    print("name is set: " .. name) -- this runs — any non-nil, non-false value is truthy
end

local count = 0
if count then
    print("this runs too — remember, 0 is truthy in Lua!")
end
```

## No switch/case statement

Lua doesn't have a built-in `switch`/`case` construct (unlike many C-family languages). The idiomatic replacements are a chain of `if`/`elseif`, or — for matching against a fixed, known set of values — a **table used as a lookup**, which is often cleaner:

```lua
local function describe_day(day)
    local descriptions = {
        Monday = "start of the week",
        Friday = "almost the weekend",
        Saturday = "weekend!",
        Sunday = "weekend!",
    }
    return descriptions[day] or "a regular day"
end

print(describe_day("Friday"))    -- "almost the weekend"
print(describe_day("Tuesday"))     -- "a regular day"
```

This table-lookup pattern (covered fully once we reach [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/)) is a genuinely idiomatic and common Lua alternative to a switch statement, especially when each "case" maps directly to a value rather than needing complex logic.

## Nested if statements

```lua
local age = 25
local has_license = true

if age >= 18 then
    if has_license then
        print("can drive")
    else
        print("too young to drive, or no license")
    end
else
    print("too young to drive")
end
```

For deeply nested conditions like this, combining conditions with `and`/`or` is often cleaner:

```lua
if age >= 18 and has_license then
    print("can drive")
else
    print("cannot drive")
end
```

Next: [While and Repeat Loops](/lua/while-and-repeat-loops/).
Control Flow.While and Repeat Loops:
## while: condition-checked-first loop

```lua
local i = 1
while i <= 5 do
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
end
```

Checks the condition before each iteration (including the first) — if the condition is false to begin with, the loop body never runs at all, same as `while` in most languages.

## repeat...until: condition-checked-last loop

```lua
local i = 1
repeat
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
until i > 5
```

`repeat...until` is Lua's equivalent of a **do-while** loop in C-family languages — the body always runs **at least once**, since the condition is checked *after* the body, not before. This is genuinely useful whenever you need "do this, then check if we should stop" logic, such as reading input until a sentinel value appears.

```lua
local input
repeat
    io.write("Enter a number (0 to quit): ")
    input = tonumber(io.read())
    print("You entered: " .. tostring(input))
until input == 0
```

## A subtlety: repeat...until's condition can see the loop body's locals

This is a small but genuinely useful Lua-specific detail: unlike `while`, where the condition is evaluated in the *outer* scope, `repeat...until`'s condition is evaluated **inside** the loop body's own scope — meaning it can reference `local` variables declared in the body:

```lua
local i = 0
repeat
    i = i + 1
    local done = (i >= 5) -- a local, declared INSIDE the loop body
until done -- valid! "done" is still in scope here, specifically because of repeat...until's design
```

Trying the equivalent with `while` wouldn't work, since `while`'s condition is checked before the body even starts, so a `local` declared inside the body wouldn't exist yet.

## break: exiting a loop early

Both `while` and `repeat` (and `for`, covered next) support `break`, which exits the innermost enclosing loop immediately:

```lua
local i = 1
while true do -- an intentional infinite loop
    if i > 5 then
        break
    end
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
end
```

## No continue keyword — the goto workaround

Lua notably has **no `continue` keyword** (unlike most other mainstream languages) for skipping to the next iteration. The idiomatic workarounds:

```lua
-- Option 1: invert the condition and wrap the rest of the body in an if
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 == 0 then -- only proceed for odd numbers
        print(i)
    end
end

-- Option 2 (Lua 5.2+): goto, jumping to a label at the end of the loop body
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 ~= 0 then goto continue end
    print(i)
    ::continue::
end
```

In practice, Option 1 (restructuring with a guard condition, or an early-exit helper function) is far more common and generally considered more readable — reach for `goto` only when the guard-condition restructuring would be significantly more awkward, which is relatively rare.

Next: [Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/).
Control Flow.Numeric For Loops:
Lua's numeric `for` loop iterates over a numeric range directly — no separate range type or iterator needed, unlike Rust's `0..5` or Python's `range()`.

## Basic syntax

```lua
for i = 1, 5 do
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

`for i = start, stop do ... end` iterates `i` from `start` to `stop`, **inclusive on both ends** — this is another important difference from Rust's exclusive `0..5` range or Python's `range(5)`; Lua's `for i = 1, 5` genuinely includes `5`.

## With an explicit step

```lua
for i = 1, 10, 2 do -- step of 2
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

for i = 10, 1, -1 do -- negative step, counting down
    print(i)
end
-- prints 10, 9, 8, ..., 1
```

The third value (step) defaults to `1` if omitted. It can be any number, including negative (for counting down) or fractional:

```lua
for i = 1, 2, 0.5 do
    print(i) -- 1.0, 1.5, 2.0
end
```

## The loop variable is local and scoped to the loop

```lua
for i = 1, 3 do
    print(i)
end
-- print(i) -- ERROR: i doesn't exist out here — it's scoped to the loop body only
```

Unlike a manually-declared `local i` before a `while` loop (which persists after the loop ends, still holding its last value), the numeric `for` loop's control variable is automatically local to the loop and disappears entirely once the loop finishes.

## New in Lua 5.5: the control variable is now read-only

In Lua 5.5, both the numeric `for` loop's control variable and the generic `for` loop's control variables (covered on the next page) are implicitly `const` — reassigning them inside the loop body is now a **compile-time error**, rather than the silently-allowed-but-confusing behavior of earlier versions:

```lua
for i = 1, 5 do
    print(i)
    i = i + 10 -- ERROR in Lua 5.5: attempt to assign to const variable 'i'
end
```

In Lua 5.1-5.4, that reassignment was legal but had **no effect on the loop's actual iteration** — the loop still counted through its original sequence regardless of what you assigned to `i` inside the body, which was a common source of confusion for newcomers who expected it to skip iterations or change the loop's range. Lua 5.5 turns that "legal but misleading" pattern into an explicit error, catching the mistake immediately instead of letting it silently do nothing. If you need a mutable counter influenced by loop-body logic, use a separate `local` variable declared outside (or at the top of) the loop body instead of trying to reassign the control variable itself.

## Common patterns: iterating array-like tables by index

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

for i = 1, #fruits do
    print(i, fruits[i])
end
-- 1  apple
-- 2  banana
-- 3  cherry
```

`#fruits` gives the table's length (covered fully in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/)). This pattern — iterating `1` to `#table` — works, but in most idiomatic Lua code, you'll actually reach for the **generic for loop with `ipairs`** instead (covered on the next page), which is slightly more idiomatic and handles some edge cases more gracefully. Both are correct and you'll see both in real code; understanding the numeric form first makes the generic form's mechanics easier to grasp.

Next: [Generic For Loops](/lua/generic-for-loops/).
Control Flow.Generic For Loops:
The **generic for loop** is Lua's more flexible iteration construct — used for iterating over tables (both array-style and dictionary-style), and anything else that provides an "iterator function." This is the loop you'll actually use most often in real Lua code once you're working with tables (which is almost always).

## ipairs: iterating array-like tables in order

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

for index, value in ipairs(fruits) do
    print(index, value)
end
-- 1  apple
-- 2  banana
-- 3  cherry
```

`ipairs(t)` iterates from index `1` upward, **in guaranteed order**, stopping at the first `nil` it encounters — this makes it the correct choice for genuinely array-like tables (sequential integer keys, no gaps), and it's the idiomatic replacement for the manual `for i = 1, #t do` pattern from the previous page.

## pairs: iterating every key in a table

```lua
local person = {name = "Alice", age = 30, city = "NYC"}

for key, value in pairs(person) do
    print(key, value)
end
-- order is NOT guaranteed — could print name/age/city in any order
```

`pairs(t)` iterates over **every** key in the table (both array-style integer keys and dictionary-style string/other keys), but makes **no guarantee about order** — this is the direct Lua equivalent of the "no guaranteed order" caveat on Rust's `HashMap`, covered in the Rust guide's [HashMap and HashSet](/rust/hashmap-and-hashset/) page. If you need a specific order, either use `ipairs` for a genuinely array-like table, or collect and sort the keys yourself (covered in [Table Library Functions](/lua/table-library-functions/)).

## ipairs vs pairs: which to use

| | Iterates | Order | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ipairs(t)` | Integer keys `1, 2, 3, ...`, stopping at the first `nil` | Guaranteed, sequential | Array-like tables (lists) |
| `pairs(t)` | Every key in the table | Not guaranteed | Dictionary-like tables (maps), or a table with a genuinely mixed structure |

```lua
local mixed = {"a", "b", "c", name = "example"}

for i, v in ipairs(mixed) do
    print(i, v) -- only prints the array part: 1 a, 2 b, 3 c
end

for k, v in pairs(mixed) do
    print(k, v) -- prints everything: 1 a, 2 b, 3 c, AND name example (order not guaranteed)
end
```

## How the generic for loop actually works, briefly

`for var1, var2 in iterator_function, state, control do ... end` is the full generic form — `ipairs`/`pairs` are themselves just regular functions that return an iterator function (plus some internal state) fitting this protocol. You can write your own custom iterators the same way; this is covered in [Coroutines for Generators and Iterators](/lua/coroutines-for-generators-and-iterators/) once coroutines have been introduced, since Lua's most elegant custom iterators are often built using them.

```lua
-- a minimal custom iterator, for illustration:
local function count_to(n)
    local i = 0
    return function() -- this returned function IS the iterator
        i = i + 1
        if i <= n then return i end
    end
end

for i in count_to(3) do
    print(i) -- 1, 2, 3
end
```

This wraps up control flow. Next: [Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/).

Functions.Defining Functions:
## Basic function definition

```lua
local function greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end

print(greet("Lua")) -- "Hello, Lua!"
```

`local function name(...) ... end` is shorthand for `local name = function(...) ... end` — functions are genuinely **values** in Lua, just like numbers or strings, assignable to variables exactly like anything else (this is explored fully once we reach closures, later on this page).

## Functions are first-class values

```lua
local function square(x)
    return x * x
end

local operation = square -- assign a function to another variable
print(operation(5)) -- 25

local function apply(f, value)
    return f(value)
end

print(apply(square, 6)) -- 36 — pass a function as an argument
```

## No type annotations — Lua is dynamically typed

Unlike Rust, Lua function parameters have no type annotations at all — any value of any type can be passed for any parameter, and it's up to your function's logic to handle (or validate) whatever it actually receives:

```lua
local function describe(x)
    return type(x) .. ": " .. tostring(x)
end

print(describe(42))       -- "number: 42"
print(describe("hi"))       -- "string: hi"
print(describe(true))         -- "boolean: true"
```

## Method-call syntax: the colon `:`

When a function is stored as a field in a table and called as a "method" on that table, Lua offers colon syntax as sugar for automatically passing the table itself as the first argument:

```lua
local account = {balance = 100}

function account.deposit(self, amount)
    self.balance = self.balance + amount
end

account.deposit(account, 50)  -- explicit form: pass account as the first arg manually
print(account.balance) -- 150

function account:withdraw(amount) -- colon in the DEFINITION: implicitly adds a "self" parameter
    self.balance = self.balance - amount
end

account:withdraw(30) -- colon in the CALL: implicitly passes account as the first arg
print(account.balance) -- 120
```

`function t:method(...)` is exactly equivalent to `function t.method(self, ...)`, and `t:method(...)` is exactly equivalent to `t.method(t, ...)` — the colon is purely syntactic convenience for the extremely common pattern of a function needing access to "the table it was called on," which becomes the foundation of Lua's object-oriented programming patterns, covered fully in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/).

## Anonymous functions

```lua
local numbers = {5, 3, 8, 1}

table.sort(numbers, function(a, b) -- an anonymous function, passed directly as an argument
    return a > b -- descending order
end)

print(table.concat(numbers, ", ")) -- "8, 5, 3, 1"
```

Anonymous functions passed directly as arguments are extremely common in Lua — used constantly with `table.sort`, custom iterators, and callback-style APIs (very common in game engines and GUI frameworks that embed Lua).

Next: [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/).
Functions.Multiple Return Values:
A genuinely distinctive Lua feature: **functions can return multiple values directly**, with no need for a tuple, array, or wrapper object — unlike most languages, where "returning multiple values" means packaging them into some compound structure first.

## Basic multiple returns

```lua
local function min_max(numbers)
    local min, max = numbers[1], numbers[1]
    for _, n in ipairs(numbers) do
        if n < min then min = n end
        if n > max then max = n end
    end
    return min, max
end

local smallest, largest = min_max({4, 1, 9, 2})
print(smallest, largest) -- 1  9
```

## What happens with a mismatched number of variables

Lua handles this gracefully in both directions, following the same "adjust" rules as multiple assignment from [Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/):

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

local a = two_values()        -- a = 1, second value silently discarded
print(a) -- 1

local a, b, c = two_values()  -- c = nil, since two_values only returned 2 values
print(a, b, c) -- 1  2  nil
```

## Multiple returns are truncated to ONE value in most contexts

This is the part that surprises newcomers: extra return values are only preserved when the function call is the **last** (or only) expression in a list. In any other position, only the *first* return value is kept:

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

print(two_values())          -- 1  2  — last/only expr in the argument list, ALL values kept
print(two_values(), "x")      -- 1  x — NOT last, only first value (1) kept
local t = {two_values(), two_values()} -- {1, 1, 2} — only the LAST call expands fully
```

If you specifically need to force a multi-value expression down to exactly one value (discarding the rest) in a context where it would otherwise expand, wrap it in parentheses:

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

print((two_values())) -- prints just "1" — the extra parentheses truncate to one value
```

## A common real-world use: pcall and error handling

This pattern is used pervasively in Lua's error-handling idiom, covered fully in [pcall and xpcall](/lua/pcall-and-xpcall/) — `pcall` returns a boolean success flag, **plus** whatever the called function itself returned (or the error value, on failure):

```lua
local function divide(a, b)
    if b == 0 then
        error("division by zero")
    end
    return a / b
end

local success, result = pcall(divide, 10, 2)
print(success, result) -- true  5.0

local success, err = pcall(divide, 10, 0)
print(success, err) -- false  "...: division by zero"
```

## select(): inspecting a variable number of values

```lua
local function count_args(...)
    return select("#", ...) -- "#" gives the total count of arguments passed
end

print(count_args(1, 2, 3)) -- 3

local function second_onward(...)
    return select(2, ...) -- everything from the 2nd argument onward
end

print(second_onward("a", "b", "c")) -- b  c
```

`select` is covered further alongside variadic functions on the next page, since the two features are almost always used together.

Next: [Variadic Functions](/lua/variadic-functions/).
Functions.Variadic Functions:
A **variadic** function accepts any number of arguments, using `...` (three dots) in its parameter list.

## Basic variadic functions

```lua
local function sum(...)
    local total = 0
    for _, n in ipairs({...}) do -- {...} packs the varargs into a table
        total = total + n
    end
    return total
end

print(sum(1, 2, 3))       -- 6
print(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))  -- 15
print(sum())                -- 0
```

`{...}` collects every extra argument into a table, which you can then iterate, index, or pass elsewhere. This has been the standard, most portable way to work with varargs across every Lua version — Lua 5.5 adds a more convenient option for it, covered next.

## New in Lua 5.5: named vararg tables

Lua 5.5 lets you give `...` a name directly in the parameter list, which binds it as a genuine table-like value (with a `.n` field giving the exact count, including any embedded `nil`s) — no manual `{...}` packing needed:

```lua
local function sum(...args)
    local total = 0
    for i = 1, args.n do
        total = total + args[i]
    end
    return total
end

print(sum(1, 2, 3))       -- 6
print(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))  -- 15
```

`args.n` is the key improvement here over plain `{...}`: as covered below, `#{...}` has always been unreliable when `nil` values are present among the arguments, while `args.n` (much like `select("#", ...)`) is always exactly correct, and — unlike `select("#", ...)` — it's available as a simple field lookup rather than a separate function call. If you're writing Lua 5.5-only code, `...name` is generally the more convenient, readable choice for anything beyond the simplest cases; if you need compatibility with 5.1-5.4 (per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), the `{...}`/`select` patterns below remain the portable approach.

## Using ... directly, without packing into a table

```lua
local function print_all(...)
    print(...) -- passes every vararg directly through to print
end

print_all("a", "b", "c") -- a  b  c
```

`...` behaves like a multi-value expression itself (similar to a multi-return function call) — passing it directly to another function forwards all the values, following the same "last position expands fully" rule from the previous page.

## Getting the count and individual values with select

```lua
local function describe(...)
    local count = select("#", ...)
    print("Received " .. count .. " arguments:")
    for i = 1, count do
        print(i, (select(i, ...))) -- select(i, ...) returns the i-th value ONWARD;
                                     -- extra parens truncate to just that one value
    end
end

describe("x", "y", "z")
```

**Important gotcha (relevant on any Lua version)**: `select("#", ...)` (the count) is more reliable than `#{...}` (the length of a packed table) when `nil` values might be present among the varargs — a table's length operator (`#`) has undefined behavior around embedded `nil`s (covered further in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/)), while `select("#", ...)` (and, in 5.5, a named vararg table's `.n` field) always correctly reports the true argument count, including trailing `nil`s.

```lua
local function count_args(...)
    return select("#", ...)
end

print(count_args(1, nil, 3)) -- 3 — correct, even with a nil in the middle
```

## Combining fixed and variadic parameters

```lua
local function greet(greeting, ...)
    local names = {...}
    for _, name in ipairs(names) do
        print(greeting .. ", " .. name .. "!")
    end
end

greet("Hello", "Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
-- Hello, Alice!
-- Hello, Bob!
-- Hello, Charlie!
```

`...` (named or not) must always come **last** in a parameter list — you can have any number of regular named parameters before it, but nothing can follow it.

## A practical example: a simple logging function

```lua
local function log(level, ...)
    local message = table.concat({...}, " ")
    print("[" .. level .. "] " .. message)
end

log("INFO", "Server started on port", 8080)
log("ERROR", "Failed to connect:", "timeout")
```

Next: [Closures and Upvalues](/lua/closures-and-upvalues/).
Functions.Closures and Upvalues:
A **closure** is a function that "remembers" variables from the scope it was defined in, even after that scope has technically finished executing. Lua's term for such a captured variable is an **upvalue**.

## A basic closure

```lua
local function make_counter()
    local count = 0 -- this becomes an upvalue for the inner function

    return function()
        count = count + 1
        return count
    end
end

local counter = make_counter()
print(counter()) -- 1
print(counter()) -- 2
print(counter()) -- 3
```

Every time `make_counter()` is called, it creates a **fresh** `count` variable and a fresh inner function closing over it — the inner function retains access to that specific `count`, persisting between calls, completely independent of any other counter you might create:

```lua
local counter1 = make_counter()
local counter2 = make_counter()

print(counter1()) -- 1
print(counter1()) -- 2
print(counter2())   -- 1 — a totally separate count, unaffected by counter1
```

## Why this is useful: encapsulated, private state

Closures are Lua's primary mechanism for genuinely **private** state — since `count` in the example above is a `local` inside `make_counter`, there is no way for any code outside the closure to directly read or modify it except by calling the returned function. This is a common and idiomatic pattern for building simple, encapsulated objects without needing the full machinery of tables-as-classes (covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)):

```lua
local function make_bank_account(initial_balance)
    local balance = initial_balance -- private, only accessible through the closures below

    return {
        deposit = function(amount)
            balance = balance + amount
        end,
        withdraw = function(amount)
            if amount > balance then
                print("Insufficient funds")
                return false
            end
            balance = balance - amount
            return true
        end,
        get_balance = function()
            return balance
        end,
    }
end

local account = make_bank_account(100)
account.deposit(50)
account.withdraw(30)
print(account.get_balance()) -- 120
-- there is no way to access `balance` directly from outside — genuinely private
```

## Closures capture variables by reference, not by value

This is worth being explicit about, since it's a common source of subtle bugs: a closure captures the **variable itself**, not a snapshot of its value at creation time. If the outer variable changes later, the closure sees the updated value:

```lua
local function make_adders()
    local adders = {}
    for i = 1, 3 do
        local captured = i -- IMPORTANT: a fresh local each iteration
        adders[i] = function(x) return x + captured end
    end
    return adders
end

local fns = make_adders()
print(fns[1](10)) -- 11
print(fns[2](10)) -- 12
print(fns[3](10)) -- 13
```

Because Lua's numeric `for` loop creates a **fresh** `i` (and, here, a fresh `captured`) on each iteration (as noted in [Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/)), each closure correctly captures its own value — this specific gotcha (all closures accidentally sharing one final loop variable) is a classic bug in some other languages' older loop semantics, but Lua's per-iteration fresh variable avoids it here.

Next: [Recursion](/lua/recursion/).
Functions.Recursion:
A function that calls itself. Lua supports recursion naturally, with one small but important detail around naming.

## Basic recursion

```lua
local function factorial(n)
    if n <= 1 then
        return 1
    end
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
end

print(factorial(5)) -- 120
```

## The local function self-reference gotcha

This is a genuine Lua-specific pitfall worth knowing about explicitly. Consider:

```lua
local factorial = function(n) -- NOTE: plain assignment, not "local function"
    if n <= 1 then
        return 1
    end
    return n * factorial(n - 1) -- ERROR at runtime: factorial is nil here!
end
```

This fails because, at the moment the function body is being *defined*, the `local factorial` on the left-hand side doesn't exist yet as far as the function body's own reference to `factorial` is concerned — when Lua looks up `factorial` inside the function body, it finds either nothing (an error) or an outer, different `factorial`, not the one currently being defined.

**The fix**: use `local function name(...)` syntax specifically (as in the very first example on this page) rather than `local name = function(...)`. This is not just a stylistic choice — `local function name(...)` is defined by the language to be sugar for:

```lua
local factorial       -- 1. declare the local FIRST, so it exists (as nil) already
factorial = function(n) -- 2. THEN assign the function, which can now see itself
    if n <= 1 then return 1 end
    return n * factorial(n - 1) -- this now correctly refers to the local declared above
end
```

**Practical rule: always use `local function name(...)` for any function that might need to call itself.** For non-recursive functions it doesn't matter which style you use, but it's a good habit to default to `local function` consistently.

## Mutual recursion

Two functions that call each other require a slightly different pattern, since neither can be fully defined before the other exists:

```lua
local is_even, is_odd -- forward-declare BOTH locals first

is_even = function(n)
    if n == 0 then return true end
    return is_odd(n - 1)
end

is_odd = function(n)
    if n == 0 then return false end
    return is_even(n - 1)
end

print(is_even(10)) -- true
print(is_odd(7))     -- true
```

Forward-declaring both `local`s before either assignment lets each function's body correctly see the other, even though one is necessarily defined "after" the other in the source.

## Recursion depth and stack limits

Lua does **not** guarantee tail-call optimization will always apply automatically the way some functional languages do by default, but it does support **proper tail calls** for calls in tail position (where a function's very last action is `return some_function(...)`, with nothing left to do afterward) — these genuinely reuse the current stack frame rather than growing the stack, allowing effectively unlimited recursion depth for correctly-written tail-recursive functions:

```lua
local function count_down(n)
    if n <= 0 then
        return "done"
    end
    return count_down(n - 1) -- a proper tail call — this will NOT grow the stack
end

print(count_down(1000000)) -- works fine, despite a million recursive calls
```

Compare this to the `factorial` example earlier, where `return n * factorial(n - 1)` is **not** a tail call (there's still a multiplication to do *after* the recursive call returns) — deep enough recursion with that version would eventually hit Lua's normal stack limit and error with `"stack overflow"`.

This wraps up functions. Next: [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) — Lua's single, do-everything data structure.

Tables.Tables as Arrays:
Tables are Lua's **only** built-in data structure — and understanding them thoroughly is probably the single highest-leverage thing you can do while learning Lua, since arrays, dictionaries, sets, objects, and modules are all, underneath, just tables used in different ways. This page covers the array-like use case.

## Creating an array-like table

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

print(fruits[1]) -- "apple" — REMEMBER: Lua tables are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed!
print(fruits[2]) -- "banana"
print(fruits[3]) -- "cherry"
print(#fruits)    -- 3, the length
```

This 1-based indexing (also seen in [Strings](/lua/strings/)) is consistent throughout Lua and is one of the most important habits to build early — reaching for `fruits[0]` out of muscle memory from another language is probably the single most common beginner mistake in Lua.

## Adding and removing elements

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}

table.insert(fruits, "cherry")      -- appends to the end: {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
table.insert(fruits, 1, "mango")     -- inserts at index 1, shifting everything else: {"mango", "apple", "banana", "cherry"}

table.remove(fruits, 1)                -- removes "mango", shifting everything back
local last = table.remove(fruits)        -- removes and returns the LAST element (no index needed)

fruits[#fruits + 1] = "kiwi" -- an alternative, common idiom for appending directly
```
