Project.Where to Go Next:
You've now covered Lua's syntax, types, control flow, tables, metatables and OOP, modules, error handling, coroutines, the standard library, package management, and embedding — a genuinely complete foundation. Here's where to go from here.

## Build things

The most effective way to solidify everything in this guide is to build real projects. Some ideas, roughly ordered by increasing scope:

- Extend the [to-do list project](/lua/build-a-to-do-list-cli-app/) with due dates, priority levels (an enum-like pattern using a table of constants), or filtering by status.
- **A small game with Love2D** — genuinely one of the most fun, motivating ways to practice Lua, and directly builds on the material in [Using Lua With Game Engines](/lua/using-lua-with-game-engines/). Love2D's own documentation and tutorials are excellent and beginner-friendly.
- **A Neovim plugin or configuration** — if you already use (or want to start using) Neovim, writing your own configuration in Lua is a genuinely practical way to use everything from this guide on something you'll interact with daily.
- **A text-processing or automation script** — something that solves a real annoyance in your own workflow, leaning on [String Library Basics](/lua/string-library-basics/), [Lua Patterns](/lua/lua-patterns-luas-regex/), and file I/O.

## Deepen specific areas

- **Advanced metatables** — beyond what's covered here, metatables support even more metamethods (`__newindex` for intercepting *writes* to missing keys, `__gc` for finalizers, weak tables via `__mode`) worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics.
- **Performance optimization** — Lua's official documentation includes a well-regarded "Lua Performance Tips" guide; understanding table pre-allocation, avoiding unnecessary global lookups, and string-building patterns becomes valuable once you're working on performance-sensitive code (like game logic running every frame).
- **LuaJIT specifically** — if your target environment uses LuaJIT (per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), its FFI library (from [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) and JIT-compilation-aware coding patterns reward focused, separate study.
- **A specific game engine or host application's API** — as discussed in [Using Lua With Game Engines](/lua/using-lua-with-game-engines/), the language itself is only part of the picture for embedded contexts; deep expertise in one specific host's API (Love2D, Roblox/Luau, WoW addons, Neovim) is its own valuable, separate skill.

## Community resources

- **lua.org** — the official Lua website, including the free, authoritative **Programming in Lua** book (the first edition is freely available online) and the full **Lua 5.5 Reference Manual**, the definitive source for exact language semantics. The 5.4 Reference Manual remains available too and is worth keeping handy if you're working with an older host application.
- **lua-users.org wiki** — a long-running, community-maintained wiki with recipes, tutorials, and discussion of idioms and gotchas.
- **r/lua** on Reddit, and the **Lua Discord/Matrix communities** — active places to ask questions and share projects.
- **Your specific host application's community** — if you're scripting for Love2D, Neovim, a specific game, or another embedded context, that community's own forums/Discord will be far more relevant for API-specific questions than general Lua resources.

## A realistic expectation

Lua's core language is genuinely small and learnable relatively quickly — but idiomatic mastery (comfortable metatable use, clean module organization, knowing when coroutines are the right tool) still takes real practice, exactly as with any language. The 1-based indexing and truthiness rules in particular are worth deliberately over-practicing early, since muscle memory from other languages actively works against you there.

Next: [FAQ](/lua/faq/).
Project.FAQ:
## Is Lua a good first programming language?

It's a reasonable choice, though not the most common recommendation for absolute beginners with zero programming experience — its small, clean core syntax is genuinely approachable, but its minimal standard library and heavy reliance on tables-for-everything means a beginner has to build more from scratch (or learn LuaRocks packages) earlier than they might with a more "batteries included" language like Python. It's an excellent **second or third** language, especially if game development or embedded scripting interests you.

## Lua vs Python — which should I learn?

They serve different niches more than they compete directly. Python has an enormous standard library and ecosystem (data science, web development, automation, general-purpose scripting) and is a very common first-language recommendation. Lua is dramatically smaller and faster, and is specifically strong where **embeddability** matters — scripting inside another application (a game, an editor, a server) rather than running as a large standalone program itself. Many developers learn both, reaching for Python for general scripting/data work and Lua specifically when working with a Lua-embedding host application.

## Why doesn't Lua have more built-in functionality?

This is a deliberate design philosophy, not an oversight — Lua's designers specifically prioritized keeping the core language and standard library small, on the theory that a host application embedding Lua (a game engine, a web server) should decide what additional functionality to expose, rather than Lua imposing a large, possibly-unwanted standard library on every embedding context. This tradeoff is exactly why LuaRocks (covered in [LuaRocks and Packages](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) exists and is genuinely necessary for many real projects, unlike languages where the standard library alone covers most everyday needs.

## Why is Lua 1-indexed?

This is a genuinely debated design choice, but the common justification: it aligns with everyday human counting convention ("the first item" is item 1, not item 0) and with Lua's mathematical/scientific computing heritage (many mathematical conventions are 1-indexed). Whatever the original reasoning, it's a fixed, permanent feature of the language at this point — the practical answer is simply to build the muscle memory, since it won't change.

## Is Lua fast?

Yes, notably so among interpreted/scripting languages — the reference PUC-Lua implementation is well-regarded for its speed relative to its simplicity, and **LuaJIT** (covered in [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) is frequently among the fastest dynamic-language implementations that exist in real-world benchmarks, often approaching statically-compiled language performance for certain workloads. This speed, combined with the tiny interpreter footprint, is a major reason Lua remains popular for performance-sensitive embedded scripting (games in particular) despite competition from many other scripting languages.

## Should I write new scripts for Lua 5.5, or target an older version?

If you're writing a **standalone script or tool** that you control the environment for, use 5.5 freely — it's the current stable release, fully compatible with 5.4-era code, and its new features (`global` declarations especially) are genuinely useful. If you're writing **for a specific host application** (a game, Neovim, a Redis script, an OpenResty deployment), check that host's documentation for its actual Lua version first, per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) — most existing hosts still run 5.1 through 5.4, and 5.5-only syntax (`global`, named vararg tables) will simply fail to parse there. When in doubt, sticking to 5.1-compatible syntax is the safest choice for code you expect to be portable across many different Lua hosts.

## Should I learn standard Lua or LuaJIT-specific features?

Learn standard Lua first — everything in this guide (aside from the explicitly-labeled [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/) page) works identically across standard Lua and LuaJIT, since LuaJIT is designed to be a drop-in-compatible, faster implementation of (primarily) Lua 5.1 semantics. Only reach for LuaJIT-specific features (the FFI library specifically) once you know for certain your target environment uses LuaJIT and you have a genuine need for direct C interop from Lua.

## I'm getting "attempt to index a nil value" — what does this mean?

This is one of the most common Lua runtime errors, and it means you tried to access a field (`.something` or `[key]`) on a variable that turned out to be `nil` — usually because a table you expected to exist wasn't actually created, a function that was supposed to return a table returned `nil` instead (perhaps due to an earlier, silently-swallowed error), or a typo in a variable/field name (which `luacheck`, from [Style Guide and Linting](/lua/style-guide-and-linting/), can often catch ahead of time). The error message usually includes the specific field name and line number — start by checking whether the table you expected actually got created/returned successfully at that point in the program.

This is the end of the guide. Good luck, and welcome to Lua!

Getting Started.What Is Lua:
Lua is a lightweight, fast, embeddable scripting language, created in Brazil in 1993. It's designed from the ground up to be simple, small, and easy to embed inside larger applications written in C or other languages — which is exactly how most people actually encounter Lua, even without realizing it.

## Why Lua exists and what makes it different

- **Extremely small and fast.** The entire Lua interpreter compiles to a few hundred kilobytes and starts up almost instantly. Lua is consistently one of the fastest scripting languages in real-world benchmarks among interpreted languages, thanks to a carefully optimized register-based virtual machine.
- **Designed to be embedded.** Unlike Python or Ruby, which are usually the "main" language of a project, Lua was built from day one to be dropped *into* a larger C/C++ application as a scripting layer — this is covered in depth in [Embedding and C Interop](/lua/why-embed-lua/).
- **One core data structure: the table.** Lua doesn't have separate array, dictionary, set, and object types — a single, flexible **table** type covers all of these roles. This is one of Lua's most distinctive design decisions and gets its own extensive section, [Tables](/lua/tables-as-arrays/).
- **Small, easy-to-learn syntax.** Lua's entire language reference fits comfortably in far fewer pages than most languages' — there's remarkably little to memorize before you're productive.

## Where you'll actually encounter Lua

- **Game development** — Lua is the scripting language behind World of Warcraft's UI addons, Roblox (a heavily modified variant called Luau), the Love2D game framework, Garry's Mod, and many other game engines that expose Lua as a way to script game logic without recompiling the engine itself.
- **Neovim configuration** — modern Neovim uses Lua as its primary configuration and plugin language (replacing Vimscript for most new plugin development).
- **Nginx / OpenResty** — Lua scripting is used to customize web server request handling at a very high performance level.
- **Redis** — Lua is built into Redis for writing atomic, server-side scripts.
- **Embedded/IoT devices** — Lua's tiny footprint makes it popular for scripting on resource-constrained hardware.

## What Lua is *not* particularly suited for

Lua doesn't ship with a large "batteries included" standard library the way Python does — no built-in HTTP client, no built-in JSON parsing, no built-in database drivers. This is a deliberate design choice: Lua expects the host application embedding it (or a package from LuaRocks, Lua's package manager, covered in [LuaRocks and Packages](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) to provide whatever additional functionality is needed. This makes Lua less immediately "batteries included" than some competitors, but keeps the core language small and predictable.

## How this guide is organized

This guide assumes zero prior Lua knowledge, but assumes you've programmed before in some language. It proceeds: installation → syntax and types → control flow and functions → tables (Lua's signature feature) → strings and pattern matching → metatables and object-oriented programming → modules → error handling → coroutines → I/O → the standard library → LuaRocks packages → embedding in C → tooling → a full worked project.

Next: [Installing Lua on Linux](/lua/installing-lua-on-linux/) or [Installing Lua on Windows](/lua/installing-lua-on-windows/).
Getting Started.Installing Lua on Linux:
## Arch Linux

Lua is available directly through `pacman`:

```bash
sudo pacman -S lua
```

This installs the latest Lua 5.x release (check with `lua -v` after installing — Arch tracks upstream fairly closely, so you'll typically get a recent 5.4.x release). Arch also packages `luarocks` (Lua's package manager, covered in [Installing LuaRocks](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) separately:

```bash
sudo pacman -S luarocks
```

## Verifying the install

```bash
lua -v
# Lua 5.4.6  Copyright (C) 1994-2023 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
```

## Other Linux distributions

Most distributions package Lua similarly:

```bash
# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install lua5.4

# Fedora
sudo dnf install lua

# openSUSE
sudo zypper install lua54
```

Debian/Ubuntu in particular tend to install version-suffixed binaries (`lua5.4` rather than plain `lua`) since multiple Lua versions can coexist — see [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) for why this matters and how to handle it.

## Building from source (getting the latest version, or a specific one)

Package managers sometimes lag behind the latest upstream release, or you may specifically want an older version for compatibility with a particular project or game engine. Building from source is simple, since Lua has no external dependencies beyond a C compiler:

```bash
curl -R -O https://www.lua.org/ftp/lua-5.4.6.tar.gz
tar zxf lua-5.4.6.tar.gz
cd lua-5.4.6
make linux test
sudo make install
```

`make linux` builds with the correct platform-specific flags (readline support for the interactive prompt, dynamic library flags, etc.); `make test` runs a quick sanity check; `sudo make install` installs to `/usr/local` by default.

## Checking which Lua you're actually running

If you have multiple Lua installations (e.g. a distro package and a from-source build), confirm which one is first on your `PATH`:

```bash
which lua
lua -v
```

Next: [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/).
Getting Started.Installing Lua on Windows:
Lua doesn't have as unified an "official installer" story on Windows as some languages, but there are several straightforward, reliable options.

## Option 1: winget (simplest, recommended)

```powershell
winget install DEVCOM.Lua
```

Or search for available Lua packages:

```powershell
winget search lua
```

## Option 2: Pre-built binaries from LuaBinaries

The Lua project's official binary distribution page (`luabinaries.sourceforge.net`) provides pre-compiled Windows executables. Download the appropriate `.zip` for your system (typically `lua-5.4.x_Win64_bin.zip`), extract it somewhere permanent like `C:\lua`, and add that folder to your `PATH`:

1. Search Windows for "Edit the system environment variables."
2. Click **Environment Variables**, select **Path** under System variables, click **Edit**, then **New**, and add `C:\lua`.
3. Open a **new** PowerShell/Command Prompt window and verify:

```powershell
lua -v
```

## Option 3: Chocolatey

If you use the Chocolatey package manager:

```powershell
choco install lua
```

## Option 4: WSL

Since Lua's Windows story is a bit less polished than its Linux story, many developers prefer running Lua inside **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)** and following the Linux install instructions exactly:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

Then inside the resulting Ubuntu shell, follow [Installing Lua on Linux](/lua/installing-lua-on-linux/). This guide's examples work identically either way — pick native Windows if you're specifically scripting a Windows application (like a game that expects a native Lua DLL) or WSL if you just want a smooth, Linux-like development experience.

## A note on LuaJIT as an alternative

Many Windows Lua users, especially in game development contexts, actually want **LuaJIT** (a fast, JIT-compiled alternative implementation, covered in [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) rather than the reference "PUC-Lua" implementation covered on this page. If a specific game engine or framework's documentation mentions LuaJIT specifically, follow that framework's own bundled installation instructions rather than installing standalone Lua — the versions need to match what the engine expects.

## Verifying the install

```powershell
lua -v
```

Next: [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/).
Getting Started.Your Editor Setup:
## VS Code

Install the **Lua** extension by **sumneko** (also published as "Lua Language Server," now maintained under the `LuaLS` organization) — this is the de facto standard Lua tooling for VS Code, providing autocompletion, inline diagnostics, go-to-definition, and hover documentation.

1. Open the Extensions panel (`Ctrl+Shift+X`).
2. Search for "Lua" and install the one published by `sumneko`/`LuaLS`.
3. Open any `.lua` file — the language server activates automatically.

## Neovim

Since Neovim itself is configured in Lua, Lua tooling in Neovim tends to be particularly well polished. Using `nvim-lspconfig` with the `lua_ls` language server:

```lua
require('lspconfig').lua_ls.setup({})
```

On Arch Linux, `lua-language-server` is available directly via pacman:

```bash
sudo pacman -S lua-language-server
```

## Other editors

- **Sublime Text** — the "Lua" package (via Package Control) provides syntax highlighting; combine with a LSP client package for full language server features.
- **IntelliJ / JetBrains IDEs** — the "Lua" plugin (search the JetBrains Marketplace) adds full Lua support.
- **ZeroBrane Studio** — a dedicated, lightweight Lua IDE, purpose-built for Lua (and popular in game development circles for its built-in debugger support with several game engines).

## Installing the language server standalone

If your editor needs the language server binary directly, the `lua-language-server` project provides prebuilt binaries on its GitHub releases page for Linux, Windows, and macOS — extract it and point your editor's LSP client configuration at the extracted binary.

## Formatting: StyLua

Lua doesn't have an official formatter bundled with the language itself (unlike Rust's `rustfmt`), but **StyLua** has become the de facto community standard:

```bash
cargo install stylua   # if you have a Rust toolchain (see the Rust guide!)
# or download a prebuilt binary from StyLua's GitHub releases
```

```bash
stylua my_script.lua        # format a file in place
stylua --check my_script.lua  # check without modifying, useful for CI
```

Most editor Lua extensions can be configured to run StyLua automatically on save, similar to how `rustfmt` works for Rust.

Next: [Hello World](/lua/hello-world/).
Getting Started.Hello World:
## Your first script

Create a file called `hello.lua`:

```lua
print("Hello, world!")
```

Run it:

```bash
lua hello.lua
```

That's genuinely the entire program — no `main` function required, no imports needed for basic output. Lua scripts execute top-to-bottom as a sequence of statements, starting immediately at the top of the file.

## The interactive prompt (REPL)

Lua ships with an interactive interpreter, useful for quick experiments:

```bash
lua
```

```
Lua 5.4.6  Copyright (C) 1994-2023 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
> print("Hello, world!")
Hello, world!
> 2 + 2
4
> local x = 10
> print(x * 2)
20
> os.exit()
```

Typing an expression alone (like `2 + 2`) at the REPL prints its value automatically — useful for quickly checking how something behaves without writing a full script.

## A slightly larger first example

```lua
-- a simple greeting script
local function greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end

print(greet("Lua"))

for i = 1, 3 do
    print("Count: " .. i)
end
```

```bash
lua hello.lua
```

```
Hello, Lua!
Count: 1
Count: 2
Count: 3
```

A few things to notice right away, each covered fully in upcoming pages: `--` starts a comment ([Comments and Formatting](/lua/comments-and-formatting/)), `..` concatenates strings ([Operators](/lua/operators/)), `local` declares a variable scoped to the current block ([Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/)), and `for i = 1, 3 do ... end` is Lua's numeric for-loop syntax ([Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/)).

Next: [The lua and luac Commands](/lua/the-lua-and-luac-commands/).
Getting Started.The lua and luac Commands:
## lua: running scripts

```bash
lua script.lua              # run a script
lua                           # start the interactive REPL
lua -e "print(2 + 2)"          # run a one-line snippet directly from the command line
lua -i script.lua                # run a script, THEN drop into an interactive prompt
                                    # (useful for inspecting state after the script runs)
```

## Passing arguments to a script

```bash
lua script.lua arg1 arg2 arg3
```

Inside `script.lua`, these are available via the global `arg` table:

```lua
print(arg[1]) -- "arg1"
print(arg[2]) -- "arg2"
print(#arg)   -- 3 (the number of arguments)
```

This is covered fully in [Command Line Arguments](/lua/command-line-arguments/).

## luac: compiling to bytecode

`luac` compiles Lua source into precompiled bytecode — this doesn't make Lua "compiled" in the sense of producing a standalone native executable (it still requires a Lua interpreter to run the bytecode), but it can speed up startup for large scripts by skipping the parsing step, and is sometimes used to obscure source code (though bytecode is still fairly easy to decompile, so don't rely on it for genuine security).

```bash
luac -o script.luac script.lua   # compile to bytecode
lua script.luac                    # run the compiled bytecode directly — the lua
                                      # interpreter accepts both source and bytecode
```

```bash
luac -p script.lua   # parse-only, check for syntax errors without producing output —
                        # useful as a quick "does this even parse" check, similar in
                        # spirit to Rust's `cargo check`
```

## A note on the standalone interpreter's name

Depending on how Lua was packaged for your system, the executable might be named `lua`, `lua5.4`, `lua5.1`, etc. (Debian/Ubuntu in particular tend to version-suffix it, since multiple Lua versions can be installed side by side). If a plain `lua` command isn't found, try `lua5.4`, or check what got installed with `ls /usr/bin/lua*` on Linux.

Next: [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/).
Getting Started.Lua Versions Explained:
Understanding Lua's version landscape early will save you real confusion later, since — unlike many languages — several genuinely different Lua versions and implementations remain in active, simultaneous use across different ecosystems.

## The official versions: 5.1 through 5.4

Lua has no "Lua 2" or radically different major version the way Python 2→3 was — instead, it's had a steady sequence of 5.x releases, each introducing some new features and occasionally small breaking changes:

- **Lua 5.1** (2006) — still widely used because it's the version **LuaJIT** (covered below) is based on, and many game engines and embedded systems standardized on it years ago and never moved.
- **Lua 5.2** (2011) — introduced `goto`, removed some deprecated 5.1 features.
- **Lua 5.3** (2015) — added a genuine integer subtype (previously all numbers were floats) and built-in bitwise operators.
- **Lua 5.4** (2020) — the current stable version as of this guide, adding integer-division operator `//`, to-be-closed variables, and generational garbage collection improvements. **This guide's examples target 5.4** unless otherwise noted, but almost everything shown works unchanged on 5.1-5.3 too.

## LuaJIT: a separate, extremely popular implementation

**LuaJIT** is not "a newer Lua" — it's a completely separate implementation (by Mike Pall) of the **Lua 5.1** language, with a highly optimized Just-In-Time compiler that makes it, in many benchmarks, one of the fastest dynamic language implementations that exists. LuaJIT is extremely widely used specifically *because* of its speed — it powers Neovim's Lua runtime, many game engines, and OpenResty/Nginx's Lua scripting.

The practical implication: if you're scripting for a specific engine or tool (Neovim, a game engine, OpenResty), **check which Lua/LuaJIT version it actually uses** before assuming every feature from this guide's Lua 5.4 examples is available — LuaJIT is based on 5.1 syntax/semantics, with some 5.2 features backported, but doesn't have Lua 5.3/5.4-only features like the native integer type or the `//` operator without special handling.

## Why this fragmentation happens, and how to navigate it

Because Lua is designed to be embedded, the application embedding it "owns" the decision of which Lua version to ship — a game released in 2012 might have permanently locked in Lua 5.1 (or LuaJIT) for its entire lifetime, regardless of what's currently "latest" upstream. This is completely normal in the Lua ecosystem, unlike languages where a single, centrally-controlled runtime version is expected.

**Practical rule of thumb**: when writing a script for a specific host application (a game, Neovim, Redis), check that application's own documentation for which Lua version it targets, and write compatible code for that version specifically — don't assume "latest Lua" features are available. When writing standalone scripts/tools with the `lua` command on your own machine, you control the version and can freely use whatever your installed `lua -v` reports.

Syntax Basics.Comments and Formatting:
## Comments

```lua
-- a single-line comment

--[[
   a multi-line block comment
   spanning several lines
--]]

--[==[
   a block comment that itself contains ]] safely,
   using extra = signs to avoid ambiguity
]==]
```

Single-line comments start with `--` and run to the end of the line. Block comments use `--[[ ... ]]`. The `--[==[ ... ]==]` variant (matching numbers of `=` signs between the brackets) exists specifically so a block comment can safely contain a literal `]]` inside it without prematurely closing.

## No enforced formatting standard, but strong conventions

Unlike Rust (which has one dominant official formatter), Lua has no built-in formatter and a looser community convention overall — but the following are close to universal:

- **Indentation**: either 2 or 4 spaces, fairly evenly split by community preference; pick one and be consistent within a project. (**StyLua**, from [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/), defaults to 4 spaces if you want an automated formatter to just decide for you.)
- **snake_case** for variables and functions: `local user_name`, `function calculate_total()`.
- **PascalCase** is commonly used for "class"-like tables (covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)): `local Animal = {}`.
- **SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE** for genuine constants, though Lua has no built-in `const` keyword (covered next page) — this is purely a naming convention signaling intent.

```lua
local MAX_RETRIES = 5
local user_name = "ferris"

local function calculate_total(items)
    -- ...
end
```

## `end` closes blocks — no braces

Unlike C-family languages, Lua doesn't use `{ }` to delimit blocks — every block-opening keyword (`function`, `if`, `for`, `while`, `do`) is closed with a matching `end`:

```lua
if x > 0 then
    print("positive")
end

function greet()
    print("hello")
end
```

This is one of the first visual differences newcomers notice, and it's consistent throughout the entire language — every block construct covered in upcoming pages follows this same `keyword ... end` pattern.

Syntax Basics.Variables and Scope:
## Global by default — a crucial early distinction

This is one of the most important things to learn early, and it's the **opposite** default from most modern languages: a variable assignment in Lua is **global** unless you explicitly declare it `local`.

```lua
x = 10        -- GLOBAL, visible everywhere, including other files/chunks
local y = 20   -- LOCAL, scoped to the current block only

print(x, y)   -- 10   20
```

## Why you should almost always use local

Global variables in Lua are stored in a shared global table (accessible as `_G`), meaning every global you create is visible from literally anywhere in your program, including other files, other libraries, and code you didn't write — a recipe for accidental name collisions and hard-to-track bugs in any program beyond a trivial script.

```lua
-- BAD habit, avoid this:
count = 0
function increment()
    count = count + 1  -- modifies the GLOBAL count — any other code using "count" breaks
end

-- GOOD habit:
local count = 0
local function increment()
    count = count + 1  -- modifies the local count, safely scoped
end
```

**Practical rule: always write `local` in front of every variable declaration unless you have a specific, deliberate reason to create a global.** This single habit prevents the large majority of scoping bugs beginners hit in Lua.

## Block scoping

`local` variables are scoped to the innermost enclosing block (`do...end`, a function body, a loop body, an `if` body):

```lua
local x = 10

do
    local x = 20 -- a NEW local variable, shadows the outer x within this block
    print(x)      -- 20
end

print(x) -- 10, unaffected — the outer x was never touched
```

```lua
if true then
    local message = "inside the if"
    print(message)
end

-- print(message) -- ERROR: message doesn't exist here, it went out of scope
```

## Declaring multiple variables at once

```lua
local a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
print(a, b, c) -- 1  2  3

local x, y = 10          -- y is nil — fewer values than variables is fine
print(x, y)              -- 10  nil

local p, q = 1, 2, 3     -- extra value (3) is simply discarded
print(p, q)              -- 1  2
```

Lua handles mismatched counts gracefully in both directions: missing values become `nil` (covered next page), and extra values are silently dropped. This behavior — used deliberately and constantly throughout idiomatic Lua — is explored further in [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/).

## Checking if a global exists (a common defensive pattern)

```lua
if type(some_global) == "nil" then
    print("not defined")
end

-- or, more idiomatically:
if some_global == nil then
    print("not defined")
end
```

Syntax Basics.Chunks and Blocks:
## What a "chunk" is

In Lua terminology, a **chunk** is simply a piece of Lua code — typically, an entire file, but also a string passed to `load()`, or code typed at the REPL. Every chunk is, internally, treated as the body of an anonymous function — this is why you'll sometimes see Lua's own error messages or documentation refer to "the main chunk" as if it were a function; it effectively is one.

```lua
-- this whole file is "a chunk" — implicitly wrapped as a function body
local x = 10
print(x)
```

This matters practically in one specific way: a chunk can `return` a value, just like a function, and this is exactly the mechanism [modules](/lua/writing-a-module/) use — a module file is a chunk that returns a table of functions.

```lua
-- greet.lua — this chunk returns a value
return function(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end
```

## Blocks

A **block** is a sequence of statements, optionally ending in a `return` or `break` — you've already seen several kinds: the body of a `function`, the body of an `if`, the body of a loop, or an explicit `do...end`.

```lua
do
    -- this is a block, with its own local scope — a standalone
    -- grouping construct with no loop or condition attached
    local temp = compute_something()
    print(temp)
end
-- temp is gone here — it only existed within the do...end block
```

A bare `do...end` block, with no attached `if`/`for`/`while`, is a genuinely useful tool purely for scoping — it lets you introduce `local` variables that are guaranteed to disappear afterward, keeping your broader scope clean of temporary helper variables.

## Statement separators

Semicolons are **entirely optional** in Lua, and rarely used in practice (unlike JavaScript or C, where they're either required or near-universal by convention):

```lua
local x = 1
local y = 2
print(x + y)

-- also completely valid, though unusual style:
local x = 1; local y = 2; print(x + y)
```

The only time a semicolon is genuinely useful is disambiguating certain edge cases involving function calls that start with `(`, where Lua's parser might otherwise interpret two consecutive lines as one expression — this is a rare enough edge case that most Lua style guides simply recommend never using semicolons at all, for consistency.

Syntax Basics.Operators:
## Arithmetic

```lua
print(5 + 3)   -- 8
print(5 - 3)   -- 2
print(5 * 3)   -- 15
print(5 / 3)   -- 1.6666666666667 — ALWAYS produces a float, even for integer operands!
print(5 // 3)  -- 1 — floor (integer) division, Lua 5.3+
print(5 % 3)   -- 2 — modulo
print(5 ^ 2)   -- 25.0 — exponentiation, always produces a float
print(-5)      -- unary negation
```

**Important**: `/` always produces a float result in Lua, even when both operands are integers (`5 / 3` is `1.6666...`, not `1`) — this is different from many languages where integer division truncates by default. Use `//` (floor division, Lua 5.3+) when you specifically want integer-style division.

## Comparison

```lua
print(5 == 3)   -- false
print(5 ~= 3)   -- true  -- NOTE: Lua uses ~= for "not equal", not != or <>
print(5 > 3)    -- true
print(5 < 3)    -- false
print(5 >= 5)   -- true
print(5 <= 4)   -- false
```

`~=` for "not equal" is one of Lua's more distinctive syntax choices — easy to forget if you're coming from a C-family language expecting `!=`.

## Logical operators: and, or, not

Lua spells out its logical operators as words, not symbols:

```lua
print(true and false)  -- false
print(true or false)   -- true
print(not true)         -- false
```

`and`/`or` in Lua don't just return `true`/`false` — they return one of their **actual operands**, evaluated with short-circuiting, which makes them useful for more than plain boolean logic (this is covered thoroughly in the section on `nil`/booleans, since it relies on understanding truthiness first — see [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/)).

```lua
local x = nil
local y = x or "default"  -- "default", since x is falsy
print(y)

local a = 5
local b = a and "positive" -- "positive", since a is truthy — the RESULT of `and`
                              -- is the second operand when the first is truthy
print(b)
```

## String concatenation: ..

```lua
local greeting = "Hello, " .. "World!"
print(greeting) -- "Hello, World!"

local name = "Lua"
local version = 5.4
print("Using " .. name .. " " .. version) -- numbers are auto-converted to strings
```

`..` is Lua's dedicated string concatenation operator — `+` is reserved purely for arithmetic and will error (or attempt numeric coercion and fail) if used on non-numeric strings.

## The length operator: #

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(#s) -- 5, the string's byte length

local t = {10, 20, 30}
print(#t) -- 3, the table's "array part" length — covered in Tables
```

## Operator precedence, briefly

Lua follows fairly standard precedence (`not`/unary minus highest, then `^`, then `*`/`/`/`//`/`%`, then `+`/`-`, then `..`, then comparisons, then `and`, then `or` lowest) — when in doubt, use parentheses for clarity; there's no penalty for being explicit.

Syntax Basics.Expressions and Statements:
Like most languages, Lua distinguishes between **expressions** (things that produce a value) and **statements** (things that perform an action). This distinction is more relaxed in Lua than in Rust, but still worth understanding clearly.

## Statements

```lua
local x = 5          -- an assignment statement
if x > 0 then         -- an if statement
    print("positive")
end
for i = 1, 3 do        -- a for statement
    print(i)
end
```

Statements don't produce a usable value — you can't do `local y = (if x > 0 then ... end)` the way you might in some functional languages; `if` in Lua is purely a control-flow statement, not an expression (unlike Rust, where `if` *does* produce a value — this is a genuine difference between the two languages worth remembering if you're learning both).

## Expressions

```lua
5 + 3              -- an arithmetic expression
"hello" .. "world" -- a concatenation expression
x > 0               -- a comparison expression, evaluates to true/false
some_function()      -- a function call expression, evaluates to its return value(s)
```

## Simulating "if as an expression" with and/or

Because Lua's `if` is a statement, not an expression, a common idiom for a quick conditional value uses `and`/`or`'s short-circuiting behavior instead (leaning on the truthiness rules from [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/)):

```lua
local age = 15
local category = (age >= 18) and "adult" or "minor"
print(category) -- "minor"
```

This reads as: *"if `age >= 18` is truthy, evaluate to `"adult"`; otherwise, evaluate to `"minor"`."* It works because of how `and`/`or` short-circuit and return actual operand values, not just booleans. **Caveat**: this idiom breaks if the "true" branch's value could itself be `false` or `nil` — `condition and false or "other"` always evaluates to `"other"`, regardless of `condition`, because `condition and false` itself is falsy, so Lua falls through to the `or` branch regardless. For anything beyond simple, always-truthy values in both branches, prefer a plain `if`/`else` assigning to a `local` declared beforehand:

```lua
local category
if age >= 18 then
    category = "adult"
else
    category = "minor"
end
```

## Function calls as statements vs expressions

A function call can be used as a standalone statement (when you only care about its side effects) or as part of a larger expression (when you care about its return value):

```lua
print("hello")              -- statement: called purely for its side effect

local result = math.max(3, 7) -- expression: the return value is used
print(math.max(3, 7) + 1)      -- expression, nested inside another expression
```

This wraps up syntax basics. Next: [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/).

Types and Values.Nil and Booleans:
## nil: Lua's "nothing" value

```lua
local x
print(x) -- nil — an uninitialized local is nil by default

local y = nil
print(y == nil) -- true
```

`nil` represents the absence of a useful value — similar in spirit to Python's `None`, JavaScript's `null`/`undefined`, or (conceptually, though implemented very differently) Rust's `Option::None`. Any variable that hasn't been assigned a value is `nil`. Assigning `nil` to a table field effectively **deletes** that key entirely (covered fully in [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/)).

## Booleans: true and false

```lua
local is_active = true
local is_done = false

print(type(is_active)) -- "boolean"
```

## Truthiness: the rule that trips up every newcomer

This is one of the most important rules in the entire language, and it differs from almost every other language you might already know: **in Lua, everything is truthy except `false` and `nil`.**

```lua
if 0 then print("0 is truthy!") end          -- prints! 0 is NOT falsy in Lua
if "" then print("empty string is truthy!") end -- prints! "" is NOT falsy in Lua
if {} then print("empty table is truthy!") end   -- prints! {} is NOT falsy in Lua

if false then print("won't print") end
if nil then print("won't print") end
```

If you're coming from Python, JavaScript, C, or most other languages, this will trip you up at least once — `0` and `""` are falsy in many of those languages, but **not** in Lua. Only the literal values `false` and `nil` are falsy; everything else, including `0`, empty strings, and empty tables, counts as true in a boolean context.

## How this affects and/or idioms

This rule is exactly why the `x or default` idiom from the previous page works cleanly for `nil` checks but can misfire if `0` or `""` are meant to be valid, intentional values:

```lua
local count = 0
local display_count = count or 10  -- display_count is 0, NOT 10 — 0 is truthy!
print(display_count) -- 0
```

If you specifically need to distinguish "no value was given" (`nil`) from "a falsy-looking but legitimate value was given" (`0`, `false`), compare against `nil` explicitly rather than relying on `or`:

```lua
local function get_count(count)
    if count == nil then
        count = 10 -- only fall back to a default if genuinely not provided
    end
    return count
end

print(get_count(0))  -- 0, correctly preserved
print(get_count())    -- 10, the default
```

Types and Values.Numbers:
## One number type, with two subtypes

Since Lua 5.3, the `number` type has two internal subtypes: **integer** and **float**. Before 5.3, Lua had only floats internally. This page covers 5.3+ behavior, which is what you'll encounter on any modern Lua install (including LuaJIT-based Lua 5.1 environments, integers are always represented as floats — see [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/) if you need to work with an older target).

```lua
print(type(10))     -- "number" — both integers and floats report the SAME type() result
print(math.type(10))   -- "integer" — math.type() distinguishes the subtype
print(math.type(10.0)) -- "float"
print(math.type(10/2)) -- "float" — / ALWAYS produces a float, as covered in Operators
```

`type()` treats integers and floats as one unified `"number"` type — you only need `math.type()` if you specifically need to distinguish the internal representation, which is relatively rare in everyday scripting.

## Integer vs float literals

```lua
local a = 10      -- integer literal
local b = 10.0    -- float literal (the .0 makes it a float)
local c = 1e3      -- float literal, scientific notation: 1000.0
local d = 0x1F       -- integer literal, hexadecimal: 31
```

## Arithmetic and automatic promotion

```lua
print(5 + 3)     -- 8 (integer + integer = integer)
print(5 + 3.0)   -- 8.0 (integer + float = float — "promoted")
print(5 / 2)     -- 2.5 (/ ALWAYS produces a float)
print(5 // 2)    -- 2 (// floor division stays integer if both operands are integers)
print(5.0 // 2)   -- 2.0 (// on a float operand produces a float)
```

## Common math functions

```lua
print(math.floor(3.7))   -- 3
print(math.ceil(3.2))     -- 4
print(math.abs(-5))        -- 5
print(math.max(3, 7, 2))    -- 7
print(math.min(3, 7, 2))     -- 2
print(math.sqrt(16))          -- 4.0
print(math.pi)                  -- 3.1415926535898
print(math.huge)                  -- inf, positive infinity
```

A full reference of `math` library functions is in [math Library](/lua/math-library/).

## Converting between strings and numbers

```lua
print(tonumber("42"))     -- 42
print(tonumber("3.14"))    -- 3.14
print(tonumber("abc"))      -- nil — not a valid number, returns nil rather than erroring
print(tonumber("10", 2))     -- 2 — parse "10" as base-2 (binary): 10 binary = 2 decimal

print(tostring(42))    -- "42"
print(tostring(3.14))   -- "3.14"
```

`tonumber` returning `nil` (rather than throwing an error) on invalid input is a common and useful pattern for validating user input — check for `nil` before using the result:

```lua
local input = "not a number"
local n = tonumber(input)
if n == nil then
    print("Invalid number: " .. input)
else
    print("Got: " .. n)
end
```

## Integer overflow behavior

Lua integers wrap around silently on overflow (similar to Rust's release-mode behavior, but always, not just in an "optimized" build) — there's no panic or error:

```lua
print(math.maxinteger)          -- 9223372036854775807 (on a typical 64-bit build)
print(math.maxinteger + 1)        -- -9223372036854775808 — wraps around silently
```

Types and Values.Strings:
## String literals

```lua
local s1 = "double quotes"
local s2 = 'single quotes' -- functionally identical to double quotes in Lua
local s3 = [[
a long string literal,
spanning multiple lines,
with no escape processing at all
]]
```

Unlike some languages, Lua treats `'single'` and `"double"` quoted strings as **completely equivalent** — pick whichever you prefer, though most style guides lean toward double quotes for consistency. The `[[...]]` "long string" syntax is useful for multi-line text (like embedded SQL, help text, or templates) and — notably — does **not** process escape sequences like `\n` inside it; it's taken completely literally, including actual line breaks.

## Escape sequences (in quoted strings, not long strings)

```lua
print("Line 1\nLine 2")    -- newline
print("Tab:\there")          -- tab
print("Quote: \"quoted\"")    -- escaped double quote
print('It\'s here')             -- escaped single quote
print("Backslash: \\")           -- literal backslash
print("Unicode: \u{1F600}")        -- unicode escape (Lua 5.3+)
```

## Strings are immutable

Just like in Rust, Python, and most other languages, Lua strings are **immutable** — every "modification" (concatenation, uppercasing, replacing) actually produces a brand new string, leaving the original unchanged:

```lua
local s = "hello"
local upper = s:upper() -- creates a NEW string
print(s)      -- "hello" — unchanged
print(upper)  -- "HELLO"
```

## String indexing and length

Unlike Rust (which deliberately disallows byte-indexing a `String` for UTF-8 safety reasons, as covered in the Rust guide's [Working With Text](/rust/working-with-text/)), Lua strings are simpler: they're just raw byte sequences, with no built-in Unicode awareness at the language level.

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(#s)         -- 5, the byte length
print(s:sub(1,1))  -- "h" — Lua string indices are 1-BASED, not 0-based!
print(s:sub(-1))    -- "o" — negative indices count from the end
print(s:sub(2,4))    -- "ell"
```

**Lua strings (and, as you'll see in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/), Lua's array-like tables) are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed.** This is a fundamental, pervasive difference from almost every C-family language, Python, JavaScript, and Rust — the very first element is index `1`, not `0`. This trips up virtually every newcomer to Lua at least once; it's worth deliberately internalizing early.

## Method-call syntax on strings

You may have noticed `s:upper()` and `s:sub(1,1)` above using a colon `:` rather than a dot `.`. This is Lua's **method call syntax**, equivalent to calling `string.upper(s)` but more convenient — this shorthand is covered in full in [Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/) once you understand how functions and tables interact, and used extensively once we reach [Tables](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) and object-oriented patterns.

```lua
local s = "hello"
print(s:upper())        -- "HELLO", shorthand for:
print(string.upper(s))  -- "HELLO", the equivalent explicit form
```

The full string library is covered in depth starting with [String Library Basics](/lua/string-library-basics/).
