Types and Values.The type Function and Type Coercion:
## The type() function

Lua has exactly **eight** basic types, and `type()` tells you which one any value is:

```lua
print(type(nil))          -- "nil"
print(type(true))          -- "boolean"
print(type(42))             -- "number"
print(type("hello"))         -- "string"
print(type({}))               -- "table"
print(type(print))             -- "function"
print(type(coroutine.create(function() end))) -- "thread"
-- the 8th type, "userdata", represents opaque data from host C code —
-- you won't create these directly in pure Lua scripts, but you'll encounter
-- them when embedding Lua in C (see Embedding and C Interop) or using libraries
-- that wrap C objects (like file handles)
```

That's the entire type system — dramatically smaller than most languages. There's no separate integer/float *type* at the `type()` level (both report `"number"`, as covered in [Numbers](/lua/numbers/)), no separate array/dictionary/object types (all are `"table"`), and no class type (classes are a pattern built on tables, covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)).

## Automatic coercion: string ↔ number

Lua automatically converts between strings and numbers in certain contexts — this is convenient but can also be a source of subtle bugs if you're not aware of it:

```lua
print("10" + 5)      -- 15 — the string "10" is coerced to a number
print("10" .. 5)       -- "105" — the number 5 is coerced to a string, then concatenated
print("3.14" * 2)       -- 6.28

print("abc" + 1)        -- ERROR: attempt to perform arithmetic on a string value
                           -- (coercion only works if the string actually looks like a number)
```

Arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, etc.) automatically try to coerce string operands to numbers. Concatenation (`..`) automatically coerces number operands to strings. This is genuinely convenient for quick scripts, but relying on it heavily in larger programs can make bugs harder to spot — being explicit with `tonumber()`/`tostring()` (from the previous page) is generally considered better practice once code grows beyond a quick script.

## No coercion for comparisons

Unlike arithmetic and concatenation, **comparison operators do not coerce types**:

```lua
print(10 == "10")  -- false! different types are NEVER equal, no coercion happens here
print(10 == 10)     -- true
```

This is a deliberate and important exception — `==` in Lua always returns `false` when comparing values of different types, with zero exceptions, unlike JavaScript's infamous `==` coercion rules. If you want to compare a string and a number for equality, convert one explicitly first:

```lua
local input = "10"
if tonumber(input) == 10 then
    print("matches!")
end
```

## Checking multiple types safely

```lua
local function describe(value)
    local t = type(value)
    if t == "number" then
        return "a number: " .. value
    elseif t == "string" then
        return "a string: " .. value
    elseif t == "nil" then
        return "nothing"
    else
        return "something else: a " .. t
    end
end

print(describe(42))       -- "a number: 42"
print(describe("hi"))       -- "a string: hi"
print(describe(nil))          -- "nothing"
print(describe({}))             -- "something else: a table"
```

This wraps up types and values. Next: [If, Then, Else](/lua/if-then-else/).

Control Flow.If, Then, Else:
```lua
local number = 7

if number < 5 then
    print("less than five")
elseif number == 5 then
    print("exactly five")
else
    print("greater than five")
end
```

Every branch keyword — `if`, `elseif`, `else` — and the whole construct is closed with one final `end`. Note `elseif` is a single word (not `else if`), and there's no limit to how many `elseif` branches you can chain.

## The condition can be any value — remember truthiness

Unlike Rust (which requires a literal `bool`), Lua's `if` condition accepts **any** value, evaluated according to the truthiness rule from [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/) — only `false` and `nil` are falsy:

```lua
local name = "Ferris"

if name then
    print("name is set: " .. name) -- this runs — any non-nil, non-false value is truthy
end

local count = 0
if count then
    print("this runs too — remember, 0 is truthy in Lua!")
end
```

## No switch/case statement

Lua doesn't have a built-in `switch`/`case` construct (unlike many C-family languages). The idiomatic replacements are a chain of `if`/`elseif`, or — for matching against a fixed, known set of values — a **table used as a lookup**, which is often cleaner:

```lua
local function describe_day(day)
    local descriptions = {
        Monday = "start of the week",
        Friday = "almost the weekend",
        Saturday = "weekend!",
        Sunday = "weekend!",
    }
    return descriptions[day] or "a regular day"
end

print(describe_day("Friday"))    -- "almost the weekend"
print(describe_day("Tuesday"))     -- "a regular day"
```

This table-lookup pattern (covered fully once we reach [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/)) is a genuinely idiomatic and common Lua alternative to a switch statement, especially when each "case" maps directly to a value rather than needing complex logic.

## Nested if statements

```lua
local age = 25
local has_license = true

if age >= 18 then
    if has_license then
        print("can drive")
    else
        print("too young to drive, or no license")
    end
else
    print("too young to drive")
end
```

For deeply nested conditions like this, combining conditions with `and`/`or` is often cleaner:

```lua
if age >= 18 and has_license then
    print("can drive")
else
    print("cannot drive")
end
```

Next: [While and Repeat Loops](/lua/while-and-repeat-loops/).
Control Flow.While and Repeat Loops:
## while: condition-checked-first loop

```lua
local i = 1
while i <= 5 do
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
end
```

Checks the condition before each iteration (including the first) — if the condition is false to begin with, the loop body never runs at all, same as `while` in most languages.

## repeat...until: condition-checked-last loop

```lua
local i = 1
repeat
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
until i > 5
```

`repeat...until` is Lua's equivalent of a **do-while** loop in C-family languages — the body always runs **at least once**, since the condition is checked *after* the body, not before. This is genuinely useful whenever you need "do this, then check if we should stop" logic, such as reading input until a sentinel value appears.

```lua
local input
repeat
    io.write("Enter a number (0 to quit): ")
    input = tonumber(io.read())
    print("You entered: " .. tostring(input))
until input == 0
```

## A subtlety: repeat...until's condition can see the loop body's locals

This is a small but genuinely useful Lua-specific detail: unlike `while`, where the condition is evaluated in the *outer* scope, `repeat...until`'s condition is evaluated **inside** the loop body's own scope — meaning it can reference `local` variables declared in the body:

```lua
local i = 0
repeat
    i = i + 1
    local done = (i >= 5) -- a local, declared INSIDE the loop body
until done -- valid! "done" is still in scope here, specifically because of repeat...until's design
```

Trying the equivalent with `while` wouldn't work, since `while`'s condition is checked before the body even starts, so a `local` declared inside the body wouldn't exist yet.

## break: exiting a loop early

Both `while` and `repeat` (and `for`, covered next) support `break`, which exits the innermost enclosing loop immediately:

```lua
local i = 1
while true do -- an intentional infinite loop
    if i > 5 then
        break
    end
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
end
```

## No continue keyword — the goto workaround

Lua notably has **no `continue` keyword** (unlike most other mainstream languages) for skipping to the next iteration. The idiomatic workarounds:

```lua
-- Option 1: invert the condition and wrap the rest of the body in an if
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 == 0 then -- only proceed for odd numbers
        print(i)
    end
end

-- Option 2 (Lua 5.2+): goto, jumping to a label at the end of the loop body
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 ~= 0 then goto continue end
    print(i)
    ::continue::
end
```

In practice, Option 1 (restructuring with a guard condition, or an early-exit helper function) is far more common and generally considered more readable — reach for `goto` only when the guard-condition restructuring would be significantly more awkward, which is relatively rare.

Next: [Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/).
Control Flow.Numeric For Loops:
Lua's numeric `for` loop iterates over a numeric range directly — no separate range type or iterator needed, unlike Rust's `0..5` or Python's `range()`.

## Basic syntax

```lua
for i = 1, 5 do
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

`for i = start, stop do ... end` iterates `i` from `start` to `stop`, **inclusive on both ends** — this is another important difference from Rust's exclusive `0..5` range or Python's `range(5)`; Lua's `for i = 1, 5` genuinely includes `5`.

## With an explicit step

```lua
for i = 1, 10, 2 do -- step of 2
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

for i = 10, 1, -1 do -- negative step, counting down
    print(i)
end
-- prints 10, 9, 8, ..., 1
```

The third value (step) defaults to `1` if omitted. It can be any number, including negative (for counting down) or fractional:

```lua
for i = 1, 2, 0.5 do
    print(i) -- 1.0, 1.5, 2.0
end
```

## The loop variable is local and scoped to the loop

```lua
for i = 1, 3 do
    print(i)
end
-- print(i) -- ERROR: i doesn't exist out here — it's scoped to the loop body only
```

Unlike a manually-declared `local i` before a `while` loop (which persists after the loop ends, still holding its last value), the numeric `for` loop's control variable is automatically local to the loop and disappears entirely once the loop finishes.

## Common patterns: iterating array-like tables by index

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

for i = 1, #fruits do
    print(i, fruits[i])
end
-- 1  apple
-- 2  banana
-- 3  cherry
```

`#fruits` gives the table's length (covered fully in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/)). This pattern — iterating `1` to `#table` — works, but in most idiomatic Lua code, you'll actually reach for the **generic for loop with `ipairs`** instead (covered on the next page), which is slightly more idiomatic and handles some edge cases more gracefully. Both are correct and you'll see both in real code; understanding the numeric form first makes the generic form's mechanics easier to grasp.

Next: [Generic For Loops](/lua/generic-for-loops/).
Control Flow.Generic For Loops:
The **generic for loop** is Lua's more flexible iteration construct — used for iterating over tables (both array-style and dictionary-style), and anything else that provides an "iterator function." This is the loop you'll actually use most often in real Lua code once you're working with tables (which is almost always).

## ipairs: iterating array-like tables in order

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

for index, value in ipairs(fruits) do
    print(index, value)
end
-- 1  apple
-- 2  banana
-- 3  cherry
```

`ipairs(t)` iterates from index `1` upward, **in guaranteed order**, stopping at the first `nil` it encounters — this makes it the correct choice for genuinely array-like tables (sequential integer keys, no gaps), and it's the idiomatic replacement for the manual `for i = 1, #t do` pattern from the previous page.

## pairs: iterating every key in a table

```lua
local person = {name = "Alice", age = 30, city = "NYC"}

for key, value in pairs(person) do
    print(key, value)
end
-- order is NOT guaranteed — could print name/age/city in any order
```

`pairs(t)` iterates over **every** key in the table (both array-style integer keys and dictionary-style string/other keys), but makes **no guarantee about order** — this is the direct Lua equivalent of the "no guaranteed order" caveat on Rust's `HashMap`, covered in the Rust guide's [HashMap and HashSet](/rust/hashmap-and-hashset/) page. If you need a specific order, either use `ipairs` for a genuinely array-like table, or collect and sort the keys yourself (covered in [Table Library Functions](/lua/table-library-functions/)).

## ipairs vs pairs: which to use

| | Iterates | Order | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ipairs(t)` | Integer keys `1, 2, 3, ...`, stopping at the first `nil` | Guaranteed, sequential | Array-like tables (lists) |
| `pairs(t)` | Every key in the table | Not guaranteed | Dictionary-like tables (maps), or a table with a genuinely mixed structure |

```lua
local mixed = {"a", "b", "c", name = "example"}

for i, v in ipairs(mixed) do
    print(i, v) -- only prints the array part: 1 a, 2 b, 3 c
end

for k, v in pairs(mixed) do
    print(k, v) -- prints everything: 1 a, 2 b, 3 c, AND name example (order not guaranteed)
end
```

## How the generic for loop actually works, briefly

`for var1, var2 in iterator_function, state, control do ... end` is the full generic form — `ipairs`/`pairs` are themselves just regular functions that return an iterator function (plus some internal state) fitting this protocol. You can write your own custom iterators the same way; this is covered in [Coroutines for Generators and Iterators](/lua/coroutines-for-generators-and-iterators/) once coroutines have been introduced, since Lua's most elegant custom iterators are often built using them.

```lua
-- a minimal custom iterator, for illustration:
local function count_to(n)
    local i = 0
    return function() -- this returned function IS the iterator
        i = i + 1
        if i <= n then return i end
    end
end

for i in count_to(3) do
    print(i) -- 1, 2, 3
end
```

This wraps up control flow. Next: [Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/).

Functions.Defining Functions:
## Basic function definition

```lua
local function greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end

print(greet("Lua")) -- "Hello, Lua!"
```

`local function name(...) ... end` is shorthand for `local name = function(...) ... end` — functions are genuinely **values** in Lua, just like numbers or strings, assignable to variables exactly like anything else (this is explored fully once we reach closures, later on this page).

## Functions are first-class values

```lua
local function square(x)
    return x * x
end

local operation = square -- assign a function to another variable
print(operation(5)) -- 25

local function apply(f, value)
    return f(value)
end

print(apply(square, 6)) -- 36 — pass a function as an argument
```

## No type annotations — Lua is dynamically typed

Unlike Rust, Lua function parameters have no type annotations at all — any value of any type can be passed for any parameter, and it's up to your function's logic to handle (or validate) whatever it actually receives:

```lua
local function describe(x)
    return type(x) .. ": " .. tostring(x)
end

print(describe(42))       -- "number: 42"
print(describe("hi"))       -- "string: hi"
print(describe(true))         -- "boolean: true"
```

## Method-call syntax: the colon `:`

When a function is stored as a field in a table and called as a "method" on that table, Lua offers colon syntax as sugar for automatically passing the table itself as the first argument:

```lua
local account = {balance = 100}

function account.deposit(self, amount)
    self.balance = self.balance + amount
end

account.deposit(account, 50)  -- explicit form: pass account as the first arg manually
print(account.balance) -- 150

function account:withdraw(amount) -- colon in the DEFINITION: implicitly adds a "self" parameter
    self.balance = self.balance - amount
end

account:withdraw(30) -- colon in the CALL: implicitly passes account as the first arg
print(account.balance) -- 120
```

`function t:method(...)` is exactly equivalent to `function t.method(self, ...)`, and `t:method(...)` is exactly equivalent to `t.method(t, ...)` — the colon is purely syntactic convenience for the extremely common pattern of a function needing access to "the table it was called on," which becomes the foundation of Lua's object-oriented programming patterns, covered fully in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/).

## Anonymous functions

```lua
local numbers = {5, 3, 8, 1}

table.sort(numbers, function(a, b) -- an anonymous function, passed directly as an argument
    return a > b -- descending order
end)

print(table.concat(numbers, ", ")) -- "8, 5, 3, 1"
```

Anonymous functions passed directly as arguments are extremely common in Lua — used constantly with `table.sort`, custom iterators, and callback-style APIs (very common in game engines and GUI frameworks that embed Lua).

Next: [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/).
Functions.Multiple Return Values:
A genuinely distinctive Lua feature: **functions can return multiple values directly**, with no need for a tuple, array, or wrapper object — unlike most languages, where "returning multiple values" means packaging them into some compound structure first.

## Basic multiple returns

```lua
local function min_max(numbers)
    local min, max = numbers[1], numbers[1]
    for _, n in ipairs(numbers) do
        if n < min then min = n end
        if n > max then max = n end
    end
    return min, max
end

local smallest, largest = min_max({4, 1, 9, 2})
print(smallest, largest) -- 1  9
```

## What happens with a mismatched number of variables

Lua handles this gracefully in both directions, following the same "adjust" rules as multiple assignment from [Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/):

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

local a = two_values()        -- a = 1, second value silently discarded
print(a) -- 1

local a, b, c = two_values()  -- c = nil, since two_values only returned 2 values
print(a, b, c) -- 1  2  nil
```

## Multiple returns are truncated to ONE value in most contexts

This is the part that surprises newcomers: extra return values are only preserved when the function call is the **last** (or only) expression in a list. In any other position, only the *first* return value is kept:

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

print(two_values())          -- 1  2  — last/only expr in the argument list, ALL values kept
print(two_values(), "x")      -- 1  x — NOT last, only first value (1) kept
local t = {two_values(), two_values()} -- {1, 1, 2} — only the LAST call expands fully
```

If you specifically need to force a multi-value expression down to exactly one value (discarding the rest) in a context where it would otherwise expand, wrap it in parentheses:

```lua
local function two_values()
    return 1, 2
end

print((two_values())) -- prints just "1" — the extra parentheses truncate to one value
```

## A common real-world use: pcall and error handling

This pattern is used pervasively in Lua's error-handling idiom, covered fully in [pcall and xpcall](/lua/pcall-and-xpcall/) — `pcall` returns a boolean success flag, **plus** whatever the called function itself returned (or the error value, on failure):

```lua
local function divide(a, b)
    if b == 0 then
        error("division by zero")
    end
    return a / b
end

local success, result = pcall(divide, 10, 2)
print(success, result) -- true  5.0

local success, err = pcall(divide, 10, 0)
print(success, err) -- false  "...: division by zero"
```

## select(): inspecting a variable number of values

```lua
local function count_args(...)
    return select("#", ...) -- "#" gives the total count of arguments passed
end

print(count_args(1, 2, 3)) -- 3

local function second_onward(...)
    return select(2, ...) -- everything from the 2nd argument onward
end

print(second_onward("a", "b", "c")) -- b  c
```

`select` is covered further alongside variadic functions on the next page, since the two features are almost always used together.

Next: [Variadic Functions](/lua/variadic-functions/).
Functions.Variadic Functions:
A **variadic** function accepts any number of arguments, using `...` (three dots) in its parameter list.

## Basic variadic functions

```lua
local function sum(...)
    local total = 0
    for _, n in ipairs({...}) do -- {...} packs the varargs into a table
        total = total + n
    end
    return total
end

print(sum(1, 2, 3))       -- 6
print(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))  -- 15
print(sum())                -- 0
```

`{...}` collects every extra argument into a table, which you can then iterate, index, or pass elsewhere. This is the most common and straightforward way to work with varargs.

## Using ... directly, without packing into a table

```lua
local function print_all(...)
    print(...) -- passes every vararg directly through to print
end

print_all("a", "b", "c") -- a  b  c
```

`...` behaves like a multi-value expression itself (similar to a multi-return function call) — passing it directly to another function forwards all the values, following the same "last position expands fully" rule from the previous page.

## Getting the count and individual values with select

```lua
local function describe(...)
    local count = select("#", ...)
    print("Received " .. count .. " arguments:")
    for i = 1, count do
        print(i, (select(i, ...))) -- select(i, ...) returns the i-th value ONWARD;
                                     -- extra parens truncate to just that one value
    end
end

describe("x", "y", "z")
```

**Important gotcha**: `select("#", ...)` (the count) is more reliable than `#{...}` (the length of a packed table) when `nil` values might be present among the varargs — a table's length operator (`#`) has undefined behavior around embedded `nil`s (covered further in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/)), while `select("#", ...)` always correctly reports the true argument count, including trailing `nil`s.

```lua
local function count_args(...)
    return select("#", ...)
end

print(count_args(1, nil, 3)) -- 3 — correct, even with a nil in the middle
```

## Combining fixed and variadic parameters

```lua
local function greet(greeting, ...)
    local names = {...}
    for _, name in ipairs(names) do
        print(greeting .. ", " .. name .. "!")
    end
end

greet("Hello", "Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
-- Hello, Alice!
-- Hello, Bob!
-- Hello, Charlie!
```

`...` must always come **last** in a parameter list — you can have any number of regular named parameters before it, but nothing can follow it.

## A practical example: a simple logging function

```lua
local function log(level, ...)
    local message = table.concat({...}, " ")
    print("[" .. level .. "] " .. message)
end

log("INFO", "Server started on port", 8080)
log("ERROR", "Failed to connect:", "timeout")
```

Next: [Closures and Upvalues](/lua/closures-and-upvalues/).
Functions.Closures and Upvalues:
A **closure** is a function that "remembers" variables from the scope it was defined in, even after that scope has technically finished executing. Lua's term for such a captured variable is an **upvalue**.

## A basic closure

```lua
local function make_counter()
    local count = 0 -- this becomes an upvalue for the inner function

    return function()
        count = count + 1
        return count
    end
end

local counter = make_counter()
print(counter()) -- 1
print(counter()) -- 2
print(counter()) -- 3
```

Every time `make_counter()` is called, it creates a **fresh** `count` variable and a fresh inner function closing over it — the inner function retains access to that specific `count`, persisting between calls, completely independent of any other counter you might create:

```lua
local counter1 = make_counter()
local counter2 = make_counter()

print(counter1()) -- 1
print(counter1()) -- 2
print(counter2())   -- 1 — a totally separate count, unaffected by counter1
```

## Why this is useful: encapsulated, private state

Closures are Lua's primary mechanism for genuinely **private** state — since `count` in the example above is a `local` inside `make_counter`, there is no way for any code outside the closure to directly read or modify it except by calling the returned function. This is a common and idiomatic pattern for building simple, encapsulated objects without needing the full machinery of tables-as-classes (covered in [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/)):

```lua
local function make_bank_account(initial_balance)
    local balance = initial_balance -- private, only accessible through the closures below

    return {
        deposit = function(amount)
            balance = balance + amount
        end,
        withdraw = function(amount)
            if amount > balance then
                print("Insufficient funds")
                return false
            end
            balance = balance - amount
            return true
        end,
        get_balance = function()
            return balance
        end,
    }
end

local account = make_bank_account(100)
account.deposit(50)
account.withdraw(30)
print(account.get_balance()) -- 120
-- there is no way to access `balance` directly from outside — genuinely private
```

## Closures capture variables by reference, not by value

This is worth being explicit about, since it's a common source of subtle bugs: a closure captures the **variable itself**, not a snapshot of its value at creation time. If the outer variable changes later, the closure sees the updated value:

```lua
local function make_adders()
    local adders = {}
    for i = 1, 3 do
        local captured = i -- IMPORTANT: a fresh local each iteration
        adders[i] = function(x) return x + captured end
    end
    return adders
end

local fns = make_adders()
print(fns[1](10)) -- 11
print(fns[2](10)) -- 12
print(fns[3](10)) -- 13
```

Because Lua's numeric `for` loop creates a **fresh** `i` (and, here, a fresh `captured`) on each iteration (as noted in [Numeric For Loops](/lua/numeric-for-loops/)), each closure correctly captures its own value — this specific gotcha (all closures accidentally sharing one final loop variable) is a classic bug in some other languages' older loop semantics, but Lua's per-iteration fresh variable avoids it here.

Next: [Recursion](/lua/recursion/).
Functions.Recursion:
A function that calls itself. Lua supports recursion naturally, with one small but important detail around naming.

## Basic recursion

```lua
local function factorial(n)
    if n <= 1 then
        return 1
    end
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
end

print(factorial(5)) -- 120
```

## The local function self-reference gotcha

This is a genuine Lua-specific pitfall worth knowing about explicitly. Consider:

```lua
local factorial = function(n) -- NOTE: plain assignment, not "local function"
    if n <= 1 then
        return 1
    end
    return n * factorial(n - 1) -- ERROR at runtime: factorial is nil here!
end
```

This fails because, at the moment the function body is being *defined*, the `local factorial` on the left-hand side doesn't exist yet as far as the function body's own reference to `factorial` is concerned — when Lua looks up `factorial` inside the function body, it finds either nothing (an error) or an outer, different `factorial`, not the one currently being defined.

**The fix**: use `local function name(...)` syntax specifically (as in the very first example on this page) rather than `local name = function(...)`. This is not just a stylistic choice — `local function name(...)` is defined by the language to be sugar for:

```lua
local factorial       -- 1. declare the local FIRST, so it exists (as nil) already
factorial = function(n) -- 2. THEN assign the function, which can now see itself
    if n <= 1 then return 1 end
    return n * factorial(n - 1) -- this now correctly refers to the local declared above
end
```

**Practical rule: always use `local function name(...)` for any function that might need to call itself.** For non-recursive functions it doesn't matter which style you use, but it's a good habit to default to `local function` consistently.

## Mutual recursion

Two functions that call each other require a slightly different pattern, since neither can be fully defined before the other exists:

```lua
local is_even, is_odd -- forward-declare BOTH locals first

is_even = function(n)
    if n == 0 then return true end
    return is_odd(n - 1)
end

is_odd = function(n)
    if n == 0 then return false end
    return is_even(n - 1)
end

print(is_even(10)) -- true
print(is_odd(7))     -- true
```

Forward-declaring both `local`s before either assignment lets each function's body correctly see the other, even though one is necessarily defined "after" the other in the source.

## Recursion depth and stack limits

Lua does **not** guarantee tail-call optimization will always apply automatically the way some functional languages do by default, but it does support **proper tail calls** for calls in tail position (where a function's very last action is `return some_function(...)`, with nothing left to do afterward) — these genuinely reuse the current stack frame rather than growing the stack, allowing effectively unlimited recursion depth for correctly-written tail-recursive functions:

```lua
local function count_down(n)
    if n <= 0 then
        return "done"
    end
    return count_down(n - 1) -- a proper tail call — this will NOT grow the stack
end

print(count_down(1000000)) -- works fine, despite a million recursive calls
```

Compare this to the `factorial` example earlier, where `return n * factorial(n - 1)` is **not** a tail call (there's still a multiplication to do *after* the recursive call returns) — deep enough recursion with that version would eventually hit Lua's normal stack limit and error with `"stack overflow"`.

This wraps up functions. Next: [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) — Lua's single, do-everything data structure.

Tables.Tables as Arrays:
Tables are Lua's **only** built-in data structure — and understanding them thoroughly is probably the single highest-leverage thing you can do while learning Lua, since arrays, dictionaries, sets, objects, and modules are all, underneath, just tables used in different ways. This page covers the array-like use case.

## Creating an array-like table

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

print(fruits[1]) -- "apple" — REMEMBER: Lua tables are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed!
print(fruits[2]) -- "banana"
print(fruits[3]) -- "cherry"
print(#fruits)    -- 3, the length
```

This 1-based indexing (also seen in [Strings](/lua/strings/)) is consistent throughout Lua and is one of the most important habits to build early — reaching for `fruits[0]` out of muscle memory from another language is probably the single most common beginner mistake in Lua.

## Adding and removing elements

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}

table.insert(fruits, "cherry")      -- appends to the end: {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
table.insert(fruits, 1, "mango")     -- inserts at index 1, shifting everything else: {"mango", "apple", "banana", "cherry"}

table.remove(fruits, 1)                -- removes "mango", shifting everything back
local last = table.remove(fruits)        -- removes and returns the LAST element (no index needed)

fruits[#fruits + 1] = "kiwi" -- an alternative, common idiom for appending directly
```

`fruits[#fruits + 1] = value` (append by writing one-past-the-current-end) is an extremely common, idiomatic Lua pattern for growing an array-like table — you'll see it constantly in real code, as an alternative to `table.insert`.

## Iterating

```lua
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}

for i, fruit in ipairs(fruits) do
    print(i, fruit)
end
```

As covered in [Generic For Loops](/lua/generic-for-loops/), `ipairs` is the idiomatic choice for genuinely array-like, gapless tables.

## What "array-like" actually means internally

This is worth understanding, since it explains several behaviors: a Lua table doesn't have a truly separate "array part" as a distinct type — it's really one general-purpose hash table under the hood, but Lua's implementation specifically **optimizes** the case where keys are a dense, gapless sequence of integers starting at `1` (giving it array-like storage and performance in that specific case). This is why `{"apple", "banana", "cherry"}` behaves efficiently like an array, while a table with scattered or non-sequential integer keys does not get that optimization.

## The danger of gaps: nil "holes"

```lua
local t = {"a", "b", nil, "d"}
print(#t) -- UNDEFINED behavior! Could be 2 or 4, depending on Lua's internal table layout
```

**Assigning `nil` into the middle of what should be a sequential array creates a "hole,"** and the `#` operator's result becomes officially undefined by the Lua language specification in this case — it might return 2, or 4, or something else, and this can even vary between Lua versions or implementations. **Practical rule: avoid leaving `nil` gaps in array-like tables.** If you need to represent "no value at this array slot," use a dedicated sentinel value instead (a special marker table, or a string like `"__EMPTY__"`), or restructure to avoid gaps entirely, rather than relying on `nil`.

## Copying an array-like table

Assigning a table to another variable does **not** copy it — both variables reference the exact same underlying table (this is covered fully, with the reasoning, in [Nested Tables](/lua/nested-tables/)). To make a genuine, independent copy:

```lua
local function copy_array(t)
    local result = {}
    for i, v in ipairs(t) do
        result[i] = v
    end
    return result
end

local original = {1, 2, 3}
local duplicate = copy_array(original)
duplicate[1] = 99
print(original[1], duplicate[1]) -- 1  99 — genuinely independent
```

Next: [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/).
Tables.Tables as Dictionaries:
The exact same `table` type doubles as a key-value dictionary (equivalent to a Python `dict`, a Rust `HashMap`, or a JavaScript object) — you've already glimpsed this in earlier pages; this page covers it directly.

## Creating a dictionary-like table

```lua
local person = {
    name = "Alice",
    age = 30,
    city = "New York",
}

print(person.name)     -- "Alice" — dot syntax, shorthand for string keys
print(person["age"])    -- 30 — bracket syntax, works for any key type
print(person["city"])    -- "New York"
```

`person.name` is exactly equivalent to `person["name"]` — the dot syntax is convenient shorthand specifically for string keys that are also valid Lua identifiers (no spaces, don't start with a digit, etc.). Bracket syntax is required for keys with spaces, keys that are themselves variables, or non-string keys.

## Keys can be almost any type

```lua
local t = {}
t["a string key"] = 1
t[42] = "a number key"
t[true] = "a boolean key"

local key_var = "dynamic"
t[key_var] = "set via a variable key"

print(t["a string key"])  -- 1
print(t[42])                -- "a number key"
print(t[true])                -- "a boolean key"
print(t["dynamic"])             -- "set via a variable key"
```

The only restriction: a key cannot be `nil` (attempting `t[nil] = value` raises an error), and using `NaN` (not-a-number, from certain floating point operations) as a key produces undefined behavior — beyond those two edge cases, strings, numbers, booleans, tables, and even functions are all valid keys.

## Adding, updating, and removing entries

```lua
local person = {name = "Alice"}

person.age = 30         -- add a new key
person.name = "Alicia"   -- update an existing key
person.age = nil          -- REMOVE the key entirely — assigning nil deletes it
```

**Assigning `nil` to a table key removes that key from the table entirely** — this is a genuinely important and distinctive Lua idiom, different from most languages where you'd call a separate `delete`/`remove`/`del` operation. There's no real distinction in Lua between "a key that doesn't exist" and "a key explicitly set to nil" — both simply return `nil` when read, and both are absent from `pairs()` iteration.

## Checking if a key exists

```lua
local person = {name = "Alice", age = 30}

if person.email then
    print("has an email: " .. person.email)
else
    print("no email set")
end

print(person.email == nil) -- true — the standard way to check for absence
```

Since indexing a missing key simply returns `nil` (never an error, unlike some languages that throw a "key not found" exception), checking for a key's presence and reading its value are effectively the same operation.

## Iterating with pairs

```lua
local person = {name = "Alice", age = 30, city = "NYC"}

for key, value in pairs(person) do
    print(key .. ": " .. tostring(value))
end
-- order NOT guaranteed, as covered in Generic For Loops
```

## Using a table as a lookup/set

A common, idiomatic pattern: use a table's keys purely for fast membership checking, with the values as placeholders (often `true`):

```lua
local valid_statuses = {
    active = true,
    pending = true,
    closed = true,
}

local function is_valid(status)
    return valid_statuses[status] == true
end

print(is_valid("active"))    -- true
print(is_valid("archived"))    -- false
```

This "table as a set" pattern is genuinely idiomatic Lua, directly analogous to Rust's `HashSet` (covered in the Rust guide's [HashMap and HashSet](/rust/hashmap-and-hashset/)) — Lua simply doesn't have a separate set type, so a table with meaningless (or `true`) values fills that role.

Next: [Nested Tables](/lua/nested-tables/).
Tables.Nested Tables:
Tables can contain other tables as values, at any depth — this is how you build more complex data structures: nested objects, trees, JSON-like data, and more.

## Basic nesting

```lua
local company = {
    name = "Acme Corp",
    address = {
        street = "123 Main St",
        city = "Springfield",
        zip = "12345",
    },
    employees = {
        {name = "Alice", role = "Engineer"},
        {name = "Bob", role = "Designer"},
    },
}

print(company.address.city)          -- "Springfield"
print(company.employees[1].name)       -- "Alice"
print(company.employees[2].role)         -- "Designer"
```

## Tables are reference types — a crucial concept to internalize

This is one of the most important things to understand about Lua tables, and it trips up beginners constantly: **assigning a table to a new variable does not copy it.** Both variables end up referencing the exact same underlying table in memory:

```lua
local original = {name = "Alice"}
local alias = original -- alias now refers to the SAME table, not a copy

alias.name = "Bob"
print(original.name) -- "Bob" — the original changed too! They're the same table.
```

This is directly analogous to how objects work in Python, JavaScript, or Java (as opposed to Rust's ownership/move semantics from the Rust guide's [Ownership Rules](/rust/ownership-rules/), or C's value-type structs) — if you're coming from Rust specifically, this is a genuine mental shift: Lua tables behave like shared, mutable references by default, always, with no borrow checker to help you reason about who else might be holding a reference to the same table.

## Passing tables to functions

Because of the above, passing a table to a function does **not** create a copy — the function receives a reference to the same table, and can mutate it, with the changes visible to the caller after the function returns:

```lua
local function add_employee(company, name, role)
    table.insert(company.employees, {name = name, role = role})
end

local company = {employees = {}}
add_employee(company, "Charlie", "Manager")
print(#company.employees) -- 1 — the original table was mutated directly
```

This is often exactly what you want (efficient, no unnecessary copying) but is worth being deliberate about — if you need a function to *not* modify the caller's table, you must explicitly create a copy first (a "deep copy," covered below), since Lua provides no automatic protection here.

## Deep copying nested tables

The simple copy loop from [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) only copies one level deep (a "shallow copy") — nested tables inside it would still be shared references. A genuine deep copy needs to recurse:

```lua
local function deep_copy(original)
    if type(original) ~= "table" then
        return original -- not a table — numbers, strings, etc. are already "copied" by value
    end

    local copy = {}
    for key, value in pairs(original) do
        copy[key] = deep_copy(value) -- recurse for nested tables
    end
    return copy
end

local original = {name = "Alice", address = {city = "NYC"}}
local duplicate = deep_copy(original)

duplicate.address.city = "LA"
print(original.address.city)  -- "NYC" — genuinely unaffected, thanks to the deep copy
print(duplicate.address.city)   -- "LA"
```

## Comparing tables: == checks identity, not contents

```lua
local a = {1, 2, 3}
local b = {1, 2, 3}
local c = a

print(a == b) -- false! Different tables, even with identical contents
print(a == c) -- true — same underlying table
```

`==` on tables checks whether both sides refer to the **exact same table in memory**, not whether their contents happen to match — this is another point where Lua behaves like Java's default `==` on objects, or Python's `is` (rather than `==`), if that comparison helps. Comparing table *contents* for equality requires writing your own recursive comparison function, or using a table library from LuaRocks that provides one.

Next: [Table Library Functions](/lua/table-library-functions/).
Tables.Table Library Functions:
The built-in `table` library provides the standard operations for working with array-like tables. This page is a consolidated reference.

## table.insert and table.remove

```lua
local t = {1, 2, 3}

table.insert(t, 4)         -- append: {1, 2, 3, 4}
table.insert(t, 1, 0)        -- insert at position 1: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}

local removed = table.remove(t)     -- remove and return the LAST element: 4
local first = table.remove(t, 1)      -- remove and return element at position 1: 0

print(table.concat(t, ", ")) -- "1, 2, 3"
```

## table.concat: joining elements into a string

```lua
local words = {"Hello", "from", "Lua"}
print(table.concat(words, " "))     -- "Hello from Lua"
print(table.concat(words))            -- "HellofromLua" — no separator given
print(table.concat(words, ", ", 1, 2)) -- "Hello, from" — join only a sub-range
```

`table.concat` only works on tables containing strings or numbers (it can't concatenate nested tables or other types) — genuinely useful for building CSV lines, joined paths, or simple report output.

## table.sort

```lua
local numbers = {5, 2, 8, 1, 9}
table.sort(numbers) -- sorts in place, ascending by default
print(table.concat(numbers, ", ")) -- "1, 2, 5, 8, 9"

table.sort(numbers, function(a, b) return a > b end) -- custom comparator: descending
print(table.concat(numbers, ", ")) -- "9, 8, 5, 2, 1"

local people = {{name = "Bob", age = 25}, {name = "Alice", age = 30}}
table.sort(people, function(a, b) return a.name < b.name end)
for _, p in ipairs(people) do print(p.name) end -- Alice, then Bob
```

`table.sort` sorts **in place** (mutating the original table directly) and takes an optional comparator function — same pattern as Rust's `.sort_by(...)`, if that's a helpful comparison.

## table.unpack (or unpack, on older Lua versions)

Expands a table's array elements into multiple separate values — the inverse operation of `{...}` packing varargs into a table:

```lua
local coords = {10, 20, 30}
print(table.unpack(coords)) -- 10  20  30, as three separate values

local function sum3(a, b, c) return a + b + c end
print(sum3(table.unpack(coords))) -- 60
```

Note: in Lua 5.1, this function is a plain global `unpack(...)`; from Lua 5.2 onward, it moved to `table.unpack(...)` — if you're targeting an older environment (like some LuaJIT-based hosts, per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), check which form is available.

## table.pack

The inverse: packs multiple values (like varargs) into a table, also storing the count in a `n` field:

```lua
local function pack_args(...)
    return table.pack(...)
end

local result = pack_args(1, 2, 3)
print(result.n)     -- 3
print(result[1])      -- 1
```

## Getting all keys from a dictionary-style table, sorted

A common pattern combining several of the above, useful when `pairs`' unordered iteration isn't acceptable:

```lua
local scores = {Charlie = 85, Alice = 92, Bob = 78}

local names = {}
for name in pairs(scores) do
    table.insert(names, name)
end
table.sort(names)

for _, name in ipairs(names) do
    print(name, scores[name])
end
-- Alice   92
-- Bob     78
-- Charlie 85
```

Next: [Iterating Tables: pairs and ipairs](/lua/iterating-tables-pairs-and-ipairs/).
Tables.Iterating Tables: pairs and ipairs:
This page consolidates everything about table iteration into one clear reference, since it's genuinely one of the most common things you'll do in real Lua programs, and the distinction between the two functions matters.

## The two iteration functions, side by side

```lua
local t = {"a", "b", "c", extra = "dictionary-style value"}

print("--- ipairs ---")
for i, v in ipairs(t) do
    print(i, v)
end
-- 1  a
-- 2  b
-- 3  c
-- (stops here — "extra" is not a sequential integer key, so ipairs never sees it)

print("--- pairs ---")
for k, v in pairs(t) do
    print(k, v)
end
-- 1  a
-- 2  b
-- 3  c
-- extra  dictionary-style value
-- (order among these is NOT guaranteed, except that this is a typical/common result)
```

## Decision guide

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| You know the table is a plain, gapless array/list | `ipairs` |
| You need guaranteed, predictable order | `ipairs` (for arrays) or collect-and-sort keys (for dicts) |
| The table is a dictionary/map with arbitrary keys | `pairs` |
| The table might have both array and dictionary parts, and you need everything | `pairs` |
| Performance-critical iteration of a large array | `ipairs`, or a manual numeric `for i = 1, #t` loop — both are typically faster than `pairs` for pure arrays |

## A manual numeric loop as a third option

```lua
local t = {"a", "b", "c"}

for i = 1, #t do
    print(i, t[i])
end
```

This is functionally equivalent to `ipairs` for a well-formed array (no `nil` holes), and is occasionally preferred in performance-sensitive code (since it avoids the small overhead of calling the `ipairs` iterator function on every step) — but `ipairs` is generally considered more idiomatic and readable for everyday code, and the performance difference is rarely significant enough to matter outside genuinely hot loops.

## Modifying a table while iterating it — a real danger

**Do not add or remove keys from a table while iterating it with `pairs`** — the behavior is undefined by the Lua specification and can cause skipped elements, repeated elements, or outright errors:

```lua
local t = {a = 1, b = 2, c = 3}

-- DON'T do this:
for k, v in pairs(t) do
    if v == 2 then
        t[k] = nil -- modifying the table mid-iteration — undefined behavior!
    end
end
```

**Setting an existing key's value to something other than `nil`** during iteration is safe. **Adding new keys, or removing keys (setting to `nil`),** during iteration is not. The safe pattern is to collect the keys you want to remove first, then remove them in a separate pass after the iteration completes:

```lua
local t = {a = 1, b = 2, c = 3}

local to_remove = {}
for k, v in pairs(t) do
    if v == 2 then
        table.insert(to_remove, k)
    end
end

for _, k in ipairs(to_remove) do
    t[k] = nil -- safe now — this is a separate loop, not modifying during pairs iteration
end

for k, v in pairs(t) do print(k, v) end -- a=1, c=3
```

This wraps up tables — Lua's single most important and distinctive feature. Next: [String Library Basics](/lua/string-library-basics/).

Strings and Patterns.String Library Basics:
The `string` library provides the core operations for working with text. This page covers the everyday, non-pattern-matching functions; Lua's pattern-matching (its regex-like feature) gets its own two pages after this.

## Case conversion and whitespace

```lua
print(string.upper("hello"))  -- "HELLO"
print(string.lower("HELLO"))   -- "hello"

-- method-call syntax (equivalent, more common in practice):
print(("hello"):upper())        -- "HELLO"
local s = "hello"
print(s:upper())                  -- "HELLO"
```

Note that Lua's standard library, unlike many languages, doesn't include a built-in `trim` function for stripping whitespace — the idiomatic way to trim is a pattern-matching one-liner, covered on the pattern-matching pages, or a small helper function you write once and reuse:

```lua
local function trim(s)
    return s:match("^%s*(.-)%s*$")
end

print(trim("   hello world   ") .. "|") -- "hello world|"
```

## Length, substrings, and searching

```lua
local s = "Hello, World!"

print(#s)              -- 13
print(s:len())            -- 13, equivalent to #s
print(s:sub(1, 5))          -- "Hello"
print(s:sub(8))               -- "World!" — from index 8 to the end
print(s:sub(-6))                -- "World!" — negative indices count from the end
print(s:find("World"))            -- 8  12 — start and end positions of the match
print(s:find("xyz"))                -- nil — not found
```

`string.find` returns `nil` (not an error, not `-1`) when the substring isn't present — always check for `nil` before using the result, similar to Lua's general pattern of returning `nil` for "not found" across the standard library, rather than raising exceptions.

## Repeating and reversing

```lua
print(string.rep("ab", 3))       -- "ababab"
print(string.rep("ab", 3, "-"))    -- "ab-ab-ab" — with a separator
print(string.reverse("hello"))       -- "olleh"
```

## Byte/character conversion

```lua
print(string.byte("A"))      -- 65 — the byte value of the first character
print(string.char(65, 66, 67)) -- "ABC" — the inverse: bytes to a string
```

## String formatting with string.format

```lua
print(string.format("Name: %s, Age: %d", "Alice", 30))
-- "Name: Alice, Age: 30"

print(string.format("%.2f", 3.14159))     -- "3.14"
print(string.format("%5d", 42))             -- "   42" — width 5, right-aligned
print(string.format("%-5d|", 42))             -- "42   |" — left-aligned
print(string.format("%05d", 42))                -- "00042" — zero-padded
print(string.format("%x", 255))                   -- "ff" — hexadecimal
```

`string.format` follows the same format-specifier conventions as C's `printf` — if you've used `printf`-style formatting in C, Python (`%` formatting), or many other languages, this will feel immediately familiar. Full formatting coverage is on the next page, [String Formatting](/lua/string-formatting/).

Next: [String Formatting](/lua/string-formatting/).
Strings and Patterns.String Formatting:
## string.format: the full reference

```lua
string.format("%s is %d years old", "Alice", 30)
-- "Alice is 30 years old"
```

## Format specifiers

| Specifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%s` | string (calls `tostring()` on the value automatically) |
| `%d` or `%i` | integer |
| `%f` | floating point |
| `%.Nf` | floating point, N decimal places |
| `%x` / `%X` | hexadecimal (lower/upper case) |
| `%o` | octal |
| `%e` | scientific notation |
| `%g` | shortest of %f/%e that represents the value cleanly |
| `%%` | a literal percent sign |
| `%c` | a character, from its byte value |

```lua
print(string.format("%s", 42))          -- "42" — %s auto-converts non-strings via tostring
print(string.format("Pi is %.4f", math.pi)) -- "Pi is 3.1416"
print(string.format("%x", 255))               -- "ff"
print(string.format("%X", 255))                -- "FF"
print(string.format("100%%"))                    -- "100%"
```

## Width and alignment

```lua
print(string.format("[%10s]", "hi"))    -- "[        hi]" — width 10, right-aligned (default)
print(string.format("[%-10s]", "hi"))     -- "[hi        ]" — left-aligned
print(string.format("[%5d]", 42))           -- "[   42]"
print(string.format("[%-5d]", 42))            -- "[42   ]"
print(string.format("[%05d]", 42))              -- "[00042]" — zero-padded
```

## Building a formatted table/report

A common practical use — aligning columns for readable console output:

```lua
local items = {
    {name = "Widget", price = 9.99, qty = 3},
    {name = "Gadget", price = 24.50, qty = 1},
}

for _, item in ipairs(items) do
    print(string.format("%-10s $%6.2f  x%d", item.name, item.price, item.qty))
end
-- Widget     $  9.99  x3
-- Gadget     $ 24.50  x1
```

## print() vs string.format vs io.write

```lua
print("a", "b", 42)          -- "a\tb\t42\n" — tab-separated, adds a trailing newline automatically,
                                --  and auto-converts every argument via tostring()

io.write("a", "b", 42)          -- "ab42" — NO separators, NO automatic newline, and
                                   --  arguments must already be strings/numbers (no auto-tostring
                                   --  for other types — io.write errors on e.g. a table or nil)

local s = string.format("a=%d, b=%s", 1, "x") -- builds a formatted string, doesn't print at all
print(s)
```

`print` is the quick, convenient choice for debugging and simple output (tab-separated, newline included, forgiving about types). `io.write` gives precise control with no automatic formatting or separators — useful when you need exact output, like building a prompt that shouldn't have a trailing newline (as seen in the Rust guide's io-flushing example, [Reading Input](/lua/reading-and-writing-files/) covers Lua's `io` library fully). `string.format` is for building a formatted string value you'll use elsewhere (store it, concatenate it, write it to a file) rather than print immediately.

Next: [Lua Patterns (Lua's Regex)](/lua/lua-patterns-luas-regex/).
Strings and Patterns.Lua Patterns (Lua's Regex):
Lua does **not** use standard regular expressions (PCRE/POSIX-style, like Rust's `regex` crate from the Rust guide's [regex](/rust/regex/) page). Instead, it has its own, simpler, lighter-weight system called **Lua patterns** — less powerful than full regex in some ways (no true alternation `|`, no general-purpose backreferences), but fast, small, and sufficient for the vast majority of everyday text-processing tasks.

## Character classes

| Class | Matches |
|---|---|
| `.` | any character |
| `%a` | any letter |
| `%d` | any digit |
| `%l` | any lowercase letter |
| `%u` | any uppercase letter |
| `%s` | any whitespace character |
| `%w` | any alphanumeric character |
| `%p` | any punctuation character |
| `%A`, `%D`, `%L`, `%U`, `%S`, `%W`, `%P` | the **complement** (opposite) of the above — e.g. `%A` is "not a letter" |

```lua
print(("hello123"):match("%a+"))  -- "hello" — one or more letters
print(("hello123"):match("%d+"))    -- "123" — one or more digits
```

## Quantifiers

| Quantifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `*` | zero or more (greedy) |
| `+` | one or more (greedy) |
| `-` | zero or more (**lazy/non-greedy** — this is different from most regex flavors, where `-` isn't a quantifier at all!) |
| `?` | zero or one |

```lua
print(("<a><b>"):match("<.*>"))  -- "<a><b>" — greedy: matches as much as possible
print(("<a><b>"):match("<.->"))   -- "<a>" — lazy: matches as little as possible
```

**This is a genuine, important difference from standard regex**: in most regex flavors, `-` isn't a special character at all, and non-greedy matching uses `*?`/`+?` instead. In Lua patterns, `-` itself *is* the lazy/non-greedy version of `*` — there's no separate lazy-quantifier syntax layered on top of `*`/`+`.

## Anchors

```lua
print(("hello"):match("^h"))    -- "h" — ^ anchors to the start of the string
print(("hello"):match("o$"))     -- "o" — $ anchors to the end of the string
print(("hello"):match("^hello$")) -- "hello" — anchored on both ends, matches the whole string
```

## Character sets: [...]

```lua
print(("hello123"):match("[0-9]+"))    -- "123" — a custom character range
print(("hello123"):match("[a-z]+"))      -- "hello"
print(("hello123"):match("[^0-9]+"))       -- "hello" — [^...] negates the set
```

## Capture groups: (...)

```lua
local date = "2024-03-15"
local year, month, day = date:match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)")
print(year, month, day) -- "2024"  "03"  "15"
```

Parentheses in a Lua pattern create a **capture** — when the pattern matches, each captured group is returned as a separate value from `:match(...)`, following the same multiple-return-values mechanics from [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/).

## Escaping special/magic characters

Characters with special meaning in patterns (`. % + - * ? [ ] ^ $ ( )`) need to be escaped with `%` when you want to match them literally:

```lua
print(("3.14"):match("%d+%.%d+"))  -- "3.14" — %. matches a literal dot, not "any character"
print(("100%"):match("%d+%%"))       -- "100%" — %% matches a literal percent sign
```

Next: [gmatch, gsub and find](/lua/gmatch-gsub-and-find/).
Strings and Patterns.gmatch, gsub and find:
The three workhorse pattern-matching functions in the `string` library, building directly on the pattern syntax from the previous page.

## string.match: extracting the first match

```lua
local s = "My email is alice@example.com, contact me there."

local email = s:match("%a+@%a+%.%a+")
print(email) -- "alice@example.com"

local year, month, day = ("2024-03-15"):match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)")
print(year, month, day) -- "2024"  "03"  "15"
```

`:match(pattern)` finds the **first** match and returns it — or, if the pattern has capture groups (parentheses), returns each captured group as a separate value instead of the whole match. Returns `nil` if there's no match at all.

## string.gmatch: iterating over every match

```lua
local s = "cat, dog, bird, fish"

for word in s:gmatch("%a+") do
    print(word)
end
-- cat
-- dog
-- bird
-- fish
```

`:gmatch(pattern)` returns an **iterator function** suitable for a generic `for` loop (the same protocol as `pairs`/`ipairs`, covered in [Generic For Loops](/lua/generic-for-loops/)) — it yields each successive match in turn, which makes it the idiomatic choice for "find every occurrence" tasks.

```lua
local csv_line = "Alice,30,Engineer"
local fields = {}
for field in csv_line:gmatch("[^,]+") do
    table.insert(fields, field)
end
print(table.concat(fields, " | ")) -- "Alice | 30 | Engineer"
```

`[^,]+` — "one or more characters that are NOT a comma" — is a common and genuinely useful idiom for simple, naive CSV-style splitting (it doesn't handle quoted fields containing commas; for real CSV parsing, use a proper library, as covered in [Popular Lua Libraries](/lua/popular-lua-libraries/)).

## string.gsub: search and replace

```lua
local s = "Hello, World!"

local result = s:gsub("World", "Lua")
print(result) -- "Hello, Lua!"

local count
result, count = s:gsub("o", "0")
print(result, count) -- "Hell0, W0rld!"  2
```

`:gsub(pattern, replacement)` returns **two** values: the resulting string, and the number of replacements made — a common gotcha is forgetting the second return value is there, which usually doesn't cause a bug (since extra return values in a non-final position are simply discarded, per [Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/)) but is worth knowing about.

## gsub with capture-group references in the replacement

```lua
local s = "John Smith"
local result = s:gsub("(%a+) (%a+)", "%2 %1") -- swap first and last name
print(result) -- "Smith John"

local s2 = "price: 100"
local result2 = s2:gsub("(%d+)", function(n) -- replacement can also be a FUNCTION
    return tostring(tonumber(n) * 2)
end)
print(result2) -- "price: 200"
```

`%1`, `%2` in a `gsub` replacement string refer to captured groups, similar to Rust's regex crate's `$1`/`$2` syntax from the Rust guide's [regex](/rust/regex/) page. The replacement can also be a function, called with each match's captures as arguments, returning the string to substitute — extremely flexible for anything beyond simple literal substitution.

## A practical trim function, explained

Returning to the `trim` helper from the previous page:

```lua
local function trim(s)
    return s:match("^%s*(.-)%s*$")
end
```

Reading this pattern piece by piece: `^%s*` (skip leading whitespace) `(.-)` (lazily capture everything in between — as little as possible) `%s*$` (skip trailing whitespace, anchored to the end). The laziness of `.-` is essential here — a greedy `.* ` would try to capture as much as possible, potentially swallowing trailing whitespace into the capture instead of leaving it to be matched (and discarded) by the final `%s*$`.

This wraps up strings and patterns. Next: [What Are Metatables](/lua/what-are-metatables/) — Lua's mechanism for customizing table behavior.

Metatables and OOP.What Are Metatables:
**Metatables** are Lua's mechanism for customizing how a table behaves — enabling operator overloading, inheritance, custom indexing behavior, and ultimately, object-oriented programming, all built on top of Lua's one basic data structure with no additional syntax needed at the language level.

## The basic idea

Every table can have an associated **metatable** — itself just a regular table — containing special keys (called **metamethods**, always starting with two underscores, like `__index` or `__add`) that tell Lua how to handle certain operations on the original table.

```lua
local t = {1, 2, 3}
print(getmetatable(t)) -- nil — a plain table has no metatable by default

local mt = {} -- an empty table, which we'll use as a metatable
setmetatable(t, mt)
print(getmetatable(t) == mt) -- true
```

By itself, an empty metatable changes nothing — metatables only affect behavior once you populate them with specific metamethod keys, covered starting on this page and continuing through the next few.

## __tostring: customizing how a table prints

A simple, illustrative first metamethod:

```lua
local point = {x = 3, y = 4}

print(point) -- something like "table: 0x55b8f2a1c3d0" — not very useful!

setmetatable(point, {
    __tostring = function(self)
        return "(" .. self.x .. ", " .. self.y .. ")"
    end
})

print(point) -- "(3, 4)" — print() calls tostring() internally, which checks for __tostring
print(tostring(point)) -- "(3, 4)" — same effect, called explicitly
```

`__tostring` is checked automatically by both `print()` and `tostring()` whenever they're given a table that has it defined — this is directly analogous to implementing Rust's `Display` trait (from the Rust guide's [String Formatting](/rust/string-formatting/) page) to customize how a type prints.

## __index: the most important metamethod

This is the metamethod that enables inheritance (covered fully on the next page) — when you access a key on a table that **doesn't exist**, Lua checks the table's metatable for an `__index` entry before giving up and returning `nil`:

```lua
local defaults = {color = "black", size = "medium"}

local shirt = {size = "large"} -- shirt only specifies "size"
setmetatable(shirt, {__index = defaults})

print(shirt.size)   -- "large" — found directly on shirt itself
print(shirt.color)    -- "black" — NOT found on shirt, so Lua checks the metatable's __index
```

When `shirt.color` is accessed, Lua first checks `shirt` directly — it's not there, so it then checks the metatable's `__index`, finds `defaults`, and looks up `color` there instead, finding `"black"`. This single mechanism is the foundation for everything covered in [__index and Inheritance](/lua/__index-and-inheritance/) and [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/).

## rawget and rawset: bypassing metamethods

```lua
local t = setmetatable({}, {__index = function() return "default" end})

print(t.anything)          -- "default" — goes through __index
print(rawget(t, "anything")) -- nil — bypasses the metatable entirely, checks t directly
```

Useful occasionally for debugging, or for implementing metamethods themselves without infinite recursion (covered in the next page's inheritance chains).

Next: [Operator Overloading With Metamethods](/lua/operator-overloading-with-metamethods/).
Metatables and OOP.Operator Overloading With Metamethods:
Just like Rust's `std::ops::Add` trait (from the Rust guide's [Operator Overloading](/rust/operator-overloading/) page), Lua lets you customize what operators like `+`, `-`, `==`, and `<` do on your own tables — via metamethods.

## Overloading + with __add

```lua
local Vector = {}
Vector.__index = Vector

local function new_vector(x, y)
    return setmetatable({x = x, y = y}, Vector)
end

Vector.__add = function(a, b)
    return new_vector(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y)
end

Vector.__tostring = function(v)
    return "(" .. v.x .. ", " .. v.y .. ")"
end

local v1 = new_vector(1, 2)
local v2 = new_vector(3, 4)
local v3 = v1 + v2 -- calls Vector.__add(v1, v2) automatically

print(v3) -- "(4, 6)"
```

Writing `v1 + v2` automatically looks for an `__add` metamethod on `v1`'s (or, if not found there, `v2`'s) metatable and calls it — exactly the same principle as Rust's operator traits, just achieved through metatables instead of a trait system.

## The full set of arithmetic and comparison metamethods

| Metamethod | Operator |
|---|---|
| `__add` | `+` |
| `__sub` | `-` |
| `__mul` | `*` |
| `__div` | `/` |
| `__mod` | `%` |
| `__pow` | `^` |
| `__unm` | unary `-` (negation) |
| `__concat` | `..` |
| `__len` | `#` |
| `__eq` | `==` |
| `__lt` | `<` |
| `__le` | `<=` |

```lua
Vector.__eq = function(a, b)
    return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y
end

Vector.__lt = function(a, b)
    return (a.x^2 + a.y^2) < (b.x^2 + b.y^2) -- compare by magnitude
end

local v1 = new_vector(1, 1)
local v2 = new_vector(1, 1)
print(v1 == v2) -- true — calls Vector.__eq, since both are tables with the SAME metatable

local v3 = new_vector(5, 5)
print(v1 < v3) -- true — calls Vector.__lt
```

**Important caveat on `__eq`**: it's only invoked when comparing two values that are **both tables** and share the **same metatable** — comparing a `Vector` to a plain table, or to a number, never triggers `__eq` at all; `==` on mismatched types simply returns `false` immediately, per the rules from [The type Function and Type Coercion](/lua/the-type-function-and-type-coercion/).

## __concat: customizing string concatenation

```lua
Vector.__concat = function(a, b)
    local a_str = (type(a) == "table") and tostring(a) or tostring(a)
    local b_str = (type(b) == "table") and tostring(b) or tostring(b)
    return a_str .. b_str
end

local v = new_vector(1, 2)
print("Vector: " .. v) -- "Vector: (1, 2)" — calls __concat
```

## __call: making a table callable like a function

```lua
local callable = setmetatable({}, {
    __call = function(self, ...)
        print("called with:", ...)
    end
})

callable(1, 2, 3) -- "called with:  1  2  3" — the table itself is invoked as if it were a function
```

This is genuinely useful for building objects that should behave like functions — for example, a "class" table that's called directly to construct new instances, a common pattern covered in the next page's inheritance material.

Metatables and OOP.__index and Inheritance:
Building on the `__index` basics from the first page of this section, this page covers **inheritance** — building a chain of "fallback" tables, similar in spirit to prototype chains in JavaScript.

## __index as a table vs a function

`__index` can be either a table (as seen previously — a simple "look here next" fallback) or a **function** (for computed/dynamic fallback logic):

```lua
local t = setmetatable({}, {
    __index = function(table, key)
        return "no value for '" .. key .. "'"
    end
})

print(t.anything) -- "no value for 'anything'" — the function is called with (table, key)
```

Function-form `__index` is powerful (it can compute a value dynamically, log access, or even generate lazily), but for straightforward inheritance, table-form `__index` (as below) is far more common and simpler.

## A multi-level inheritance chain

```lua
local Animal = {}
Animal.__index = Animal

function Animal.new(name)
    return setmetatable({name = name}, Animal)
end

function Animal:speak()
    print(self.name .. " makes a sound")
end

local Dog = setmetatable({}, {__index = Animal}) -- Dog "inherits" from Animal
Dog.__index = Dog

function Dog.new(name)
    local self = Animal.new(name)   -- reuse Animal's constructor logic
    return setmetatable(self, Dog)   -- but set the metatable to Dog, not Animal
end

function Dog:speak() -- Dog OVERRIDES Animal's speak method
    print(self.name .. " barks")
end

local generic_animal = Animal.new("Generic Animal")
local rex = Dog.new("Rex")

generic_animal:speak() -- "Generic Animal makes a sound"
rex:speak()               -- "Rex barks" — Dog's own speak, found directly on Dog
```

## Following the lookup chain for an inherited (non-overridden) method

Suppose `Dog` *hadn't* defined its own `speak`. Here's exactly what happens when you call `rex:speak()`:

1. Lua looks for `speak` directly on `rex` (the instance table) — not found.
2. Lua checks `rex`'s metatable's `__index`, which is `Dog` — checks `Dog.speak` — not found (in this hypothetical where Dog doesn't override it).
3. Lua checks `Dog`'s **own** metatable's `__index` (remember, `Dog` itself was created with `setmetatable({}, {__index = Animal})`) — which is `Animal` — checks `Animal.speak` — **found!**

This chain can extend to any depth — `Dog` could have a `Puppy` "subclass" set up the same way, extending the chain further. This mechanism (a table's metatable's `__index` pointing to another table, which might itself have its own metatable pointing further up) is genuinely how essentially every Lua OOP library and framework implements inheritance under the hood — there's no separate, built-in "class" or "extends" keyword in the language; it's entirely built from metatables.

## Why self:speak() needs self.name, not just name

Recall from [Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/) that colon syntax (`function Dog:speak()`) is shorthand for an implicit first `self` parameter. Every method needs to reference instance-specific data through `self` explicitly — there's no implicit "current object" scope the way `this`/`self` might work automatically in some other languages; `self` is just a regular, explicitly-passed parameter that happens to be populated automatically by colon-call syntax.

The next page assembles all of this into a clean, reusable pattern for defining classes, and the page after that walks through a complete, realistic example.

Metatables and OOP.Object-Oriented Programming in Lua:
This page consolidates the previous pages' metatable mechanics into the **standard, idiomatic pattern** for defining a "class" in Lua — a pattern you'll recognize (with minor variations) across essentially every Lua codebase and library that uses OOP.

## The standard class pattern

```lua
-- 1. Define the "class" as a table
local Animal = {}
Animal.__index = Animal -- CRUCIAL: this makes Animal act as its own __index fallback

-- 2. A constructor function
function Animal.new(name, sound)
    local self = setmetatable({}, Animal) -- new instance, with Animal as its metatable
    self.name = name
    self.sound = sound
    return self
end

-- 3. Methods, using colon syntax
function Animal:make_sound()
    print(self.name .. " says " .. self.sound)
end

function Animal:get_name()
    return self.name
end

-- Usage:
local cat = Animal.new("Whiskers", "Meow")
cat:make_sound() -- "Whiskers says Meow"
print(cat:get_name()) -- "Whiskers"
```

The key line to understand deeply is `Animal.__index = Animal` — this makes `Animal` serve as its own fallback table. When you call `cat:make_sound()`, Lua looks for `make_sound` on `cat` itself (not found — `cat` only has `name` and `sound`), then checks `cat`'s metatable (which is `Animal`) for `__index`, finds it's `Animal` itself, and looks up `make_sound` there — found.

## Why setmetatable(self, Animal) and not something else

`setmetatable({}, Animal)` sets `Animal` *itself* (not `{__index = Animal}`) as the new instance's metatable — this works specifically *because* `Animal.__index = Animal` was set up in step 2. Lua's metatable lookup mechanism specifically checks the metatable's `__index` field, and since `Animal.__index` points back to `Animal`, using `Animal` directly as the metatable achieves the same effect as the more verbose `{__index = Animal}` would, while also allowing `Animal` to hold its own metamethods (like `__tostring`, `__add`) directly alongside its regular methods, all in one place.

## Adding inheritance to this pattern

```lua
local function class(parent)
    local cls = {}
    cls.__index = cls
    if parent then
        setmetatable(cls, {__index = parent})
    end
    return cls
end

local Animal = class()
function Animal.new(name)
    return setmetatable({name = name}, Animal)
end
function Animal:speak()
    print(self.name .. " makes a sound")
end

local Dog = class(Animal) -- Dog inherits from Animal
function Dog.new(name)
    local self = Animal.new(name)
    return setmetatable(self, Dog)
end
function Dog:speak()
    print(self.name .. " barks")
end

local rex = Dog.new("Rex")
rex:speak() -- "Rex barks"
```

This small `class(parent)` helper function is a common pattern to reduce the boilerplate of the manual `__index` wiring — many real Lua projects define a helper close to this (or pull in a small library that does, like `middleclass` or `classic`, mentioned in [Popular Lua Libraries](/lua/popular-lua-libraries/)) rather than writing the raw metatable code inline every time.

## When (not) to reach for OOP in Lua

Lua's flexibility means OOP is a genuine, well-supported *option*, not a requirement the way it is in Java — plenty of idiomatic Lua code is written in a plainer, more functional or table-of-functions style (a "module," covered in [Writing a Module](/lua/writing-a-module/)) without ever using metatables or `self` at all. Reach for the class pattern on this page when you genuinely need multiple independent instances sharing behavior (many `Dog`s, many game entities, many UI widgets) — for a single, unique piece of functionality (a math utility module, a config loader), a plain table of functions is usually simpler and just as idiomatic.
