LuaRocks and Packages.Publishing Your Own Rock:
Publishing a Lua library to LuaRocks makes it installable by anyone via `luarocks install your_package` — the Lua equivalent of the Rust guide's [Publishing to crates.io](/rust/publishing-to-crates-io/) page.

## The rockspec file

Every LuaRocks package needs a **rockspec** — a Lua file describing the package's metadata, dependencies, and how to build it:

```lua
-- my_library-1.0-1.rockspec
package = "my_library"
version = "1.0-1"

source = {
    url = "git+https://github.com/you/my_library.git",
    tag = "v1.0",
}

description = {
    summary = "A short, one-line description of what this does.",
    detailed = "A longer, more detailed description.",
    homepage = "https://github.com/you/my_library",
    license = "MIT",
}

dependencies = {
    "lua >= 5.1",
}

build = {
    type = "builtin",
    modules = {
        my_library = "src/my_library.lua",
        ["my_library.utils"] = "src/utils.lua",
    },
}
```

## Understanding the version naming convention

Rockspec filenames follow `package-version-revision.rockspec` — the `version` corresponds to your library's actual release version, and the `revision` (the final `-1`, `-2`, etc.) is incremented if you need to fix the **rockspec itself** (a build script bug, a metadata typo) without releasing a genuinely new version of the underlying code.

## The build.modules mapping

The `modules` table maps each **module name** (what users will `require(...)`) to its **source file path** — this is what makes `require("my_library.utils")` correctly find `src/utils.lua`, regardless of your actual folder layout, decoupling the public module naming from your internal file organization.

## Testing your rockspec locally before publishing

```bash
luarocks make my_library-1.0-1.rockspec   # builds and installs FROM the local rockspec
lua -e "print(require('my_library'))"       # verify it works
luarocks remove my_library                    # clean up the test install
```

## Getting an API key and publishing

1. Create an account at `luarocks.org`.
2. Go to your account settings and generate an API key.
3. Configure the key locally:

```bash
luarocks upload my_library-1.0-1.rockspec --api-key=YOUR_KEY
```

`luarocks upload` builds the rock from your rockspec and uploads it directly — after a short processing delay, it becomes installable by anyone via `luarocks install my_library`.

## Publishing a new version

Create a new rockspec file with the updated version number (`my_library-1.1-1.rockspec`), update the `source.tag` to point at the new release tag in your repository, and upload again — LuaRocks keeps every published version available (similar to crates.io's permanence, from the Rust guide's [Publishing to crates.io](/rust/publishing-to-crates-io/) page), so users can pin to a specific older version if needed.

## A note on rockspec source options

The `source.url` above used a git tag; LuaRocks also supports plain `.tar.gz`/`.zip` archive URLs, or even a local directory during development (`source = { url = "file://./" }` — mainly useful for the local testing step above, not for actual publishing).

This wraps up LuaRocks and packages. Next: [Why Embed Lua](/lua/why-embed-lua/).

Embedding and C Interop.Why Embed Lua:
As noted back in [What Is Lua](/lua/what-is-lua/), embeddability is Lua's core design purpose — this page explains *why* embedding is valuable and what it actually looks like conceptually, before the next two pages get into real code.

## What "embedding" means

Embedding Lua means taking the Lua interpreter (a small, self-contained C library) and linking it directly into your own application, written in C, C++, or another language with C interop — your application becomes the "host," and Lua becomes a scripting layer inside it, with your host code controlling exactly what Lua scripts are allowed to see and do.

## Why embed a scripting language at all

- **Letting non-programmers (or less-technical team members) customize behavior** without recompiling the host application — a game designer can tweak enemy AI behavior in a `.lua` file and see changes immediately, without waiting for a programmer to rebuild the entire game engine.
- **Safe, sandboxable extensibility** — a host application can expose only a carefully chosen, limited set of functions to Lua scripts, meaning user-provided or mod-provided Lua code can't do anything the host hasn't explicitly allowed (no arbitrary file access, no arbitrary network access, unless the host specifically exposes those).
- **Fast iteration** — changing a Lua script and re-running it is close to instant, compared to a full C/C++ recompile — genuinely valuable during game development, where designers iterate on behavior constantly.
- **A small footprint** — unlike embedding, say, a full Python interpreter, Lua's reference implementation is famously tiny (the entire interpreter is often under a megabyte), making it practical even for resource-constrained environments.

## The two directions of interaction

Embedding Lua involves communication in **both** directions, each covered on the following pages:

1. **C calling Lua** ([Calling Lua From C: the Basics](/lua/calling-lua-from-c-the-basics/)) — your host application loads and runs a Lua script, and calls specific Lua functions from your C code (e.g., "call the `on_player_death` function defined in this mod's Lua script").
2. **Lua calling C** ([Calling C From Lua](/lua/calling-c-from-lua/)) — you expose specific C functions to Lua scripts, so Lua code can call back into your host application (e.g., a Lua script calls a `spawn_enemy(x, y)` function that's actually implemented in your game engine's C code).

## The C API: Lua's core embedding mechanism

All of this communication happens through Lua's **C API** — a set of C functions (all prefixed `lua_`, like `lua_pushnumber`, `lua_pcall`, `lua_gettop`) that manipulate a **stack**-based interface between C and Lua. Every value passed between the two languages goes through this stack — this design (rather than, say, directly mapping C structs to Lua tables) is deliberately simple and consistent, though it does take some getting used to if you're used to more "direct" language interop mechanisms.

## When you'd actually write this code yourself

If you're using Lua purely as an end-user scripter — writing Neovim configs, WoW addons, or Love2D game logic — you'll likely never touch the C API directly at all; the host application (Neovim, WoW, Love2D) has already done this embedding work for you, and simply exposes a rich Lua API for you to call. The next two pages are relevant specifically if you're building the **host** application yourself (writing a C/C++ program that embeds Lua as its own scripting layer) — a more advanced, but genuinely common and valuable skill in game development and systems programming contexts.

Next: [Calling Lua From C: the Basics](/lua/calling-lua-from-c-the-basics/).
Embedding and C Interop.LuaJIT and FFI:
**LuaJIT**, briefly introduced in [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/), offers a dramatically simpler alternative to the manual C API registration shown on the previous pages, for one specific, common use case: calling existing C library functions directly from Lua.

## The FFI library

LuaJIT's built-in `ffi` library lets Lua code declare a C function's signature and call it **directly** — no C wrapper code, no `luaL_Reg` registration tables, no manual stack manipulation at all:

```lua
local ffi = require("ffi")

ffi.cdef[[
    int printf(const char *fmt, ...);
    double sqrt(double x);
]]

ffi.C.printf("Hello from C's printf, called directly from Lua!\n")
print(ffi.C.sqrt(16.0)) -- 4.0
```

`ffi.cdef[[...]]` takes a C declaration (literally just the function signatures, as they'd appear in a C header file) and makes the corresponding functions available under `ffi.C`. This works because LuaJIT can call into **any** C function whose signature you declare this way — no wrapper code needs to be written or compiled at all, since LuaJIT's FFI generates the necessary calling code dynamically, at runtime.

## Loading a specific shared library

```lua
local ffi = require("ffi")

ffi.cdef[[
    typedef struct { double x, y; } Point;
    double distance(Point a, Point b);
]]

local mylib = ffi.load("mylib") -- loads libmylib.so (Linux) / mylib.dll (Windows)

local p1 = ffi.new("Point", {x = 0, y = 0})
local p2 = ffi.new("Point", {x = 3, y = 4})

print(mylib.distance(p1, p2)) -- calls the C function directly, e.g. 5.0
```

`ffi.new("Point", {...})` creates a genuine, correctly-laid-out C struct instance directly from Lua — this is a level of low-level interop the standard C API from the previous two pages simply doesn't offer without substantial manual wrapper code.

## FFI vs the traditional C API: when to use which

| | Traditional C API (`lua_pushnumber`, etc.) | LuaJIT FFI |
|---|---|---|
| Requires writing/compiling C wrapper code | Yes, for every exposed function | No — just declare the signature in Lua |
| Works with standard PUC-Lua (5.1-5.4) | Yes | No — **LuaJIT only** |
| Best for | Building a host application FROM SCRATCH that embeds Lua as its scripting layer | Calling into EXISTING C libraries from Lua scripts, with minimal glue code |
| Performance | Good | Often better — LuaJIT's JIT compiler can inline and optimize FFI calls aggressively |

**The critical caveat**: FFI is a **LuaJIT-specific** feature — it does not exist in standard PUC-Rio Lua (the reference implementation covered throughout most of this guide) at all. If you're targeting standard Lua 5.1-5.4 (which is what you get from the installation instructions in [Installing Lua on Linux](/lua/installing-lua-on-linux/)/[Installing Lua on Windows](/lua/installing-lua-on-windows/)), FFI simply isn't available, and the traditional C API from the previous pages is your only option for C interop. Check which Lua implementation your target environment actually uses (per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)) before relying on FFI in any code you intend to share.

## Why this matters for game development specifically

Many game engines that embed **LuaJIT** specifically (rather than standard Lua) do so partly *because* of FFI — it enables extremely fast, low-overhead communication between game logic (often in Lua, for iteration speed) and performance-critical engine internals (in C/C++), without the overhead of the traditional stack-based C API for every single call.

This wraps up embedding and C interop. Next: [Running and Debugging Scripts](/lua/running-and-debugging-scripts/).

Tooling and Building.Running and Debugging Scripts:
## Debugging with print statements

The simplest, most universal debugging tool in Lua — as in most scripting languages — is strategic use of `print`:

```lua
local function calculate(x, y)
    print("DEBUG: calculate called with x=" .. tostring(x) .. " y=" .. tostring(y))
    local result = x * y + 10
    print("DEBUG: result=" .. tostring(result))
    return result
end
```

## A cleaner debug-printing helper

```lua
local DEBUG = true

local function dbg(...)
    if DEBUG then
        print("[DEBUG]", ...)
    end
end

dbg("calculating with", 5, 10)
```

Wrapping debug output in a helper like this, gated by a single toggleable flag, makes it trivial to silence all debug output at once (set `DEBUG = false`) without deleting or commenting out every individual print statement — genuinely useful as a project grows.

## Pretty-printing tables

Lua's `print(some_table)` just shows a memory address, not the table's actual contents — a small recursive pretty-printer is a near-universal utility every Lua developer eventually writes or borrows:

```lua
local function dump(value, indent)
    indent = indent or ""
    if type(value) == "table" then
        print(indent .. "{")
        for k, v in pairs(value) do
            io.write(indent .. "  " .. tostring(k) .. " = ")
            if type(v) == "table" then
                print()
                dump(v, indent .. "    ")
            else
                print(tostring(v))
            end
        end
        print(indent .. "}")
    else
        print(indent .. tostring(value))
    end
end

dump({name = "Alice", address = {city = "NYC", zip = "10001"}})
```

For a more robust version, the `inspect.lua` library (a single-file, widely-used LuaRocks package) is a common drop-in choice rather than maintaining your own.

## The debug library

Lua's built-in `debug` library provides lower-level introspection tools:

```lua
local function level_two()
    print(debug.traceback("here's where we are:"))
end

local function level_one()
    level_two()
end

level_one()
```

```lua
-- getting information about the currently executing function:
local function my_function()
    local info = debug.getinfo(1, "Sl") -- "S" = source info, "l" = current line
    print(info.source, info.currentline)
end
```

`debug.traceback()` is especially useful combined with `xpcall` (from [pcall and xpcall](/lua/pcall-and-xpcall/)) for getting a full call stack when an error occurs, rather than just the error message alone.

## Using a real debugger

For anything beyond simple print-debugging, **ZeroBrane Studio** (mentioned in [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/)) includes a genuine breakpoint-based debugger with variable inspection, step-through execution, and watch expressions — a substantial step up from print-debugging for tracking down a tricky bug, and specifically built with Lua (and several game engines' Lua environments) in mind. VS Code, with the "Local Lua Debugger" extension, offers similar breakpoint debugging for standalone Lua scripts.

Next: [Packaging a Standalone Executable](/lua/packaging-a-standalone-executable/).
Tooling and Building.Packaging a Standalone Executable:
Unlike Rust (where `cargo build --release` naturally produces a single native executable, as covered in the Rust guide's [Distributing Binaries](/rust/distributing-binaries/) page), Lua is an interpreted language by default — running a `.lua` file requires the Lua interpreter to already be installed on the target machine. This page covers the common approaches for distributing a Lua program to users who might not have Lua installed at all.

## Approach 1: bundling multiple files into one, with luastatic or a manual concat

For a simple multi-file script, the crudest but genuinely effective approach is concatenating everything into one file (handling `require` calls manually or via a bundler), so the recipient only needs one `.lua` file plus a Lua interpreter:

```bash
luarocks install luastatic
```

`luastatic` goes further — it produces a genuine **standalone native executable** by statically linking your Lua script(s) together with the Lua interpreter itself and any pure-Lua dependencies:

```bash
luastatic main.lua /usr/lib/liblua5.4.a -I/usr/include/lua5.4
```

The resulting binary requires **no Lua installation at all** on the machine running it — the interpreter itself is baked directly into the executable, similar in spirit to how a Rust binary needs no separate runtime (from the Rust guide's [Distributing Binaries](/rust/distributing-binaries/) page).

## Approach 2: srlua

**srlua** is an older, simpler, widely-used tool for exactly this purpose — it "glues" a precompiled Lua script (via `luac`, from [The lua and luac Commands](/lua/the-lua-and-luac-commands/)) onto a small stub executable:

```bash
luac -o script.luac script.lua
srlua glue script.luac my_program        # Linux
srlua glue script.luac my_program.exe      # Windows
```

The result is a single native executable that runs your script directly, with no separate Lua installation required by the end user.

## Approach 3: distributing the interpreter alongside your script

The simplest option of all — since Lua's interpreter itself is tiny (often under a megabyte), some projects simply bundle the appropriate platform's `lua`/`lua.exe` binary alongside their `.lua` script files in a folder, with a small launcher script or shortcut that invokes `lua main.lua`. This avoids any special tooling, at the cost of shipping multiple files instead of one clean executable.

## Choosing between these approaches

| Approach | Result | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Plain `.lua` file(s) | Requires Lua installed on the target machine | Scripts for developers, or environments where Lua is already guaranteed present (game mods, Neovim configs) |
| `luastatic` | A single native executable, no Lua needed | Distributing a genuine standalone CLI tool to end users |
| `srlua` | A single native executable, no Lua needed | Similar to luastatic, an older/simpler alternative |
| Bundled interpreter + scripts | Multiple files, no compilation needed | Quick, low-effort distribution when a folder is acceptable |

For most learning projects and personal scripts, plain `.lua` files (run with an already-installed `lua` command) are completely sufficient — reach for `luastatic`/`srlua` specifically when you're distributing a tool to people who shouldn't need to install Lua themselves.

Tooling and Building.Using Lua With Game Engines:
Since game development is one of Lua's most prominent real-world use cases (as noted in [What Is Lua](/lua/what-is-lua/)), this page gives a practical overview of how Lua scripting typically looks within several popular engines — useful context if you're heading in that direction after this guide.

## Love2D: Lua as the entire game logic layer

**Love2D** (often styled LÖVE) is a lightweight, open-source 2D game framework where Lua isn't just a scripting *add-on* — it's the primary language for the entire game:

```lua
-- main.lua
function love.load()
    player = {x = 400, y = 300, speed = 200}
end

function love.update(dt)
    if love.keyboard.isDown("right") then
        player.x = player.x + player.speed * dt
    end
end

function love.draw()
    love.graphics.circle("fill", player.x, player.y, 20)
end
```

`love.load`, `love.update`, `love.draw` are specific callback function names the Love2D engine (itself written in C++, with Lua embedded via the C API from [Calling C From Lua](/lua/calling-c-from-lua/)) calls automatically at the right moments — a concrete, practical example of the host-application-calls-into-Lua pattern from the previous section, but experienced entirely from the Lua side, with none of the C glue code visible to you as a game developer.

## Roblox: Luau, a modified Lua dialect

Roblox uses **Luau**, a heavily modified, gradually-typed dialect derived from Lua 5.1, adding optional static type annotations, additional standard library functions, and various performance/safety improvements specific to Roblox's needs:

```lua
-- Luau supports optional type annotations, NOT part of standard Lua
local function greet(name: string): string
    return "Hello, " .. name .. "!"
end

local part = Instance.new("Part") -- Roblox-specific API, not standard Lua at all
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
```

If you're specifically developing for Roblox, treat this guide's core language material (syntax, tables, functions, control flow) as directly applicable — Luau remains very close to Lua at its core — but expect Roblox-specific APIs (`Instance.new`, services like `game.Workspace`) and Luau's added type-annotation syntax to require Roblox's own documentation specifically, since neither is part of standard Lua.

## World of Warcraft addons

WoW's addon API exposes a large, WoW-specific set of global functions and events, with standard Lua as the underlying scripting language:

```lua
local frame = CreateFrame("Frame")
frame:RegisterEvent("PLAYER_LOGIN")
frame:SetScript("OnEvent", function(self, event)
    print("Player has logged in!")
end)
```

Again, the core Lua (variables, functions, tables, the event-callback pattern) is exactly what this guide has covered — `CreateFrame`, `RegisterEvent`, and the rest are WoW's own API surface, learned from Blizzard's addon documentation and the addon-developer community, not from a general Lua resource.

## Defold, Corona/Solar2D, and others

Several other game engines and frameworks (Defold, the now-community-maintained Solar2D, and various others) follow a broadly similar pattern: standard (or near-standard) Lua as the scripting language, plus an engine-specific API surface for graphics, physics, input, and audio. The practical takeaway across all of these: **this guide gives you the Lua language itself, which transfers directly** — but every engine layers its own substantial API on top, which you'll learn from that engine's specific documentation once you've picked one to specialize in.

Tooling and Building.Style Guide and Linting:
## luacheck: Lua's standard static analysis linter

Similar in purpose to Rust's `clippy` (from the Rust guide's [clippy and rustfmt](/rust/clippy-and-rustfmt/) page), **luacheck** analyzes Lua code for common mistakes without actually running it — catching things like unused variables, undefined globals (a direct, automated check against the "forgot `local`" gotcha from [Useful Idioms and Gotchas](/lua/useful-idioms-and-gotchas/)), and shadowed variables.

```bash
luarocks install luacheck
```

```bash
luacheck my_script.lua
luacheck src/                # check an entire directory
```

```
src/main.lua:5:1: unused variable 'temp'
src/main.lua:12:5: accessing undefined variable 'countt'  -- catches a likely typo!
```

That second warning is genuinely valuable — a typo like `countt` instead of `count` silently creates (or reads) a stray global variable in plain Lua, with no error at all, but `luacheck` flags it immediately as a likely mistake, precisely the class of bug the "always use local" advice from [Variables and Scope](/lua/variables-and-scope/) is meant to prevent.

## Configuring luacheck

A `.luacheckrc` file at your project root customizes its behavior — commonly used to declare known globals (like `love` in a Love2D project, or WoW's addon API globals) that would otherwise be incorrectly flagged as undefined:

```lua
-- .luacheckrc
std = "lua54" -- target Lua 5.4's standard library

globals = {
    "love", -- allow Love2D's global "love" table without a warning
}

max_line_length = 100
```

## StyLua: automated formatting, revisited

As introduced in [Your Editor Setup](/lua/your-editor-setup/), **StyLua** is the closest Lua equivalent to Rust's `rustfmt` — an opinionated, automatic formatter with minimal configuration:

```bash
stylua src/                   # format an entire directory in place
stylua --check src/             # check without modifying (for CI)
```

```toml
# stylua.toml — minimal customization, most projects use the defaults
column_width = 100
indent_type = "Spaces"
indent_width = 4
```

## A common style guide summary (community conventions)

Beyond what StyLua enforces automatically, these conventions are close to universal across idiomatic Lua codebases:

- **`local` by default, always** — the single most important habit, repeated throughout this guide for good reason.
- **snake_case** for variables/functions, **PascalCase** for "class" tables, **SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE** for genuine constants.
- **Prefer `ipairs` for arrays, `pairs` for dictionaries** — using the right one signals intent to readers, beyond just correctness.
- **Avoid deeply nested tables where a flatter structure works** — Lua's dynamic nature makes deeply nested access (`a.b.c.d.e`) error-prone, since any missing intermediate key produces a runtime error trying to index `nil`.
- **Document module public APIs with a comment block at the top of the file** — since Lua has no formal doc-comment standard the way Rust's `///` (from the Rust guide's [Comments and Formatting](/rust/comments-and-formatting/) page) does, a plain comment block describing a module's purpose and public functions is the common convention.

## Wiring luacheck and StyLua into CI

A typical CI check, directly analogous to the Rust guide's `cargo fmt -- --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo test` combination from [clippy and rustfmt](/rust/clippy-and-rustfmt/):

```bash
stylua --check . && luacheck . && busted
```

Project.Build a To-Do List CLI App:
Let's build a complete, working command-line to-do list application in Lua — mirroring the Rust guide's own [Build a CLI To-Do App](/rust/build-a-cli-to-do-app/) project, so you can see how the same real-world task looks in each language.

## Project structure

```
todo_cli/
├── main.lua
└── tasks.json    -- created automatically on first run
```

We'll use `dkjson` for JSON handling (see [Installing and Using Packages](/lua/installing-and-using-packages/)):

```bash
luarocks install dkjson
```

## The full implementation

```lua
-- main.lua
local json = require("dkjson")

local DATA_FILE = "tasks.json"

-- Load tasks from disk, or start with an empty list
local function load_tasks()
    local file = io.open(DATA_FILE, "r")
    if not file then
        return {tasks = {}, next_id = 1}
    end
    local contents = file:read("a")
    file:close()

    if contents == "" then
        return {tasks = {}, next_id = 1}
    end

    local data, _, err = json.decode(contents)
    if err then
        print("Warning: tasks.json is corrupted, starting fresh")
        return {tasks = {}, next_id = 1}
    end
    return data
end

-- Save the current state back to disk
local function save_tasks(state)
    local file = io.open(DATA_FILE, "w")
    file:write(json.encode(state, {indent = true}))
    file:close()
end

local function add_task(state, description)
    local id = state.next_id
    table.insert(state.tasks, {id = id, description = description, done = false})
    state.next_id = state.next_id + 1
    return id
end

local function find_task(state, id)
    for _, task in ipairs(state.tasks) do
        if task.id == id then
            return task
        end
    end
    return nil
end

local function complete_task(state, id)
    local task = find_task(state, id)
    if not task then
        return false, "no task with id " .. id
    end
    task.done = true
    return true
end

local function remove_task(state, id)
    for i, task in ipairs(state.tasks) do
        if task.id == id then
            table.remove(state.tasks, i)
            return true
        end
    end
    return false, "no task with id " .. id
end

local function list_tasks(state)
    if #state.tasks == 0 then
        print("No tasks yet!")
        return
    end
    for _, task in ipairs(state.tasks) do
        local mark = task.done and "x" or " "
        print(string.format("[%s] #%d %s", mark, task.id, task.description))
    end
end

-- Command-line handling
local state = load_tasks()
local command = arg[1]

if command == "add" then
    local description = table.concat(arg, " ", 2) -- join arg[2] through arg[#arg]
    local id = add_task(state, description)
    print("Added task #" .. id .. ": " .. description)

elseif command == "done" then
    local id = tonumber(arg[2])
    local ok, err = complete_task(state, id)
    if ok then
        print("Marked task #" .. id .. " as done")
    else
        print("Error: " .. err)
    end

elseif command == "remove" then
    local id = tonumber(arg[2])
    local ok, err = remove_task(state, id)
    if ok then
        print("Removed task #" .. id)
    else
        print("Error: " .. err)
    end

elseif command == "list" then
    list_tasks(state)

else
    print("Usage: lua main.lua <add|done|remove|list> [args]")
end

save_tasks(state)
```

## Trying it out

```bash
lua main.lua add Learn Lua tables
lua main.lua add Write a CLI app
lua main.lua list
lua main.lua done 1
lua main.lua list
lua main.lua remove 2
lua main.lua list
```

## What this example demonstrates

- **Tables as both arrays and dictionaries** ([Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/), [Tables as Dictionaries](/lua/tables-as-dictionaries/)) — `state.tasks` is an array of dictionary-style task tables.
- **Functions and closures** ([Defining Functions](/lua/defining-functions/)) — small, focused functions like `find_task`, `complete_task`.
- **Multiple return values for error handling** ([Multiple Return Values](/lua/multiple-return-values/)) — `complete_task`/`remove_task` return `(true)` or `(false, error_message)`, following the idiomatic pattern from [Writing Robust Error Handling](/lua/writing-robust-error-handling/).
- **File I/O** ([Reading and Writing Files](/lua/reading-and-writing-files/)) — loading/saving JSON to disk, with graceful handling of a missing or corrupted file.
- **Command-line arguments** ([Command Line Arguments](/lua/command-line-arguments/)) — the `arg` table drives the whole command-dispatch logic.
- **A LuaRocks package** ([Installing and Using Packages](/lua/installing-and-using-packages/)) — `dkjson` for JSON encoding/decoding.

From here, natural extensions to try on your own: wrap the class-based patterns from [Object-Oriented Programming in Lua](/lua/object-oriented-programming-in-lua/) around the task/state logic, add due dates, use `argparse` (from [Command Line Arguments](/lua/command-line-arguments/)) for more robust CLI parsing, or use `luafilesystem` to support storing tasks in a user-configurable location.

Project.Common Beginner Mistakes:
A consolidated list of mistakes almost every Lua beginner makes at least once.

## Forgetting local

Covered repeatedly throughout this guide because it's genuinely the single most impactful habit to build:

```lua
function process() end  -- creates a GLOBAL function — almost always a mistake
count = 0                  -- creates a GLOBAL variable
```

Always write `local` in front of every declaration unless a global is specifically, deliberately intended. Run `luacheck` (from [Style Guide and Linting](/lua/style-guide-and-linting/)) regularly — it catches accidental globals automatically.

## Assuming 0-based indexing

```lua
local t = {"a", "b", "c"}
print(t[0]) -- nil! Lua tables (and strings) are 1-indexed
print(t[1]) -- "a" — the correct first element
```

This is probably the single most common muscle-memory mistake for anyone coming from a C-family language, Python, JavaScript, or Rust — all of which are 0-indexed. It takes deliberate practice to internalize Lua's 1-based convention.

## Expecting 0 or "" to be falsy

```lua
local count = 0
if count then
    print("this runs — 0 is truthy in Lua!") -- surprising if you're used to C/Python/JS
end
```

Covered in depth in [Nil and Booleans](/lua/nil-and-booleans/) — only `false` and `nil` are falsy in Lua. Explicitly compare against `0`/`""` if you mean to check for those specific values.

## Confusing == with type coercion expectations

```lua
print(10 == "10") -- false — Lua NEVER coerces types for ==, unlike JavaScript's ==
```

Since Lua's `==` never coerces between types (covered in [The type Function and Type Coercion](/lua/the-type-function-and-type-coercion/)), this is actually *safer* than some languages' comparison operators — but it can surprise you if you expected automatic coercion the way arithmetic (`+`) or concatenation (`..`) provide it.

## Modifying a table while iterating it with pairs

```lua
for k, v in pairs(t) do
    if some_condition then
        t[k] = nil -- UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR — don't remove keys mid-iteration!
    end
end
```

Covered fully in [Iterating Tables: pairs and ipairs](/lua/iterating-tables-pairs-and-ipairs/) — collect keys to remove first, then remove them in a separate pass afterward.

## The local function self-reference gotcha

```lua
local factorial = function(n) -- WRONG for recursion — factorial isn't visible inside itself yet
    if n <= 1 then return 1 end
    return n * factorial(n - 1) -- errors: factorial is nil here
end
```

Covered in depth in [Recursion](/lua/recursion/) — always use `local function name(...)` syntax specifically for any function that needs to call itself.

## Assuming table equality checks contents

```lua
local a = {1, 2, 3}
local b = {1, 2, 3}
print(a == b) -- false! Different table objects, even with identical contents
```

Covered in [Nested Tables](/lua/nested-tables/) — `==` on tables checks identity (are these literally the same table in memory), not structural equality. Write your own recursive comparison function if you need content-based equality.

## Leaving nil gaps in array-like tables

```lua
local t = {"a", "b", nil, "d"}
print(#t) -- undefined! Could be 2 or 4
```

Covered in [Tables as Arrays](/lua/tables-as-arrays/) — avoid assigning `nil` into the middle of an array-like table; use a sentinel value instead if you genuinely need to represent "empty" at a specific position.

## Forgetting that / always produces a float

```lua
local half = 10 / 2
print(half) -- 5.0, not 5 (though this often doesn't matter in practice, since Lua's
              -- number formatting and further arithmetic handle this transparently)

local int_half = 10 // 2 -- 5, using floor division specifically for an integer result
```

Covered in [Numbers](/lua/numbers/) and [Operators](/lua/operators/) — reach for `//` when you specifically need integer-style division.

Project.Where to Go Next:
You've now covered Lua's syntax, types, control flow, tables, metatables and OOP, modules, error handling, coroutines, the standard library, package management, and embedding — a genuinely complete foundation. Here's where to go from here.

## Build things

The most effective way to solidify everything in this guide is to build real projects. Some ideas, roughly ordered by increasing scope:

- Extend the [to-do list project](/lua/build-a-to-do-list-cli-app/) with due dates, priority levels (an enum-like pattern using a table of constants), or filtering by status.
- **A small game with Love2D** — genuinely one of the most fun, motivating ways to practice Lua, and directly builds on the material in [Using Lua With Game Engines](/lua/using-lua-with-game-engines/). Love2D's own documentation and tutorials are excellent and beginner-friendly.
- **A Neovim plugin or configuration** — if you already use (or want to start using) Neovim, writing your own configuration in Lua is a genuinely practical way to use everything from this guide on something you'll interact with daily.
- **A text-processing or automation script** — something that solves a real annoyance in your own workflow, leaning on [String Library Basics](/lua/string-library-basics/), [Lua Patterns](/lua/lua-patterns-luas-regex/), and file I/O.

## Deepen specific areas

- **Advanced metatables** — beyond what's covered here, metatables support even more metamethods (`__newindex` for intercepting *writes* to missing keys, `__gc` for finalizers, weak tables via `__mode`) worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics.
- **Performance optimization** — Lua's official documentation includes a well-regarded "Lua Performance Tips" guide; understanding table pre-allocation, avoiding unnecessary global lookups, and string-building patterns becomes valuable once you're working on performance-sensitive code (like game logic running every frame).
- **LuaJIT specifically** — if your target environment uses LuaJIT (per [Lua Versions Explained](/lua/lua-versions-explained/)), its FFI library (from [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) and JIT-compilation-aware coding patterns reward focused, separate study.
- **A specific game engine or host application's API** — as discussed in [Using Lua With Game Engines](/lua/using-lua-with-game-engines/), the language itself is only part of the picture for embedded contexts; deep expertise in one specific host's API (Love2D, Roblox/Luau, WoW addons, Neovim) is its own valuable, separate skill.

## Community resources

- **lua.org** — the official Lua website, including the free, authoritative **Programming in Lua** book (the first edition is freely available online) and the full **Lua 5.4 Reference Manual**, the definitive source for exact language semantics.
- **lua-users.org wiki** — a long-running, community-maintained wiki with recipes, tutorials, and discussion of idioms and gotchas.
- **r/lua** on Reddit, and the **Lua Discord/Matrix communities** — active places to ask questions and share projects.
- **Your specific host application's community** — if you're scripting for Love2D, Neovim, a specific game, or another embedded context, that community's own forums/Discord will be far more relevant for API-specific questions than general Lua resources.

## A realistic expectation

Lua's core language is genuinely small and learnable relatively quickly — but idiomatic mastery (comfortable metatable use, clean module organization, knowing when coroutines are the right tool) still takes real practice, exactly as with any language. The 1-based indexing and truthiness rules in particular are worth deliberately over-practicing early, since muscle memory from other languages actively works against you there.

Project.FAQ:
## Is Lua a good first programming language?

It's a reasonable choice, though not the most common recommendation for absolute beginners with zero programming experience — its small, clean core syntax is genuinely approachable, but its minimal standard library and heavy reliance on tables-for-everything means a beginner has to build more from scratch (or learn LuaRocks packages) earlier than they might with a more "batteries included" language like Python. It's an excellent **second or third** language, especially if game development or embedded scripting interests you.

## Lua vs Python — which should I learn?

They serve different niches more than they compete directly. Python has an enormous standard library and ecosystem (data science, web development, automation, general-purpose scripting) and is a very common first-language recommendation. Lua is dramatically smaller and faster, and is specifically strong where **embeddability** matters — scripting inside another application (a game, an editor, a server) rather than running as a large standalone program itself. Many developers learn both, reaching for Python for general scripting/data work and Lua specifically when working with a Lua-embedding host application.

## Why doesn't Lua have more built-in functionality?

This is a deliberate design philosophy, not an oversight — Lua's designers specifically prioritized keeping the core language and standard library small, on the theory that a host application embedding Lua (a game engine, a web server) should decide what additional functionality to expose, rather than Lua imposing a large, possibly-unwanted standard library on every embedding context. This tradeoff is exactly why LuaRocks (covered in [LuaRocks and Packages](/lua/installing-luarocks/)) exists and is genuinely necessary for many real projects, unlike languages where the standard library alone covers most everyday needs.

## Why is Lua 1-indexed?

This is a genuinely debated design choice, but the common justification: it aligns with everyday human counting convention ("the first item" is item 1, not item 0) and with Lua's mathematical/scientific computing heritage (many mathematical conventions are 1-indexed). Whatever the original reasoning, it's a fixed, permanent feature of the language at this point — the practical answer is simply to build the muscle memory, since it won't change.

## Is Lua fast?

Yes, notably so among interpreted/scripting languages — the reference PUC-Lua implementation is well-regarded for its speed relative to its simplicity, and **LuaJIT** (covered in [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/)) is frequently among the fastest dynamic-language implementations that exist in real-world benchmarks, often approaching statically-compiled language performance for certain workloads. This speed, combined with the tiny interpreter footprint, is a major reason Lua remains popular for performance-sensitive embedded scripting (games in particular) despite competition from many other scripting languages.

## Should I learn standard Lua or LuaJIT-specific features?

Learn standard Lua first — everything in this guide (aside from the explicitly-labeled [LuaJIT and FFI](/lua/luajit-and-ffi/) page) works identically across standard Lua and LuaJIT, since LuaJIT is designed to be a drop-in-compatible, faster implementation of (primarily) Lua 5.1 semantics. Only reach for LuaJIT-specific features (the FFI library specifically) once you know for certain your target environment uses LuaJIT and you have a genuine need for direct C interop from Lua.

## I'm getting "attempt to index a nil value" — what does this mean?

This is one of the most common Lua runtime errors, and it means you tried to access a field (`.something` or `[key]`) on a variable that turned out to be `nil` — usually because a table you expected to exist wasn't actually created, a function that was supposed to return a table returned `nil` instead (perhaps due to an earlier, silently-swallowed error), or a typo in a variable/field name (which `luacheck`, from [Style Guide and Linting](/lua/style-guide-and-linting/), can often catch ahead of time). The error message usually includes the specific field name and line number — start by checking whether the table you expected actually got created/returned successfully at that point in the program.

This is the end of the guide. Good luck, and welcome to Lua!
